papers.3: Paper 3 Financial Accounting (A Level structured paper in 2022)

practice.subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is shown in the equity section of a limited company's statement of financial position?
A 6% loan notes (2033)
B share premium
C corporation tax payable
D dividends paid during the year
parts.answer: B share premium
parts.working: Share premium is a capital reserve and part of equity. Loan notes (A) are a non-current liability; dividends paid (D) appear in the statement of changes in equity as a deduction from retained earnings, not as a separate line in the SOFP.

practice.subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP
practice.stem: Shalimar Foods Limited provides the following for the year ended 31 March 2027: revenue $1,840,000; cost of sales $1,104,000; distribution costs $196,000; administrative expenses $248,000; finance costs $36,000; tax $64,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit from operations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.
parts.working: 292,000 − finance costs 36,000 = 256,000 profit before tax; − tax 64,000 = 192,000. M1 A1.

practice.subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two items that appear in the statement of profit or loss of a limited company but not in that of a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two: tax (corporation tax / income tax on company profits); directors' remuneration; auditors' fees; loan note (debenture) interest as finance costs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why dividends paid are not shown as an expense in a company's statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Dividends are an appropriation (distribution) of profit to the owners, not a cost of earning profit. They are deducted from retained earnings in the statement of changes in equity.
parts.working: 1 mark: appropriation/distribution to owners, not an expense; 1 mark: shown in SOCE/retained earnings.

practice.subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the heading under which each item appears in a limited company's statement of financial position.
(i) 9% loan notes repayable in 2035
(ii) Tax payable
(iii) General reserve
(iv) Prepaid insurance
parts.answer: (i) non-current liabilities; (ii) current liabilities; (iii) equity; (iv) current assets.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The 9% loan notes become repayable in eight months' time. State how this changes their classification.
parts.answer: They become a current liability (due within 12 months).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company has gross profit $418,000, other operating income (rent received) $9,000, distribution costs $92,000, administrative expenses $133,000 and finance costs $21,000. What is its profit from operations?
A $193,000
B $181,000
C $202,000
D $223,000
parts.working: Profit from operations = 418,000 + 9,000 − 92,000 − 133,000 = 202,000. Finance costs are deducted after profit from operations, so B (181,000) is profit before tax.

practice.subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP
practice.stem: Lyallpur Cotton Limited: revenue $742,500; returns inwards $12,600; purchases $455,800; returns outwards $8,900; carriage inwards $6,300; opening inventory $51,200; closing inventory $63,900.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales.
parts.working: 51,200 + (455,800 − 8,900) + carriage inwards 6,300 − 63,900 = 440,500. M1 net purchases, M1 carriage inwards added, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit and the gross margin, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Gross profit $289,400; gross margin 39.65%

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where carriage outwards of $14,700 would be shown.
parts.answer: As an expense (distribution costs) after gross profit, not in cost of sales.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP
practice.stem:
After preparing the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 2026, the accountant of Chenab Plastics Limited has the following figures (all adjustments for the year have been posted to profit, but not yet to the asset and liability balances below).
Land at cost $350,000 (not depreciated). Machinery at cost $280,000; accumulated depreciation at 1 January 2026 $96,000; machinery is depreciated at 20% per year on the reducing balance.
Inventory $64,200; trade receivables $52,000, against which an allowance of 5% is to be made; prepaid insurance $2,600; bank $18,300.
Trade payables $47,100; accrued expenses $3,900; tax payable $22,500; 8% loan notes (2032) $150,000.
Ordinary share capital $250,000; share premium $50,000; retained earnings is the only other reserve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of non-current assets at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net current assets at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Current assets: inventory 64,200 + receivables 52,000 − allowance 2,600 + prepayment 2,600 + bank 18,300 = 134,500 (M1). Current liabilities 47,100 + 3,900 + 22,500 = 73,500 (M1). Net 61,000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 December 2026, and state the total equity.
parts.answer: Retained earnings $108,200; total equity $408,200

practice.subtopic: Statement of profit or loss and SOFP
practice.stem:

Other balances before adjustments: wages $168,300; rent $54,000; directors' remuneration $96,000; trade receivables $73,500; allowance for irrecoverable debts at 1 July 2026 $2,100; equipment at cost $220,000; 6% loan notes $250,000 (no interest has been paid or recorded).

1 Wages of $4,700 are owing.
2 Rent includes $9,000 paid for July and August 2027.
3 A debt of $3,500 is to be written off. The allowance is to be 4% of the remaining receivables.
4 Equipment is depreciated at 15% per year on cost.
5 Tax for the year is $31,800.

practice.stem:

practice.stem:
At 1 April 2026, Ravi Textiles Limited had: ordinary shares of $0.50 each $800,000; share premium $120,000; retained earnings $410,000.
During the year ended 31 March 2027:
1 On 1 June 2026 a bonus issue of 1 share for every 4 held was made, using the share premium as far as possible and then retained earnings.
2 On 1 October 2026 a rights issue of 1 share for every 5 held was made at $0.80 per share. All rights were taken up.
3 Profit for the year was $236,000 and dividends paid were $95,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued (i) in the bonus issue and (ii) in the rights issue.
parts.answer: (i) 400,000 shares; (ii) 400,000 shares
parts.working: Shares at start 800,000 ÷ 0.50 = 1,600,000; bonus 1 for 4 = 400,000; after bonus 2,000,000; rights 1 for 5 = 400,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 31 March 2027.
parts.working: Bonus issue 200,000 (1) funded from share premium 120,000 (1) and retained earnings 80,000 (1); rights issue share capital 200,000 (1) and premium 120,000 (1); profit and dividends (1); closing balances (2).

practice.stem:
Hamza Logistics Limited, at 1 July 2026: ordinary share capital $600,000; general reserve $75,000; retained earnings $288,000.
During the year to 30 June 2027 land was revalued upwards by $140,000. Profit for the year was $112,000. Dividends of $48,000 were paid. The directors transferred $25,000 to the general reserve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 30 June 2027.
parts.answer:
Share cap.  Gen. res.Reval. res. Ret. earn.      Total
                                      $          $          $          $          $
At 1 July 2026                  600,000     75,000               288,000    963,000
Revaluation of land                                   140,000               140,000
Profit for the year                                              112,000    112,000
Dividends paid                                                  (48,000)   (48,000)
Transfer to general reserve                 25,000              (25,000)          0
At 30 June 2027                 600,000    100,000    140,000    327,000  1,167,000
parts.working: Columns and opening balances (1); revaluation reserve (1); profit (1); dividends (1); transfer shown in both columns with no effect on total (1); closing balances (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the transfer to general reserve does not change total equity.
parts.answer: It moves profit from retained earnings to another revenue reserve within equity; no assets or liabilities change, so total equity is the same.
parts.working: 1 mark: movement between reserves; 1 mark: no change to net assets.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is shown in a company's statement of changes in equity but NOT in its statement of profit or loss?
A loan note interest
B tax on profit
C dividends paid
D directors' fees
parts.answer: C dividends paid
parts.working: Dividends paid are a distribution to shareholders recorded in the SOCE (reducing retained earnings). Loan note interest (A) is a finance cost in the statement of profit or loss.

practice.stem:
Extract from the records of Thar Minerals Limited for the year ended 31 December 2026.
Retained earnings 1 January 2026 $184,500; retained earnings 31 December 2026 $226,900.
During 2026: the final dividend for 2025 of $42,000 and an interim dividend of $18,000 were paid; $30,000 was transferred to general reserve; a bonus issue used $25,000 of retained earnings. No other items affected retained earnings apart from the profit for the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Closing RE 226,900 = opening 184,500 + profit − final dividend 42,000 − interim 18,000 − transfer 30,000 − bonus 25,000. Profit = 226,900 − 184,500 + 60,000 + 30,000 + 25,000 = 157,400. M1 dividends, M1 transfer, M1 bonus, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the final dividend for 2026, proposed in February 2027, is not deducted in the 2026 statement of changes in equity.
parts.answer: A dividend proposed after the reporting date is not a liability at 31 December 2026 (no obligation exists until approved), so it is only disclosed in a note and recorded when paid/approved in 2027 (IAS 10).
parts.working: 1 mark: not a liability/obligation at year end; 1 mark: disclosed as a note.

The directors make a bonus issue of 1 share for every 3 held. They use the share premium first, then the general reserve, then retained earnings.

practice.stem: Gwadar Fisheries Limited has ordinary share capital of $450,000 in shares of $0.50 each. The market price of each share is $2.10. The company makes a rights issue of 1 new share for every 5 held at $1.60 per share. All the rights are taken up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash raised by the rights issue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in (i) share capital and (ii) share premium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a company usually offers rights shares at a price below the current market price.
parts.answer: To encourage existing shareholders to take up the shares so the issue is fully subscribed and the cash is raised; shareholders who do not wish to buy can sell their rights.
parts.working: 1 mark: attractive to shareholders / ensures take-up; 1 mark: development.

practice.stem:
Shandur Ceramics Limited has 3,000,000 ordinary shares of $1 each in issue, with a market price of $2.40. The directors are considering two options:
Option 1: a bonus issue of 1 share for every 6 held, funded from the share premium account, which has a balance of $650,000.
Option 2: a rights issue of 1 share for every 6 held at $1.80 per share.
Ayesha owns 12,000 shares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash the company would raise under Option 2, and the amount Ayesha would have to pay to take up all her rights.
parts.answer: Company: $900,000; Ayesha: $3,600

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of each option on the company's (i) cash, (ii) share capital and (iii) total equity.
parts.answer: Option 1 (bonus): (i) no change; (ii) increases by $500,000; (iii) no change. Option 2 (rights): (i) increases by $900,000; (ii) increases by $500,000; (iii) increases by $900,000.
parts.working: 1 mark per row (i), (ii), (iii) correct for both options.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The company needs $850,000 to modernise its kiln. Advise the directors which option they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Rights issue: raises 900,000, enough for the $850,000 kiln; no interest or repayment; existing holders keep their percentage if they take up rights. But shareholders must find cash, and it may depress the share price; any shortfall in take-up reduces funds. Bonus issue: costs shareholders nothing and may please them, makes shares more marketable, but raises no cash, so it does not meet the need. Decision: choose the rights issue (Option 2), as only it provides the finance required.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points on both options, using figures; 1 mark for a justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between ordinary shares and loan notes (debentures).
parts.answer: Any two: ordinary shareholders are owners, loan note holders are lenders (creditors); dividends are paid only if declared and profits allow, interest must be paid at a fixed rate whether or not there is profit; ordinary shareholders usually vote, loan note holders do not; loan notes are repaid on a set date, ordinary shares are not normally repaid; on liquidation loan note holders are repaid before shareholders; interest is an expense in the SOPL, dividends are a distribution in the SOCE.
parts.working: 2 marks per difference, clearly comparing both.

practice.stem:
Mehran Packaging Limited has 2,000,000 ordinary shares in issue and needs $500,000 for a new production line. Profit before interest and tax next year is expected to be $640,000 under either option. Tax is 25% of profit after interest.
Option A: issue 7% loan notes (2034) of $500,000.
Option B: issue 250,000 ordinary shares at $2.00 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual interest under Option A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit after tax under each option.
parts.answer: Option A: $453,750; Option B: $480,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit after tax per ordinary share, in cents to two decimal places, under each option.
parts.answer: Option A: 22.69 cents; Option B: 21.33 cents

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the directors which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option A (loan notes): higher return per share (22.69c v 21.33c); no dilution of control; interest is fixed. But interest must be paid even in a bad year and the 500,000 must be repaid; gearing rises; security may be needed. Option B (shares): no compulsory payments or repayment; lower risk. But return per share falls and control is diluted. Decision with reason, e.g. choose loan notes if profits are stable, as the profit before interest is well above the interest cost (640,000 v 35,000).
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points on both sides (using figures); 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Swat Valley Hotels Limited wants $2 million to build a new wing. Its gearing (non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities)) is already 58%. Profits are seasonal and fell in each of the last two years after floods. The directors are considering: (1) a rights issue of ordinary shares; (2) a five-year bank loan at 11% interest secured on the hotel; (3) a sale and leaseback of its existing staff accommodation annex.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each of the three sources of finance for Swat Valley Hotels Limited, and recommend which the directors should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Rights issue: no interest or repayment, no security needed, keeps gearing low (already high at 58%); but shareholders may not take up the issue after two poor years; cost of issue; dividends expected later. Bank loan (5 years): quick, interest tax-deductible, owners keep control; but interest and repayments must be met from uncertain seasonal cash flow, raises gearing further, bank may require the hotel as security and may refuse given current gearing. Sale and leaseback of the annex: releases cash from existing assets quickly; leaseback means future lease payments and loss of the asset's future value. Recommendation: a rights issue (or mixed with a smaller loan) because gearing is already high and profits are volatile, so fixed interest increases risk.
parts.working: Level 3 (8–10): balanced discussion of all three sources applied to the hotel (gearing, seasonality, control), clear justified recommendation. Level 2 (4–7): advantages and disadvantages of at least two sources with some application, recommendation given. Level 1 (1–3): generic points about sources of finance, little application.

practice.stem: The bookkeeper of Kaghan Dairy Limited included dividends paid of $40,000 in administrative expenses. The draft profit for the year was $146,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why your correction does not change the retained earnings at the end of the year.
parts.answer: The dividend is now deducted in the statement of changes in equity instead of the statement of profit or loss, so retained earnings are reduced by the same amount either way.
parts.working: 1 mark: dividend deducted in SOCE; 1 mark: same overall effect on retained earnings.

practice.stem:
The draft profit for the year of Pothohar Steel Limited was $284,600. The following errors and omissions were found.
1 Closing inventory was overvalued by $7,800.
2 The company has $300,000 8% loan notes. Interest for the second half of the year has not been paid or recorded.
3 The allowance for irrecoverable debts should be increased by $2,200.
4 A new machine costing $16,000 was debited to repairs. Machinery is depreciated at 25% per year on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
Draft profit for the year                          284,600
1 Closing inventory overvalued                     (7,800)
2 Loan note interest owing                        (12,000)
3 Increase in allowance for irrecoverable debts     (2,200)
4 Machine treated as repairs                        16,000
4 Depreciation on machine                          (4,000)
Corrected profit for the year                      274,600
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 1–3 (7,800, 12,000 = 8% × 300,000 × 6/12, 2,200); item 4: add back 16,000 (1), depreciation 4,000 (1); corrected profit 274,600 (1) — max 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of item 4 on the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Non-current assets increase by $12,000 (cost 16,000 less depreciation 4,000); retained earnings increase by the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark NCA carrying amount; 1 mark retained earnings.

practice.stem:
Draft profit for the year ended 31 March 2027 of Margalla Software Limited was $418,300. Retained earnings at 1 April 2026 were $236,000. Dividends paid in the year were $90,000 and have been correctly recorded.
Errors found:
1 A bonus issue of $25,000, which was to be funded from share premium, was debited to general expenses and credited to share capital.
2 Rent received of $12,000 for April to June 2027 was included in income for the year.
3 Office equipment costing $64,000 was depreciated at 10% per year on cost instead of the company's policy of 15% per year on cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working:
Draft profit                                     418,300
1 Bonus issue wrongly charged as expense          25,000
2 Rent received in advance                      (12,000)
3 Extra depreciation (15% − 10%) × 64,000        (3,200)
Corrected profit                                 428,100
1 mark per adjustment (3), 1 mark corrected profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 March 2027.
parts.working: 236,000 + 428,100 − dividends 90,000 = 574,100. (The bonus issue is funded from share premium, so it does not reduce retained earnings.) M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the correct double entry for the bonus issue.
parts.answer: Dr Share premium $25,000; Cr Ordinary share capital $25,000.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a capital reserve and a revenue reserve.
parts.answer: A capital reserve arises from capital transactions (e.g. share premium, revaluation) and cannot be used to pay cash dividends. A revenue reserve arises from retained profits and can be distributed as dividends.
parts.working: 1 mark each side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of each type of reserve.
parts.answer: Capital: share premium, revaluation reserve (also capital redemption reserve). Revenue: retained earnings, general reserve.
parts.working: 1 mark for two capital, 1 mark for two revenue.

practice.stem: Lahore Leather Limited has ordinary share capital of $900,000 ($1 shares), share premium $180,000, general reserve $40,000 and retained earnings $95,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum cash dividend the company could legally pay from its reserves.
parts.working: Only revenue reserves can be distributed: retained earnings 95,000 + general reserve 40,000 = 135,000. Share premium is a capital reserve. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum bonus issue that could be made without reducing revenue reserves, and express it as a ratio of new shares to existing shares.
parts.answer: $180,000, i.e. 1 new share for every 5 held
parts.working: Share premium 180,000 ÷ share capital 900,000 = 1/5 → 1 for 5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a company might choose to keep profits in a general reserve rather than pay them as dividends.
parts.answer: To retain cash in the business for expansion or replacement of assets; to show shareholders that this profit is not intended for distribution; to strengthen the SOFP for lenders.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid reasons.

practice.stem: Saadat Hospitals Limited revalued its property at 31 December 2026. Land cost $260,000 and is now valued at $395,000. Buildings cost $480,000, with accumulated depreciation of $96,000, and are now valued at $520,000. There was no revaluation reserve before.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance on the revaluation reserve after the revaluation.
parts.working: Land 395,000 − 260,000 = 135,000; buildings 520,000 − (480,000 − 96,000) = 136,000; total 271,000. M1 (uses carrying amount for buildings) A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entries to record the revaluation of the buildings.
parts.answer:
Debit $    Credit $
Buildings: accumulated depreciation       96,000            
Buildings: cost/valuation                 40,000            
Revaluation reserve                                  136,000
parts.working: Eliminate accumulated depreciation 96,000 (1); increase buildings to valuation 40,000 (1); credit revaluation reserve 136,000 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the revaluation reserve cannot be used to pay a cash dividend.
parts.answer: The gain is unrealised — no cash has been received and the assets have not been sold — so distributing it would pay out capital and could harm creditors.
parts.working: 1 mark unrealised/no cash; 1 mark protects capital/creditors.

practice.stem:
Indus Motors Parts Limited had 1,600,000 ordinary shares of $1 each on 1 July 2026. During the year ended 30 June 2027:
• August 2026: paid the final dividend for the previous year of 6 cents per share.
• January 2027: bonus issue of 1 share for every 4 held. The bonus shares rank for any later dividends.
• April 2027: paid an interim dividend of 3.5 cents per share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total dividends paid during the year ended 30 June 2027.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether a company with a large retained earnings balance but a bank overdraft should pay a dividend.
parts.answer: Legally it may pay, as dividends come from distributable profits (retained earnings). But dividends need cash; paying would increase the overdraft and interest, and could harm liquidity and ability to pay suppliers. It may be better to pay a smaller dividend or keep cash until liquidity improves, while considering shareholders' expectations.
parts.working: 1 mark: legal — distributable reserves; 1 mark: cash/liquidity problem; 1 mark: conclusion/shareholder expectations.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm in Sialkot makes footballs. The cost card for one ball shows: direct materials $14, direct labour $9, variable overhead $4, fixed overhead absorbed $6. The normal selling price is $45. The firm has spare capacity and is offered a one-off order. What is the lowest price per ball it could accept without reducing its profit?
A $23
B $27
C $33
D $45
parts.working: Only the marginal (variable) cost is extra: 14 + 9 + 4 = $27. Fixed overhead will be paid anyway, so C ($33 full cost) is not the minimum; any price above $27 adds contribution.

practice.stem: A business in Sialkot makes school bags. Costs per bag: materials $8.50, labour $6.00, variable overhead $1.50. Fixed costs are $48,000 per month. Normal monthly output is 12,000 bags, sold at $25 each, and there is spare capacity of 3,000 bags. A charity offers to buy 2,000 bags at $19 each; it would need special delivery costing $1,400 in total.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the marginal cost of one bag.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in monthly profit if the order is accepted.
parts.answer: Contribution per bag 19 − 16 = $3; 2,000 × 3 = 6,000; less delivery 1,400 = increase of $4,600
parts.working: M1 contribution per unit; M1 deduct extra delivery cost; A1. Fixed costs ignored (no change).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two non-financial factors the business should consider before accepting the order.
parts.answer: Any two: existing customers may ask for the lower price; whether the order may lead to repeat business; effect on quality and staff workload; reliability of the new customer; damage to brand image if sold cheaply.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
A company in Gujrat makes three ceiling fans. Its statement for last year shows:
                             Standard $  Deluxe $  Premium $
Revenue                         180,000    95,000    140,000
Variable costs                  110,000    70,000     84,000
Fixed costs (apportioned)        40,000    32,000     36,000
Profit/(loss)                    30,000   (7,000)     20,000
The fixed costs would not change if a product were dropped. The directors want to stop making the Deluxe fan because it makes a loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution earned by each product.
parts.answer: Standard $70,000; Deluxe $25,000; Premium $56,000
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total profit if the Deluxe fan is discontinued.
parts.answer: Current profit 43,000; Deluxe contribution lost 25,000; new profit = $18,000
parts.working: M1 fixed costs unchanged; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether the Deluxe fan should be discontinued.
parts.answer: No: it earns a positive contribution of $25,000 towards the fixed costs, which would still have to be paid; profit would fall by that amount.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark reason based on contribution.

practice.stem: A factory in Karachi makes running shoes, sold at $50 a pair. For each pair: materials $12, labour $8, variable overhead $3, and a sales commission of 5% of the selling price. Fixed costs are $36,000 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by contribution.
parts.answer: Selling price (or revenue) less variable costs; the amount left to pay the fixed costs and then provide profit.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 1 mark use towards fixed costs and profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per pair.
parts.answer: Variable cost = 12 + 8 + 3 + 2.50 commission = 25.50; contribution = 50 − 25.50 = $24.50
parts.working: M1 commission included as a variable cost; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit for a month in which 2,400 pairs are sold.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

practice.stem: Yasmin runs a kitchen-fitting business in Islamabad and has spare capacity. A one-off contract would need materials costing $2,400 (bought specially), 120 labour hours at $15 per hour and variable overhead of $4 per labour hour. Fixed overheads are normally absorbed at $10 per labour hour; they will not change if the contract is taken.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum price Yasmin could charge for the contract.
parts.answer: Materials 2,400 + labour 120 × 15 = 1,800 + variable overhead 120 × 4 = 480 = $4,680
parts.working: M1 labour; M1 variable overhead; A1 (fixed overhead excluded).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why she might charge more than this minimum price.
parts.answer: Any two: to cover fixed costs; to make a profit; customer can afford more / market price is higher; avoid other customers expecting low prices; risk of cost over-runs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Material is in short supply. Product X earns contribution of $24 per unit and uses 4 kg of material; product Y earns $30 and uses 6 kg; product Z earns $18 and uses 2 kg. In what order should production be ranked?
A X, Y, Z
B Y, X, Z
C Z, X, Y
D Z, Y, X
parts.answer: C Z, X, Y
parts.working: Contribution per kg: X 24 ÷ 4 = $6, Y 30 ÷ 6 = $5, Z 18 ÷ 2 = $9, so Z, X, Y. B ranks by contribution per unit, which ignores the scarce resource.

practice.stem:
Noor Ceramics makes three products. Material costs $5 per kg and only 13,000 kg is available next month. Fixed costs are $52,000 per month.
Product    Price $  Material kg  Labour $  Var. overhead $  Max demand
Alpha           60            4        15                5       1,500
Beta            85            7        18                6       1,000
Gamma           48            2        16                4       2,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per kg of material for each product and rank the products.
parts.answer: Alpha: contribution 20, per kg 5.00; Beta: contribution 26, per kg 3.71; Gamma: contribution 18, per kg 9.00. Ranking: Gamma 1st, Alpha 2nd, Beta 3rd.
parts.working: M1 contribution per unit (material at $5 per kg); M1 ÷ kg; A1 ranking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the production plan that maximises profit. Make whole units only.
parts.answer: Gamma 2,000 units (4,000 kg); Alpha 1,500 units (6,000 kg); Beta 3,000 kg ÷ 7 = 428 units (2,996 kg).
parts.working: M1 meet full demand in ranking order; M1 remaining material to Beta; A1 428 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit from this plan.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

practice.stem: Rehman Motors makes 10,000 units a year of component K. Cost per unit: materials $6.40, labour $5.20, variable overhead $1.80, fixed overhead absorbed $4.60. A supplier offers component K at $15.50 per unit. If the company buys it in, the space freed can be rented out for $18,000 per year and a supervisor earning $9,000 per year would no longer be needed. Other fixed overheads would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relevant annual cost of making the component.
parts.working: M1 variable costs only; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net annual cost of buying the component and state whether the company should make or buy it.
parts.answer: 155,000 − 18,000 rent − 9,000 salary saved = $128,000. Buying is cheaper by $6,000, so buy.
parts.working: M1 purchase cost less rent; M1 less salary saved; A1 decision.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two non-financial factors to consider before buying from the supplier.
parts.answer: Any two: reliability of delivery; quality control; loss of skills/jobs and staff morale; dependence on one supplier who may raise prices; confidentiality of design.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A shop in Doha sells water filters at $50 each. Variable cost is $30 per filter and fixed costs are $90,000 per month. It sells 6,000 filters per month. The manager proposes cutting the price by 10%, which is expected to raise monthly sales by 25%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current monthly profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the monthly profit if the proposal is adopted and state the change in profit.
parts.working: M1 new price and volume; M1 contribution − fixed costs; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one factor, other than profit, the manager should consider.
parts.answer: Any one: market share gained; reaction of competitors; whether capacity can make 7,500 units; effect on brand image; reliability of the 25% estimate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Hashmi Electronics sells air purifiers at $80 each; variable cost is $44 each. Annual sales are 5,000 units and fixed costs are $130,000, including sales staff salaries of $24,000. It plans to stop paying the salaries and instead pay the sales staff a commission of 6% of the selling price. It expects sales to rise to 5,600 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current annual profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per unit and the annual profit under the commission plan.
parts.working: M1 commission as a variable cost; M1 fixed costs reduced by 24,000; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in units under each plan.
parts.working: M1 each method; A1 both, rounded up to whole units.

practice.stem: Ghazi Textiles can make 50,000 towels a year. It currently sells 38,000 towels a year in Pakistan at $22 each; variable cost $13 per towel; fixed costs $250,000 a year. A buyer in Kenya offers to buy 9,000 towels at $16 each. Shipping would cost an extra $0.80 per towel and a one-off export certificate would cost $6,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should accept the export order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The order adds $13,800 to profit and there is enough spare capacity, so accept unless the risks below are judged too great. Either decision accepted if justified.
parts.working: Calculation (max 2): contribution 9,000 × (16 − 13 − 0.80) = 19,800 less certification 6,000 = 13,800 extra profit. For (max 3): spare capacity of 12,000 units is otherwise unused; covers some fixed costs; may lead to further export orders and a new market; keeps staff employed. Against (max 3): home customers may learn of the lower price and demand the same; uses 9,000 of 12,000 spare units, leaving little room for growth at home; exchange-rate and payment risks; the price is below full cost. Decision (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A component costs $18 per unit in variable costs to make. Fixed overhead of $7 per unit is absorbed, which includes a supervisor's salary of $12,000 per year that would be saved if the component were bought in. 4,000 components are needed each year and a supplier offers them at $20.50 each. What is the effect on annual profit of buying instead of making?
A decrease of $10,000
B increase of $2,000
C increase of $12,000
D increase of $18,000
parts.answer: B increase of $2,000
parts.working: Relevant cost of making = 4,000 × 18 + 12,000 = 84,000. Buying = 4,000 × 20.50 = 82,000. Profit rises by $2,000. A ignores the salary saved; D compares with the full cost of $25, but the rest of the absorbed overhead is not saved.

practice.stem:
A workshop in Gujranwala makes two kinds of pump. Next month only 15,000 skilled labour hours are available. Fixed costs are $150,000 per month.
Pump    Price $  Variable cost $  Labour hours per unit  Maximum demand
P            90               54                      3           4,000
Q           120               78                      2           2,500
The variable cost includes labour at the normal rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per labour hour for each product and state which should be made first.
parts.answer: P: 36 ÷ 3 = $12 per hour; Q: 42 ÷ 2 = $21 per hour. Make Q first.
parts.working: 1 mark both figures; 1 mark ranking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of each product to make and the profit for the month. Make whole units only.
parts.working: M1 Q at full demand; M1 P with remaining hours; M1 total contribution; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Workers will work overtime at a premium of $6 per hour above the normal rate. Calculate the extra profit if overtime is used to meet the full demand for P.
parts.answer: Extra P = 4,000 − 3,333 = 667 units, contribution 667 × 36 = 24,012. Total hours for 4,000 P = 12,000; normal hours available for P = 10,000, so overtime = 2,000 hours (the 1 spare normal hour is used first). Premium = 2,000 × 6 = 12,000. Extra profit = 24,012 − 12,000 = $12,012
parts.working: M1 extra contribution less overtime premium on the overtime hours only; A1 $12,012 (accept $12,006 if all 2,001 hours are treated as overtime).

practice.stem: A factory in Lahore has 20,000 machine hours a month. It makes one product, selling 8,500 units a month at $40 each; variable cost $22 per unit; 2 machine hours per unit. A customer asks for 2,000 units of a modified version at $30 each. Each needs 2 machine hours and has a variable cost of $21. A one-off design cost of $2,500 would be paid. Demand for the normal product is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the spare machine hours and the number of units of the normal product that must be given up.
parts.answer: Spare = 3,000 hours; order needs 4,000 hours; 1,000 hours short = 500 normal units.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on profit of accepting the order.
parts.answer: Order contribution 2,000 × (30 − 21) = 18,000; lost contribution 500 × 18 = 9,000; design cost 2,500; increase in profit = $6,500
parts.working: M1 order contribution; M1 lost contribution; M1 design cost; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum price per unit at which the order would be worth accepting.
parts.working: M1 variable cost + opportunity and specific costs per unit; A1.

practice.stem:
Mirza Ltd makes electric kettles. It sells 8,000 kettles a year at $35 each. Variable cost is $21 per kettle and fixed costs are $80,000 a year. The directors are considering two options for next year:
Option 1: reduce the price to $32; sales are expected to rise to 10,500 kettles.
Option 2: keep the price at $35 and spend $18,000 on advertising; sales are expected to rise to 9,600 kettles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors which option, if either, they should choose. Justify your answer with calculations.
parts.answer: Current profit $32,000; Option 1 profit $35,500; Option 2 profit $36,400. On profit alone Option 2 is better by $900, but the difference is small, so either option can be recommended with justification.
parts.working: Calculations (max 3): current profit 14 × 8,000 − 80,000 = 32,000; Option 1: 11 × 10,500 − 80,000 = 35,500; Option 2: 14 × 9,600 − 98,000 = 36,400. Points (max 3): Option 1 break-even 7,273 units, margin of safety 10,500 − 7,273 = 3,227; Option 2 break-even 7,000 units, margin of safety 2,600; the lower price may start a price war and lower brand image; Option 1 needs extra capacity and workload for 2,500 more units; advertising results are uncertain but could have longer-lasting effects; the sales forecasts are estimates. Decision with reason (1).

practice.stem:
A department store in Lahore has three departments. Fixed costs of $96,000 a year are shared by floor area: clothing 50%, footwear 30%, toys 20%.
                  Clothing $  Footwear $  Toys $
Revenue              240,000     120,000  90,000
Variable costs       150,000      84,000  72,000
If the toy department closed, $5,000 of fixed costs would be saved. Its space would be given to footwear, whose revenue and variable costs would both rise by 30%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss of each department and the total profit.
parts.answer: Clothing 42,000; Footwear 7,200; Toys (1,200); total $48,000
parts.working: Apportioned fixed costs 48,000, 28,800, 19,200 (1); departmental results (1); total (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total profit if the toy department is closed and footwear expanded. State whether the plan should go ahead.
parts.answer: Contribution: clothing 90,000 + footwear 36,000 × 1.3 = 46,800 → 136,800; fixed costs 96,000 − 5,000 = 91,000; profit = $45,800. This is $2,200 lower than now, so the toy department should not be closed.
parts.working: M1 footwear contribution × 1.3; M1 toy contribution removed; M1 fixed costs reduced only by 5,000; A1 with decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A product sells for $18 and has a variable cost of $11 per unit. Fixed costs are $42,000. How many units must be sold to make a profit of $14,000?
A 6,000
B 8,000
C 3,112
D 5,091
parts.working: Required contribution = 42,000 + 14,000 = 56,000; ÷ (18 − 11) = 8,000 units. A covers only the fixed costs (break-even).

practice.stem: A company in Peshawar makes ceramic water coolers, sold at $32 each. Per unit: materials $9, labour $7, variable overhead $2. Fixed costs are $30,000 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per unit.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution to sales ratio as a percentage, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total contribution and the profit for a month in which 3,000 units are sold.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A bakery in Abu Dhabi sells boxes of pastries at $75 per box. Variable cost is $45 per box and fixed costs are $180,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per unit and the contribution to sales (C/S) ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of units needed to earn a profit of $60,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the revenue needed to earn a profit of $60,000.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the profit if 9,500 units are sold.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A workshop in Ankara makes office chairs. This year it sold 8,000 chairs at $120 each; variable cost was $70 per chair and fixed costs were $300,000. Next year fixed costs will rise by 10% and variable cost per chair by 6%. The owners want a profit of $120,000 next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate this year's profit.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of units needed next year to earn a profit of $120,000 at the current selling price.
parts.working: M1 new costs; M1 required contribution ÷ unit contribution; A1 rounded up.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price needed to earn $120,000 next year if only 8,500 units can be sold. Give your answer to the nearest cent.
parts.answer: Contribution needed per unit = 450,000 ÷ 8,500 = 52.94; price = 74.20 + 52.94 = $127.14
parts.working: M1 required contribution ÷ 8,500; M1 add variable cost; A1.

practice.stem: A company in Lahore makes solar lamps that sell for $140 each. Variable cost is $84 per lamp and fixed costs are $168,000 per year. Budgeted sales are 4,500 lamps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point in units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety in units and as a percentage of budgeted sales.
parts.working: M1 units; A1; A1 percentage.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business budgets to sell 12,000 units at $25 each. Variable cost is $15 per unit and fixed costs are $90,000. What is the margin of safety as a percentage of budgeted sales?
A 25%
B 33⅓%
C 40%
D 75%
parts.working: Break-even = 90,000 ÷ 10 = 9,000 units; margin of safety = 3,000 units; 3,000 ÷ 12,000 = 25%. B divides by break-even sales instead of budgeted sales.

practice.stem: A café in Istanbul sells many different items, so it does not calculate costs per unit. Last year revenue was $480,000, variable costs were $312,000 and fixed costs were $126,000. Assume the sales mix stays the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution to sales ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even revenue.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety as a percentage of revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem: Okafor Ltd in Lagos makes garden tools. Each tool sells for $60 with a variable cost of $36. Fixed costs are $192,000 a year and budgeted sales are 11,000 tools. A new machine would increase fixed costs by $48,000 a year and reduce variable cost by $4 per tool.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current break-even point and margin of safety in units.
parts.answer: 192,000 ÷ 24 = 8,000 units; margin of safety 11,000 − 8,000 = 3,000 units
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even point and margin of safety, in units and as a percentage of budgeted sales, if the machine is bought.
parts.answer: Contribution 60 − 32 = 28; fixed 240,000; break-even = 8,571.4 → 8,572 units; margin of safety = 2,428 units = 22.07%
parts.working: M1 new contribution and fixed costs; A1 break-even; A1 margin of safety.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the level of sales at which profit is the same with or without the machine.
parts.working: M1 equation; A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is NOT an assumption of cost–volume–profit analysis?
A Selling price per unit is constant at all levels of sales.
B Fixed costs stay the same within the relevant range.
C Variable cost per unit is constant.
D Inventory levels rise and fall during the period.
parts.answer: D Inventory levels rise and fall during the period.
parts.working: CVP assumes everything produced is sold, so inventory levels do not change. A, B and C are standard CVP assumptions (linear revenue and cost lines).

practice.stem: Zubair runs a hardware store in Mardan that sells several hundred different products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three assumptions made in cost–volume–profit analysis.
parts.answer: Any three: selling price per unit is constant; variable cost per unit is constant; fixed costs are constant within the relevant range; all costs can be split into fixed and variable; all output is sold (no change in inventory); the sales mix is constant; only volume affects costs and revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using cost–volume–profit analysis for a business that sells several products.
parts.answer: A constant sales mix must be assumed. If customers buy more low-contribution items than planned, the average contribution falls and the true break-even point is higher than calculated.
parts.working: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: The directors of Jinnah Paints have drawn a break-even chart. The total revenue line starts at the origin and rises to $900,000 at 10,000 tins. The fixed cost line is horizontal at $240,000. The total cost line starts at $240,000 and rises to $690,000 at 10,000 tins. The lines cross at 5,333 tins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways the directors could use cost–volume–profit analysis when planning next year's production.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: find the break-even output, so they know the minimum sales needed to avoid a loss; set the sales level needed for a target profit; measure risk through the margin of safety; test the effect of changes in price, costs or volume (what-if analysis) before deciding.
parts.working: 1 mark use; 1 mark explanation, × 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the actual profit at 10,000 units might differ from the profit shown by the break-even chart.
parts.answer: Any two: bulk discounts or overtime make variable cost per unit change; prices may have to be cut to sell more; fixed costs may step up when output rises; inventory may be built up instead of sold.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company produced 10,000 units and sold 8,500 units in its first month. Fixed production overhead was $60,000, absorbed on units produced. How will profit under absorption costing compare with profit under marginal costing?
A Absorption profit is $9,000 higher.
B Marginal profit is $9,000 higher.
C Absorption profit is $10,588 higher.
D The two profits are the same.
parts.answer: A Absorption profit is $9,000 higher.
parts.working: Fixed overhead per unit = 60,000 ÷ 10,000 = $6. Closing inventory 1,500 units carries 1,500 × 6 = $9,000 of fixed overhead into next month under absorption costing, so absorption profit is $9,000 higher. C wrongly divides the overhead by units sold.

practice.stem: Khyber Foods began making jars of pickle on 1 June. June data: production 5,000 jars, sales 4,200 jars at $30 each. Variable production cost $12 per jar; fixed production overhead $35,000 (absorbed on the normal output of 5,000 jars, so $7 per jar); variable selling cost $1 per jar sold; fixed administration $18,000. There was no opening inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit for June using marginal costing.
parts.answer:
Marginal costing statement
                                                   $         $
Revenue (4,200 × 30)                                   126,000
Variable cost of production (5,000 × 12)      60,000
Less closing inventory (800 × 12)            (9,600)
Variable cost of sales                                (50,400)
Variable selling costs                                 (4,200)
Contribution                                            71,400
Fixed production overhead                             (35,000)
Fixed administration                                  (18,000)
Profit                                                  18,400
parts.working: Closing inventory at 12 (1); contribution 71,400 (1); profit 18,400 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement of profit for June using absorption costing.
parts.answer:
Absorption costing statement
                                            $         $
Revenue                                         126,000
Cost of production (5,000 × 19)        95,000
Less closing inventory (800 × 19)    (15,200)
Cost of sales                                  (79,800)
Gross profit                                     46,200
Variable selling costs                          (4,200)
Fixed administration                           (18,000)
Profit                                           24,000
parts.working: Full cost 12 + 7 = 19 per unit (1); closing inventory 15,200 (1); profit 24,000 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two profit figures are different.
parts.answer: Absorption profit is $5,600 higher because 800 units of closing inventory carry 800 × $7 = $5,600 of fixed production overhead into July, whereas marginal costing charges all the fixed overhead in June.
parts.working: 1 mark figure; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem:
Ravi Plastics in Chennai absorbs fixed production overhead at $9 per unit, based on a normal output of 6,000 units a month. Actual fixed overhead is $54,000 each month. There was no inventory at the start of month 1.
                                 Month 1  Month 2
Production (units)                 6,000    5,500
Sales (units)                      5,000    6,300
Profit under marginal costing    $42,000  $55,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the closing inventory in units at the end of each month.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each month under absorption costing.
parts.answer: Month 1: 42,000 + 1,000 × 9 = $51,000. Month 2: inventory falls by 800 units, so 55,000 − 800 × 9 = $47,800. Month 2 production is 500 units below normal, so 500 × $9 = $4,500 of overhead is under-absorbed and charged as an expense; the difference between the two profits is still fully explained by the change in inventory × $9.
parts.working: M1 inventory change × $9; A1 month 1; M1 decrease deducted; A1 month 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the absorption profit is higher than the marginal profit in month 1 but lower in month 2.
parts.answer: Month 1: inventory rises, so some fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory. Month 2: inventory falls, so fixed overhead carried forward from month 1 is released into cost of sales, reducing absorption profit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

topics.name: Analysis and communication of accounting information

practice.stem:
Kiran owns a clothing boutique in Hyderabad (Sindh). Her ratios are:
                                2024      2025
Gross margin                     38%       41%
Profit margin                    14%       10%
Return on capital employed       22%       17%
Current ratio                1.9 : 1   1.8 : 1
Trade receivables turnover   34 days   29 days

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ratios that show an improvement in 2025.
parts.answer: Gross margin (rose from 38% to 41%) and the trade receivables turnover (fell from 34 to 29 days).
parts.working: 1 mark each with direction stated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the profit margin fell although the gross margin rose.
parts.answer: Operating expenses (such as rent, wages or advertising) rose faster than gross profit, so a smaller share of revenue was left as profit.
parts.working: 1 mark expenses rose; 1 mark faster than gross profit / as % of revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions Kiran could take to improve her profit margin.
parts.answer: Cut operating expenses such as advertising or energy; move to cheaper premises or renegotiate rent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible expense-control or revenue actions.

practice.stem: Esi runs a homeware shop in Kumasi. For 2025: cost of sales $384,000; inventory 1 January 2025 $40,000; inventory 31 December 2025 $56,000. In 2024 the rate of inventory turnover was 12 times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inventory turnover for 2025.
parts.answer: 8.00 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two possible reasons why the rate of inventory turnover has fallen from 12 times.
parts.answer: Sales have slowed (fewer customers); Esi bought too much inventory or some lines are out of fashion.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: lower demand/sales; overbuying/bulk purchases; slow-moving or obsolete lines; higher selling prices reduced sales; new competitor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Esi whether she should sell her slow-moving inventory at reduced prices. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Selling at a discount releases cash and storage space and avoids obsolescence, but lowers the gross margin and may train customers to wait for sales; a justified decision.
parts.working: For: cash released, less risk of obsolescence/damage, lower storage cost, turnover improves. Against: lower gross margin, damages brand image, customers wait for discounts. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Liang owns a bicycle shop in Kunming and has asked a bank for a five-year loan. At 31 December 2025: inventory $64,000; trade receivables $41,000; cash $3,000; current liabilities $72,000. Other information:
                               Liang   Industry average
Return on capital employed       21%                15%
Interest cover               6 times            5 times
Current ratio                      ?           1.80 : 1
Liquid ratio                       ?           1.00 : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to two decimal places, Liang's (i) current ratio and (ii) liquid (acid test) ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the bank whether it should grant the loan. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Profitability is strong (ROCE 21% v 15%), but liquidity is weak (0.61 v 1.00), so the bank may lend only with security or conditions.
parts.working: For: ROCE above the industry; interest cover 6 times. Against: both liquidity ratios below the industry average; may struggle to meet repayments in cash. Other: security available, purpose of loan, owner's record. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Tendai sells farm supplies in Harare. In 2025 he increased the credit period for customers from 30 to 60 days to win more business; his trade receivables turnover in 2024 was 38 days and the business now has a bank overdraft. For 2025: credit sales $730,000; credit purchases $511,000; trade receivables $122,000; trade payables $42,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for 2025, to the nearest whole day: (i) the trade receivables turnover, (ii) the trade payables turnover.
parts.answer: (i) 61 days (ii) 30 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Tendai whether to continue offering 60 days' credit. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Longer credit raised sales but customers now pay 31 days after Tendai pays suppliers, which has caused the overdraft; he should probably return to shorter credit or offer cash discounts.
parts.working: For keeping: sales grew; competitive; customer loyalty. Against: receivables days 38 → 61 while payables 30, overdraft interest, higher risk of irrecoverable debts. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Yusuf owns a restaurant in Dubai. At the start of 2025 he introduced a premium menu.
                        2024 $      2025 $
Revenue              1,250,000   1,400,000
Cost of sales          500,000     616,000
Operating expenses     450,000     560,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross margin for each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin for each year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Yusuf whether he should keep the new premium menu. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The menu raised revenue by 12% but profit fell from $300,000 to $224,000 because food and staff costs rose faster; he should change it unless prices can rise or costs be cut.
parts.working: For: revenue up 150,000; new customers/reputation; may take time to pay off. Against: GM down 4 points, PM down 8 points, profit down 76,000; expenses up 110,000. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Directors of Dune Solar Ltd review the last three years. For 2025: profit from operations $840,000; equity $4,200,000; non-current liabilities $1,400,000.
                                2023      2024      2025
Return on capital employed       19%       17%         ?
Gearing                          10%       18%       25%
Current ratio                1.9 : 1   1.6 : 1   1.3 : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed for 2025, to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the company's financial position has improved over the three years.
parts.answer: No: profitability has fallen (ROCE 19% → 15%), borrowing has risen (gearing 10% → 25%) and liquidity has weakened (current ratio 1.9 → 1.3), although gearing is still low and the borrowing may be funding growth.
parts.working: ROCE falling each year: less return per $ invested (1–2 marks). Gearing up: more risk, more interest, but still below 50% (1–2). Current ratio down: possible liquidity pressure, still above 1 (1–2). Balanced point: new investment may not yet have produced profit (1). Conclusion (1). Max 6.

practice.stem:
Meridian Furniture plc has two divisions. The directors can invest in only one of them.
                           North $     South $
Revenue                  2,400,000   1,500,000
Profit from operations     288,000     270,000
Capital employed         1,600,000   1,800,000
Profit margin               12.00%      18.00%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for each division, to two decimal places: (i) the asset turnover (revenue ÷ capital employed), (ii) the return on capital employed.
parts.answer: North: asset turnover 1.50 times, ROCE 18.00%. South: asset turnover 0.83 times, ROCE 15.00%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors which division should receive the investment. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: North earns the higher ROCE through efficient use of assets, though South has the better margin; a justified choice, usually North.
parts.working: North: higher ROCE 18% v 15%; uses assets more intensively (1.50 v 0.83). South: higher profit margin 18% v 12% – if extra capital raises its sales, it may gain more. Non-financial: market growth, competition, capacity. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Omar holds shares in Granite Peak Cement plc, which has 7,000,000 ordinary shares in issue.
                                2024         2025
Profit for the year       $2,100,000   $1,260,000
Ordinary dividends paid   $1,050,000   $1,050,000
Market price per share         $3.00        $2.40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover for each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield for each year, to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Omar whether to keep his shares. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The higher yield is only because the share price fell; with cover of 1.20 the dividend is at risk, so Omar should consider selling unless he expects profits to recover.
parts.working: For keeping: yield up to 6.25%; dividend maintained; price may recover. Against: EPS fell 30c → 18c; cover 1.20 – dividend barely covered, may be cut; falling price shows market concern. 1 mark per point (max 3, both sides), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Divya runs an electrical wholesaler in Chennai. Her current assets are inventory $60,000, trade receivables $80,000 and cash $10,000. Current liabilities are trade payables $40,000 and a bank overdraft $60,000 (current ratio 1.50 : 1; liquid ratio 0.90 : 1). A debt factor offers to buy all her trade receivables for $76,000 cash. Divya would use the cash to repay the overdraft in full.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, to two decimal places, the current ratio and the liquid ratio after the proposal.
parts.answer: Current ratio 2.15 : 1; liquid ratio 0.65 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Divya whether to accept the factor's offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The overdraft disappears and the current ratio rises, but the liquid ratio falls and the business loses $4,000 and control of debt collection; a justified decision.
parts.working: For: overdraft repaid, no overdraft interest, immediate cash, no irrecoverable debt risk. Against: cost 4,000 (5%); liquid ratio falls 0.90 → 0.65; customers dealt with by a third party; one-off – future receivables still slow. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Kilimanjaro Tea Ltd: at 31 December 2024 long-term loans were $800,000 and equity was $1,200,000 (gearing 40.00%). At 31 December 2025 long-term loans were $500,000 and equity was $1,500,000. Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the company is high or low geared in 2025 and give one advantage to ordinary shareholders of the change since 2024.
parts.answer: Low geared (below 50%). Less interest has to be paid, so more profit is available for dividends and the risk of not paying a dividend is lower.
parts.working: 1 mark low geared; 1 mark advantage (less interest/lower risk/more profit for dividends).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company has 1,200,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each. Its profit for the year was $540,000 and it has no preference shares. What is its earnings per share?
A 45 cents
B 90 cents
C 22.5 cents
D 4.5 cents
parts.answer: A 45 cents
parts.working: 540,000 ÷ 1,200,000 shares = $0.45 = 45 cents. 90 cents wrongly divides by the nominal value of the share capital ($600,000) instead of the number of shares.

practice.stem: Andes Coffee plc has 4,000,000 issued ordinary shares of $1 each and no preference shares. For the year: profit for the year $1,320,000; ordinary dividends paid $480,000. The market price of one share is $4.62.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earnings per share.
parts.answer: 33 cents

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio.
parts.answer: 14.00 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover.
parts.answer: 2.75 times

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield, to two decimal places.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain what the price earnings ratio shows an investor.
parts.answer: It shows how many years of current earnings the share price represents; a high P/E means the market expects profits to grow (or sees the share as low risk).
parts.working: 1 mark price paid per $1 of earnings / years to recover price; 1 mark high = confidence/expected growth.

practice.stem:
Extract from the statement of financial position of Baltic Fisheries Ltd at 31 March 2026:
                                 $
Ordinary share capital   2,000,000
Share premium              400,000
Retained earnings        1,100,000
8% debentures (2032)     1,500,000
Profit from operations for the year was $690,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio, to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the interest cover, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 5.75 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why both lenders and ordinary shareholders are interested in the gearing ratio.
parts.answer: Lenders: a high gearing means more risk that interest and capital will not be repaid. Shareholders: high gearing means fixed interest is paid before dividends, so dividends are more volatile, although returns can be higher when profits rise.
parts.working: 1 mark lenders' risk of non-payment/security; 1 mark shareholders: interest paid first, dividends at risk; 1 mark development (higher gearing magnifies returns in good years / ability to borrow more).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company's equity is $600,000 and its only non-current liability is a loan of $200,000. It issues a further $100,000 of debentures to buy machinery. Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100. What is the gearing ratio after the issue?
A 33.33%
B 25.00%
C 50.00%
D 42.86%
parts.working: 300,000 ÷ (600,000 + 300,000) × 100 = 33.33%. 25.00% is the gearing before the issue; 50.00% divides debt by equity only (300,000 ÷ 600,000).

practice.stem:
Ayesha, a retired teacher in Lahore, wants regular income from shares. She is choosing between two companies:
                           Crescent Foods plc   Delta Tech plc
Profit for the year                  $900,000       $1,560,000
Ordinary shares in issue            3,000,000        6,000,000
Ordinary dividends paid              $450,000         $312,000
Market price per share                  $3.60            $3.90
Dividend cover                      2.0 times        5.0 times
Gearing                                   45%              15%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dividend yield for each company, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Crescent 4.17%; Delta 1.33%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price earnings ratio for each company.
parts.answer: Crescent 12.00; Delta 15.00

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Ayesha which company's shares she should buy. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Crescent suits her need for regular income (higher yield), but its high gearing makes the dividend less safe; a justified decision either way.
parts.working: Crescent: yield 4.17% v 1.33%; pays out half its profit. Against Crescent: gearing 45% – interest comes first, dividend cover only 2.0. Delta: low gearing 15%, cover 5.0 so dividend is safe, higher P/E suggests market expects growth – but low income now. 1 mark per point to 3 (both sides needed for 3), 1 mark decision linked to her need for income.

practice.stem:
Pacifica Bottling plc has 5,000,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, equity of $7,500,000 and no borrowings. It needs $2,000,000 for a new production line, after which profit from operations is expected to be $1,400,000 a year. Ignore taxation.
Option 1: issue 1,000,000 ordinary shares at $2 each.
Option 2: borrow $2,000,000 with a 7% long-term loan.
Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected earnings per share under each option, to two decimal places (in cents).
parts.answer: Option 1 23.33 cents; option 2 25.20 cents

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio under option 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 2 gives higher EPS and keeps control with existing shareholders; gearing of 21.05% is still low, so the loan is affordable unless profits are uncertain.
parts.working: For loan: EPS 25.20c v 23.33c; no dilution of control; interest cover 10 times. Against: fixed interest must be paid even if profit falls; capital must be repaid; gearing rises. 1 mark per point (max 2), 1 mark decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business had total revenue of $520,000, of which $438,000 was on credit. Trade receivables at the year end were $54,000. What is the trade receivables turnover in days (to the nearest day)?
A 45 days
B 38 days
C 8 days
D 60 days
parts.answer: A 45 days
parts.working: 54,000 ÷ 438,000 × 365 = 45 days. 38 days wrongly uses total revenue instead of credit sales.

practice.stem: Blue Lagoon Laundry, Colombo, had revenue of $1,260,000 for 2025. The carrying amount of its non-current assets at 31 December 2025 was $420,000. Its non-current asset turnover for 2024 was 2.40 times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the non-current asset turnover for 2025, to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 3.00 times
parts.working: Revenue 1,260,000 ÷ non-current assets 420,000 (M1) = 3.00 times (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the change from 2.40 times in 2024 shows.
parts.answer: Each $1 of non-current assets generated $3.00 of revenue instead of $2.40, so the assets are being used more efficiently (or the assets are older with lower carrying amounts).
parts.working: 1 mark improved/more revenue per $1 of assets; 1 mark more efficient use (or credit the effect of depreciation lowering carrying amounts).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Opening inventory was $34,000, closing inventory was $46,000 and cost of sales was $360,000. What was the rate of inventory turnover?
A 9.00 times
B 7.83 times
C 10.59 times
D 4.50 times
parts.answer: A 9.00 times
parts.working: Average inventory = (34,000 + 46,000) ÷ 2 = 40,000; 360,000 ÷ 40,000 = 9.00 times. 7.83 times uses closing inventory only; 4.50 times divides by the total of the two inventories.

practice.stem:
Ivan Petrov owns a wholesale stationery business in Almaty. For the year ended 30 June 2026:
                                                   $
Revenue (including cash sales of $120,000)   900,000
Purchases (all on credit)                    640,000
Inventory 1 July 2025                         70,000
Inventory 30 June 2026                        80,000
Trade receivables 30 June 2026                96,000
Trade payables 30 June 2026                   70,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the rate of inventory turnover (to two decimal places), (ii) the trade receivables turnover in days, (iii) the trade payables turnover in days. Give (ii) and (iii) to the nearest whole day.
parts.answer: (i) 8.40 times (ii) 45 days (iii) 40 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the relationship between the trade receivables and trade payables periods.
parts.answer: Customers take about 45 days to pay but Ivan pays suppliers in about 40 days, so cash goes out before it comes in, which puts pressure on liquidity.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison with figures; 1 mark consequence for cash flow/working capital.

practice.stem:
Kofi Distributors provides these figures for the year (all purchases are on credit and the business buys goods only for resale; purchases equal cost of sales):
                          $
Cost of sales       474,500
Average inventory    52,000
Credit sales        584,000
Trade receivables    64,000
Trade payables       39,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the inventory turnover in days, (ii) the trade receivables turnover in days, (iii) the trade payables turnover in days.
parts.answer: (i) 40 days (ii) 40 days (iii) 30 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the working capital (cash) cycle in days.
parts.answer: 50 days

parts.label: c
parts.text: The business plans to reduce the trade receivables period to 30 days with the same credit sales. Calculate the cash released.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one risk of shortening the credit period offered to customers.
parts.answer: Customers may move to competitors that give longer credit, so sales fall.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Shifa Pharmacy, Rawalpindi, has an annual cost of sales of Rs 1,095,000 and holds average inventory of Rs 150,000. The owner wants to reduce inventory turnover to 35 days with no change in cost of sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current inventory turnover in days.
parts.answer: 50 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the reduction in average inventory needed to reach 35 days.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Holding inventory costs 12% of its value per year. Calculate the annual saving.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two risks to the pharmacy of holding less inventory.
parts.answer: Running out of medicines that patients need, losing customers to other pharmacies; losing bulk-buying discounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: stock-outs/lost sales; loss of customer goodwill (patients need medicines urgently); loss of bulk discounts; more frequent ordering costs; supplier delays.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shop had revenue of $250,000 and cost of sales of $175,000. What was its gross margin?
A 30.00%
B 42.86%
C 70.00%
D 25.00%
parts.working: Gross profit = 75,000; 75,000 ÷ 250,000 × 100 = 30.00%. 42.86% is the mark-up (gross profit ÷ cost of sales); 70.00% is cost of sales as a percentage of revenue.

practice.stem:
Tariq Electronics, Gujranwala, provides this information:
                          2024 $    2025 $
Revenue                  480,000   560,000
Gross profit             168,000   179,200
Profit from operations    57,600    50,400
Capital employed         320,000   360,000
Ratios for 2024: gross margin 35.00%, profit margin 12.00%, return on capital employed 18.00%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate for 2025, to two decimal places: (i) the gross margin, (ii) the profit margin, (iii) the return on capital employed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two possible reasons for the change in the gross margin.
parts.answer: Selling prices were cut to raise sales volume; the cost of buying goods rose and was not passed on.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: lower selling prices/discounts to customers; higher purchase prices; change in sales mix towards lower-margin goods; loss of trade discounts; more inventory losses/theft.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the change in the return on capital employed.
parts.answer: ROCE fell from 18.00% to 14.00%: each $1 invested earned less profit, because profit fell while extra capital of $40,000 was invested.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies fall (with figures); 1 mark explains (lower profit and higher capital employed / less efficient use of resources).

practice.stem: Noor Cosmetics, Islamabad, had a gross margin of 40% and a profit from operations margin of 15% for the year. Its operating expenses were Rs 72,000. There was no other income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue for the year.
parts.working: Gross profit − expenses = profit from operations: 0.40R − 72,000 = 0.15R (M1); 0.25R = 72,000 (M1); R = Rs 288,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mark-up, to two decimal places.
parts.working: Gross profit 115,200 ÷ cost of sales 172,800 × 100 (M1) = 66.67% (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which user of a business's financial statements is most interested in its liquid (acid test) ratio?
A A supplier deciding whether to offer 30 days' credit
B A shareholder comparing dividend yields
C The tax authority checking the profit figure
D A competitor comparing gross margins
parts.answer: A A supplier deciding whether to offer 30 days' credit
parts.working: A trade supplier wants to know whether the business can pay its short-term debts on time, which the liquid ratio measures. Shareholders are more interested in returns and dividends.

practice.stem: Bilal owns Sunrise Poultry Farm near Sheikhupura. He employs a farm manager and twelve workers and wants to borrow money from a bank to build a new shed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two internal users of the financial statements of Sunrise Poultry Farm.
parts.answer: The owner (Bilal) and the farm manager/employees.
parts.working: 1 mark each: owner; managers; employees (internal).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the bank would look for in the financial statements before lending to the farm.
parts.answer: Whether the farm makes enough profit and cash to pay interest and repay the loan, and what assets could be offered as security.
parts.working: 1 mark profitability/cash flow to repay; 1 mark security/gearing/existing debts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the farm's employees are interested in its financial statements.
parts.answer: To judge job security and whether the farm can afford pay rises.
parts.working: 1 mark job security/continuity; 1 mark ability to pay wages/pay rises/bonuses.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has current assets of $80,000 and current liabilities of $40,000. It then pays a trade payable $10,000 by cheque from a positive bank balance. What is the new current ratio?
A 2.33 : 1
B 2.00 : 1
C 1.75 : 1
D 1.67 : 1
parts.working: Both current assets and current liabilities fall by 10,000: 70,000 : 30,000 = 2.33 : 1. 1.75 : 1 reduces only the current assets.

practice.stem:
Grace runs a hardware store in Accra. At 31 December 2025:
                         $
Inventory           46,000

practice.stem: Hira owns a shoe retailer with two shops in Karachi. She compares her ratios with those of a large shoe retailer in Madrid that publishes its financial statements online, to decide whether her business is doing well.

parts.working: For each of three limitations: 1 mark identifying, 1 mark explaining in context. practice.stem: Hina is opening a small café in Lahore and her bank has asked for a cash budget for the first six months.
