practice.stem:
The cash budget of Saeed Packaging Ltd shows a cash deficit of $40,000 for the next three months, after which the balance becomes positive. The directors are considering two options:
Option 1: an overdraft of $40,000 for three months at an interest rate of 12% per annum.
Option 2: offer customers a 2.5% cash discount to pay one month earlier. The directors expect customers owing $64,000 to accept, which would remove the deficit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of Option 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of Option 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which option they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 1 is cheaper by $400 and does not depend on customers' behaviour; the bank may withdraw an overdraft at short notice, and it adds to interest costs. Option 2 is more expensive, customers may not all accept, and once offered the discount may be expected permanently, reducing future profit; but it lowers the risk of irrecoverable debts and needs no bank approval. Decision: choose the overdraft because it is cheaper and more certain, provided the bank agrees.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for Option 1 (cheaper by 400; certain amount; temporary). Up to 2 marks for points for/against Option 2 (uncertain take-up; permanent expectation; fewer bad debts; no security needed). 1 mark for use of figures. 1 mark for a clear decision consistent with the argument.

3 fixed production overheads of $57,000 are absorbed on budgeted production
4 opening inventory 600 units valued at $28 each; inventories are valued at full production cost
5 administration expenses $48,000; selling expenses 5% of revenue; depreciation of office equipment $6,000.

parts.answer:

Opening inventory (600 × $28)           16,800

Administration                          48,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the budgeted profit will not equal the budgeted increase in the bank balance.
parts.answer: Profit includes non-cash items such as depreciation and inventory changes, and sales or purchases on credit are counted before cash moves; capital spending and loan repayments affect cash but not profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason; 1 mark for a relevant example.

practice.stem: The owner of a chain of three pharmacies in Lahore is thinking about introducing a system of budgets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three purposes of budgeting for the business.
parts.answer: Planning: forces managers to think ahead about sales, staff and stock. Coordination: makes sure the three pharmacies and departments work to the same plan. Control: actual results can be compared with budget and variances investigated. (Also motivation and communication.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each purpose: 1 mark naming it, 1 mark applying/explaining it (max 6).

practice.stem: Al-Shifa Hospital, Karachi, currently sets departmental budgets centrally. The new finance director suggests participative budgeting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'participative budgeting'.
parts.answer: Budget holders (department managers) are involved in setting their own budgets with senior management, rather than having budgets imposed.
parts.working: 1 mark: managers take part. 1 mark: contrast with imposed/top-down.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of participative budgeting for the hospital.
parts.answer: Advantages: department heads know their patient numbers and costs, so budgets are more realistic; managers feel ownership and are more motivated to meet them; better communication between departments. Disadvantages: takes longer; managers may build in budgetary slack; targets may not match the hospital's overall goals; senior managers may still override them, causing demotivation.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for advantages and up to 3 for disadvantages, each developed in the hospital context.

practice.stem: The directors of Shah Logistics Ltd plan to pay each depot manager a bonus if the depot's actual costs are below its budget.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'budgetary slack'.
parts.answer: Deliberately overstating budgeted costs (or understating revenue) so the target is easier to achieve.
parts.working: 1 mark: deliberate overstatement/understatement. 1 mark: to make the target easy to meet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should link the bonus to the budget. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: gives managers a clear target and incentive to control costs; aligns their goals with the company's. Against: encourages budgetary slack in the budget-setting stage; managers may cut essential spending (maintenance, training) to earn the bonus; ignores factors outside their control such as fuel prices; may harm service quality. Decision: link bonuses only if budgets are reviewed for slack and include non-financial targets, or use a flexed budget; otherwise do not.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 3 marks for points against (slack, short-termism, uncontrollable costs, quality); 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: A bottling plant in Hub records electricity costs of $9,200 when output is 4,000 crates and $13,700 when output is 7,000 crates. The cost is semi-variable.

parts.label: c

parts.answer: $500 adverse

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one possible cause of this variance.
parts.answer: An increase in the electricity tariff (or machines left running when idle).
parts.working: B1 any valid cause.

practice.stem:
Thar Pumps budgeted to make and sell 8,000 pumps at $45 each. Variable cost per pump: materials $15, labour $9, variable overheads $3. Fixed costs were budgeted at $90,000.
Actual results: 6,500 pumps made and sold at $46 each; materials $101,400; labour $60,450; variable overheads $20,800; fixed costs $88,000.
The production manager says: 'Total costs were $35,350 below budget, so my department performed very well.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the flexed budget profit for the actual output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost variance compared with the flexed budget, stating whether it is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: $5,150 adverse
parts.working: Actual costs 270,650 − flexed 265,500 (M1) = 5,150 A (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the production manager's claim.
parts.answer: The $35,350 saving (306,000 − 270,650) arises mainly because 1,500 fewer pumps were made, not from efficiency. Against the flexed budget, costs were $5,150 adverse: materials $3,900 A, labour $1,950 A and variable overheads $1,300 A, partly offset by fixed costs $2,000 F. The claim is therefore misleading.
parts.working: 1 mark: original budget comparison distorted by lower volume. 1 mark: flexed comparison shows 5,150 adverse (with item detail). 1 mark: conclusion that claim is not justified.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: Any two: it gains an established customer base and reputation at once; removes a competitor; gains skilled staff, suppliers and premises; quicker than organic growth; economies of scale.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Any two: continues to share in future profits through dividends; shares may rise in value; limited liability; shares can be sold later; the company may not have enough cash.

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Purchased goodwill has a reliable cost – the amount actually paid above the fair value of net assets. Internally generated goodwill has no reliable cost or measurable value, so it is not recognised.
parts.working: 1 mark each side.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem: Farid is a sole trader whose business has made an average profit of $46,000 a year. Zenith Ltd offers to buy his business for 200,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, valued at $1.50 per share. Farid would be employed by Zenith Ltd as branch manager at a salary of $30,000 a year. Zenith Ltd has paid a dividend of $0.09 per share for the last three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Farid's expected annual income if he accepts the offer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Farid whether he should accept the offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: expected income $48,000 is $2,000 more than now; a fixed salary is less risky than trading profit; shares are worth $300,000 and can be sold; limited liability; fewer working hours and responsibilities.
Against: dividends are not guaranteed and may fall; the share price may fall; he loses control and becomes an employee who can be dismissed; he is a small minority shareholder with little say; the gain of $2,000 is small.
Decision: e.g. accept, because income rises and risk falls, provided he is satisfied with the dividend record and a service contract.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for points for, up to 3 marks for points against (max 5 for points); 1 mark for a justified decision.

The purchase consideration was: 80,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each issued at $1.20 per share; $50,000 of 6% debentures; and $40,000 in cash.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.label: d

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem: Rafiq and Sohail share partnership profits equally. The partnership has made a profit of $84,000 a year. Tern Ltd offers to buy the business. Each partner would receive 60,000 ordinary shares of $1 each and $25,000 of 7% debentures. Rafiq would be employed by Tern Ltd as manager at $28,000 a year; Sohail would retire. Tern Ltd expects to pay a dividend of 12% on its ordinary shares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's annual income before and after the sale.
parts.answer:
Before: each $42,000
After: Rafiq $36,950 (salary 28,000 + dividend 7,200 + interest 1,750); Sohail $8,950 (dividend 7,200 + interest 1,750)
parts.working: B1 before 42,000 each; B1 dividend 7,200; B1 interest 1,750; B1 Rafiq 36,950 and Sohail 8,950.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Sohail whether he should accept the offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: his income falls from $42,000 to $8,950. For: he will no longer work, so the comparison is with retirement income; he receives an asset (shares and debentures) that can be sold; debenture interest is secure and repaid at maturity; liability is limited and he is free of business risk. Decision: accept if he wishes to retire and the capital value is fair; otherwise negotiate more debentures or cash.
parts.working: 1 mark: income falls with figures; 1 mark each for up to two other relevant points; 1 mark: justified decision.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem: Kingfisher Ltd bought a partnership business. The fair value of the net assets acquired was $186,000 and goodwill of $14,000 was recorded. Kingfisher Ltd paid $40,000 in cash and issued 100,000 ordinary shares of $1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the purchase consideration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the issue price of each share.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Before the purchase the share premium account had a balance of $25,000. Costs of $3,000 for issuing the shares were written off against share premium. Calculate the new balance on the share premium account.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A year later an impairment review shows that the goodwill should be reduced by $3,500. State how this is recorded in the financial statements.
parts.answer: An impairment loss of $3,500 is charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss; goodwill is shown at $10,500 in the statement of financial position (an impairment of goodwill is never reversed).
parts.working: 1 mark: expense in profit or loss; 1 mark: goodwill reduced to 10,500.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem:
Maple Ltd's statement of financial position at 30 June 2027 showed: non-current assets $255,000; bank $18,000; other net current assets $42,000; ordinary shares of $1 each $200,000; share premium $20,000; retained earnings $95,000.
On that date Maple Ltd bought a sole trader's business, taking over non-current assets $70,000, inventory $12,000 and trade payables $9,000 (agreed values). It issued 40,000 ordinary shares at $1.75 each and paid $30,000 in cash. The cash was raised on the same day by a bank loan repayable in 2032.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Maple Ltd's total equity after the purchase.
parts.working: B1 share capital 240,000 and premium 50,000; B1 total 385,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Maple Ltd's net current assets after the purchase.
parts.working: B1 60,000 + 12,000 − 9,000; B1 loan received and cash paid cancel: 63,000.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate total non-current assets, including goodwill, and show that net assets equal equity.
parts.answer: Non-current assets $352,000; net assets 352,000 + 63,000 − loan 30,000 = 385,000 = equity.
parts.working: B1 352,000; B1 reconciliation.

practice.subtopic: Partnership or sole trader acquired by a company
practice.stem:
Heron Ltd's equity on 1 October 2026 was: ordinary shares of $1 each $400,000; share premium $60,000; retained earnings $210,000.
On 1 October 2026 it made a rights issue of 1 new share for every 5 held at $1.30 per share; all rights were taken up.
On 15 October 2026 it bought a partnership business with net assets at fair value of $148,000. It paid $90,000 in cash and issued 50,000 ordinary shares at $1.50 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash raised by the rights issue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill on the purchase of the partnership.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare the equity section of Heron Ltd's statement of financial position after both transactions.
parts.answer:
Equity
                                       $
Ordinary shares of $1 each       530,000
Share premium                    109,000
Retained earnings                210,000
Total equity                     849,000
parts.working: B1 share capital 530,000; B1 premium on rights 24,000; B1 premium on purchase 25,000 (total 109,000); B1 total 849,000.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the net effect of the two transactions on Heron Ltd's bank balance.
parts.answer: Increase of $14,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define purchased goodwill.
parts.answer: The amount by which the purchase consideration for a business exceeds the fair value of its identifiable net assets.
parts.working: 1 mark: consideration paid; 1 mark: in excess of fair value of identifiable net assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A company pays $260,000 for a business whose identifiable net assets have a fair value of $231,500. Calculate the goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the seller of a business expects to be paid for goodwill.
parts.answer: Any two: the business has loyal customers and a good reputation; a good location; skilled and experienced staff; established supplier relationships; brand names – all of which will earn the buyer future profits.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A sole trader's profits for the last four years were $42,000, $47,500, $39,000 and $51,500. A buyer agrees to value goodwill at two years' purchase of the average annual profit. The net assets of the business at fair value are $310,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total purchase price.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one limitation of valuing goodwill on past profits.
parts.answer: Past profits may not continue: the owner's personal skills or customers may leave with the owner, market conditions may change, and profits may include one-off items.
parts.working: 1 mark: future profits may differ; 1 mark: a reason.

practice.stem:
Two partners are negotiating the sale of their business. Recent profits were:
Year ended 31 December      Profit $
2024                          38,000
2025                          44,000
2026                          55,000
The 2026 profit includes a one-off gain of $4,000 on the sale of land. Goodwill is to be valued at two years' purchase of the weighted average profit, using weights of 1, 2 and 3 for 2024, 2025 and 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the adjusted profit for 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the weighted average profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a weighted average and the adjustment for the gain on land are used.
parts.answer: Weighting gives more importance to recent profits, which are a better guide to future profits. The gain on land is a one-off, non-trading item that will not recur, so it is removed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: On 1 January 2026 Cedar Ltd bought a business and recorded goodwill of $48,000. At 31 December 2026 an impairment review of the business found that its recoverable amount was $412,000. The carrying amount of its net assets, excluding goodwill, was $381,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the impairment loss.
parts.working: M1 carrying amount 429,000 compared with 412,000; A1 17,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of goodwill at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the impairment loss is treated in the financial statements.
parts.answer: It is charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss for 2026 and deducted from goodwill in the statement of financial position. It cannot be reversed in later years.
parts.working: 1 mark: expense in profit or loss; 1 mark: reduces goodwill / not reversed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why purchased goodwill is tested for impairment each year rather than written off on a fixed schedule.
parts.answer: Goodwill has no fixed useful life, so an annual impairment review (IAS 36) shows it at no more than its recoverable amount instead of using an arbitrary amortisation period.

practice.stem:
Juniper Ltd is buying the business of a sole trader. The sole trader's statement of financial position shows:
                               $
Land                      60,000
Equipment                 34,000
Inventory                 17,000
Trade receivables         11,000
Bank                       4,000
Trade payables           (9,500)
Loan                    (20,000)
Capital                   96,500
Juniper Ltd will take over all assets and liabilities except the bank balance. Agreed values: land $85,000; equipment $28,000; inventory to be reduced by $1,500; a provision for doubtful debts of 3% on trade receivables. The loan and trade payables are taken over at book value.
Consideration: 50,000 ordinary shares of $1 each issued at $1.80; $10,000 of 6% debentures; and $15,000 cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net assets acquired at agreed values.
parts.working: B1 land and equipment at agreed values; B1 inventory 15,500; B1 receivables 10,670; B1 less payables and loan: 109,670.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the goodwill.

parts.label: c

parts.label: d

parts.answer: The consideration would rise by 50,000 × $0.20 = $10,000, so goodwill would also rise by $10,000 to $15,330 (net assets are unchanged).
parts.working: 1 mark: consideration +10,000; 1 mark: goodwill 15,330.

practice.stem: Larch Ltd is considering buying a sole trader's business. The business has made a steady profit of $58,000 a year, before any payment for the owner's work. After the purchase Larch Ltd would have to employ a manager at $22,000 a year. Larch Ltd requires a return of 12.5% a year on any investment. The fair value of the net assets is $247,000. The owner is asking $300,000 for the business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum price Larch Ltd should pay to earn its required return.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum goodwill Larch Ltd should accept.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Larch Ltd whether to buy the business at the owner's asking price. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: At $300,000 the return is 36,000 ÷ 300,000 = 12%, below the 12.5% required, and goodwill of $53,000 exceeds the $41,000 justified. However, the business may grow, give synergies or remove a competitor, and the profit record is steady. Decision: do not buy at $300,000; offer up to $288,000, or buy only if future profits are expected to rise.
parts.working: 1 mark: return at asking price 12% / goodwill too high; 1 mark: non-financial or future factor; 1 mark: further relevant point; 1 mark: justified decision.

practice.stem: On 1 April 2027 Ayesha and Bilal combined their sole-trader businesses to form a partnership. The agreed value of the net assets brought in was Ayesha $84,000 and Bilal $62,000. Goodwill was valued at $16,000 for Ayesha's business and $10,000 for Bilal's, and is to be kept in the partnership books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's opening capital.
parts.answer: Ayesha $100,000; Bilal $72,000
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total net assets of the partnership, including goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the assets of each business are revalued before the merger.
parts.answer: Book values may not reflect current worth; revaluing at agreed fair values means each partner is credited with the true value of what they bring in, so neither partner gains at the other's expense.
parts.working: 1 mark: book values out of date; 1 mark: fairness between partners/correct capital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages for two sole traders of merging their businesses to form a partnership.
parts.answer:
Advantages (any two): more capital; shared workload and skills; economies of scale (bulk buying); losses and risks shared; cover for holidays and illness.
Disadvantages (any two): profits shared; decisions must be agreed and disputes may arise; unlimited liability for the other partner's actions; loss of independence.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and two disadvantages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the two owners must agree a value for goodwill before merging.
parts.answer: Each business may have built up goodwill of different value. If it is not valued and credited to the owner who created it, the other partner would share in it without paying, so capitals would be unfair.
parts.working: 1 mark: goodwill differs between businesses; 1 mark: fairness of capital/profit sharing.

practice.stem: Ellie and Faisal merged their businesses. Ellie brought in net assets of $55,000 and goodwill valued at $20,000; Faisal brought in net assets of $40,000 and goodwill valued at $8,000. They will share profits Ellie 3 : Faisal 2. Goodwill is not to be kept in the books.

parts.label: b

practice.stem: Gul and Hira merged their sole-trader businesses on 1 January 2027 to form a partnership sharing profits Gul 3 : Hira 2. Agreed values: Gul net assets $71,000 and goodwill $15,000; Hira net assets $52,500 and goodwill $6,000. Goodwill is to be written off in the new profit-sharing ratio. parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the cash each partner must pay in.

parts.label: d

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A product uses direct materials of $14 and 2.5 direct labour hours at $12 per hour. Production overheads are absorbed at $8 per direct labour hour. The selling price is full production cost plus a mark-up of 25%. What is the selling price?
A $85.33
B $80.00
C $64.00
D $55.00
parts.working: Full cost = 14 + 30 + 20 = 64; price = 64 × 1.25 = 80.00. A applies 25% as a margin on selling price (64 ÷ 0.75); C is full cost with no mark-up; D applies the mark-up to prime cost only (44 × 1.25).

practice.stem: A company in Multan packs olive-oil gift boxes. Each box uses direct materials of $8.40 and 0.5 direct labour hours at $14 per hour. Production overheads are absorbed at $18 per direct labour hour. Administration overheads are absorbed at 10% of production cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of one box.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The company wants a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. Calculate the selling price of one box.

practice.stem: A printing firm in Rawalpindi has completed a job printing school yearbooks. Direct materials cost $1,240. Direct labour was 36 hours at $13 per hour. Production overheads are absorbed at $21 per direct labour hour. The price quoted to the school was $3,080.

parts.label: b

practice.stem: Rehman Ltd prices its products at full cost plus a mark-up of 40%. Product K has a full cost of $65 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of product K.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin (profit as a percentage of selling price). Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A competitor sells a similar product for $84. Calculate the mark-up Rehman Ltd would earn if it matched this price. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of cost-plus pricing.
parts.answer: Advantage: simple, and every unit sold covers its full cost / gives a profit if budgeted volume is achieved. Disadvantage: ignores competitors' prices and customer demand; if output falls, cost per unit rises and the price may be uncompetitive.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid advantage; 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.

practice.stem: Nexa Ltd has capital employed of $600,000 and wants a return on capital employed of 15% a year. It plans to make and sell 24,000 units of its only product. The full absorption cost is $32 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit required for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price per unit needed to earn this return.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mark-up percentage on full cost. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two limitations of setting the price in this way.
parts.answer: Any two: the return is achieved only if 24,000 units are actually sold; the price ignores what customers will pay and competitors' prices; the full cost depends on the absorption basis chosen, which is arbitrary; a higher price may reduce demand, raising cost per unit.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid limitations.

practice.stem:
Indus Tiles Ltd makes floor tiles. Budgeted production is 40,000 boxes a year; the factory can make 50,000 boxes. The cost of one box at the budgeted output is:
                                       $
Direct materials                    6.00
Direct labour                       4.50
Variable production overhead        1.50
Fixed production overhead           3.00
The normal selling price is $20 per box. An overseas customer offers to buy 8,000 boxes at $13.50 per box. Special packaging costing $0.40 per box would be needed. Fixed costs will not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the full production cost of one box.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on profit of accepting the order.
parts.answer: Profit increases by $8,800
parts.working: B1 relevant cost per box 12.40 (fixed overhead excluded, packaging included); B1 contribution 1.10 per box; B1 total 8,800 increase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should accept the order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Accept, on the figures: there is spare capacity of 10,000 boxes, fixed overheads are already covered by normal sales, so the order adds $8,800 to profit even though $13.50 is below full cost of $15.00. Against: existing customers may learn of the low price and demand a reduction; the margin is very thin (1.10 per box), so a small cost rise wipes it out; currency and payment risk on an overseas customer; capacity may be needed if domestic demand grows. Decision: accept as a one-off order if it can be kept separate from the home market.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points in favour (spare capacity, positive contribution, fixed costs unchanged, possible future orders); up to 2 marks for points against (effect on regular prices, low margin, risk, capacity); 1 mark for a clear decision consistent with the points.

practice.stem:
A factory has budgeted production overheads of $180,000 for the year. Budgeted activity is 30,000 direct labour hours and 12,000 machine hours. It makes two products:
                                Product P  Product Q
Prime cost per unit                   $30        $28
Direct labour hours per unit            2          1
Machine hours per unit                0.5        1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate an overhead absorption rate per direct labour hour and per machine hour.
parts.answer: $6.00 per labour hour; $15.00 per machine hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the full production cost of each product using each absorption rate.
parts.answer:
Labour hour basis: P $42.00, Q $34.00
Machine hour basis: P $37.50, Q $50.50
parts.working: 1 mark for each cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The factory is highly automated. Explain which absorption rate should be used and the effect on pricing if the other rate were used.
parts.answer: Machine hours, because most overheads (power, depreciation, maintenance) are caused by machine running time. With the labour hour rate Q would be under-costed (34.00 instead of 50.50) and could be priced below its true cost, while P would be over-costed and priced uncompetitively.
parts.working: 1 mark: machine hour rate with reason; 1 mark: Q undercosted/underpriced and P overcosted.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Factory rent of $72,000 is apportioned on floor area. Machining occupies 2,400 m², Assembly 1,800 m² and Stores 600 m². How much rent is apportioned to Machining?
A $24,000
B $27,000
C $36,000
D $41,143
parts.working: 72,000 × 2,400 ÷ 4,800 = 36,000. D leaves the Stores area out of the total; the service department must also take its share of rent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between allocation and apportionment of overheads.
parts.answer: Allocation charges a whole overhead to one cost centre because it was incurred wholly by that centre (e.g. a supervisor who works only in assembly). Apportionment shares an overhead between several cost centres on a fair basis because it is shared (e.g. factory rent).
parts.working: 1 mark allocation – whole cost to one centre; 1 mark apportionment – shared cost split on a suitable basis.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Suggest a suitable basis of apportionment for each of the following overheads.
(i) Factory rent
(ii) Depreciation of machinery
(iii) Canteen costs
(iv) Insurance of buildings
parts.answer: (i) Floor area (ii) Cost or carrying amount of machinery (iii) Number of employees (iv) Floor area or value of buildings occupied
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Canteen overheads of $28,000 are reapportioned to the two production departments on the number of employees. Department X has 45 employees, Department Y has 25 and the canteen has 10. How much is reapportioned to Department X?
A $15,750
B $18,000
C $14,000
D $10,000
parts.working: A service department's costs are shared only between the departments it serves: 28,000 × 45 ÷ 70 = 18,000. A wrongly includes the canteen's own 10 employees in the total.

practice.stem:
A garment factory in Sialkot has two production departments, Cutting and Stitching, and one service department, Maintenance. Budgeted overheads for the year are:
Indirect materials $9,800, allocated: Cutting $4,200; Stitching $3,100; Maintenance $2,500
Rent and rates $48,000, apportioned on floor area
Depreciation of machinery $30,000, apportioned on cost of machinery
Supervisors' salaries $21,000, apportioned on number of employees
Power $16,000, apportioned on kilowatt hours
                             Cutting   Stitching Maintenance
Floor area (m²)                1,500       2,000         500
Cost of machinery ($)         90,000      50,000      10,000
Number of employees               12          24           4
Kilowatt hours                50,000      25,000       5,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare an overhead analysis sheet showing the total overheads of each department.
parts.answer:
Total   Cutting Stitching    Maint.
                                     $         $         $         $
Indirect materials               9,800     4,200     3,100     2,500
Rent and rates                  48,000    18,000    24,000     6,000
Depreciation of machinery       30,000    18,000    10,000     2,000

Total                          124,800    56,500    54,700    13,600

parts.label: b
parts.text: Maintenance spends 60% of its time on Cutting and 40% on Stitching. Calculate the total overheads of each production department after reapportionment.
parts.answer: Cutting $64,660; Stitching $60,140

practice.stem:
After primary apportionment the budgeted overheads of a plastics factory are: Moulding $84,000; Packing $52,000; Stores $18,000; Maintenance $24,000.
Stores serves Moulding 50%, Packing 30% and Maintenance 20%. Maintenance serves Moulding 70% and Packing 30%; it does no work for Stores.
Budgeted activity: Moulding 7,200 machine hours; Packing 8,000 direct labour hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Reapportion the service department overheads to the production departments.
parts.answer:
Moulding   Packing    Stores    Maint.
                                   $         $         $         $
Primary totals                84,000    52,000    18,000    24,000
Stores reapportioned           9,000     5,400  (18,000)     3,600
                                                            27,600
Maintenance reapportioned     19,320     8,280            (27,600)
Totals                       112,320    65,680         –         –
parts.working: B1 stores split 9,000/5,400/3,600; B1 maintenance total 27,600; B1 split 19,320/8,280; B1 totals 112,320 and 65,680.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate an overhead absorption rate for each production department. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Moulding $15.60 per machine hour; Packing $8.21 per direct labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Stores must be reapportioned before Maintenance.
parts.answer: Stores provides services to Maintenance, so part of Stores' cost must first be added to Maintenance; Maintenance does not serve Stores, so once Stores is cleared nothing comes back to it and every cost ends up in a production department.
parts.working: 1 mark: Stores serves Maintenance; 1 mark: otherwise Maintenance's share of stores cost would be missed / reapportioned twice.

practice.stem:
Heating costs of $60,000 in a factory are at present apportioned on floor area. The production manager says volume would be fairer.
                               Assembly        Finishing
Floor area (m²)                   1,200              800
Ceiling height (m)                    8                3
Other overheads ($)              90,000           50,000
Budgeted activity       10,000 mach hrs    8,000 lab hrs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heating cost apportioned to each department on (i) floor area and (ii) volume.
parts.answer:
(i) Assembly $36,000, Finishing $24,000
(ii) Assembly $48,000, Finishing $12,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate of each department under each method.
parts.answer:
Floor area: Assembly $12.60/mach hr, Finishing $9.25/lab hr
Volume: Assembly $13.80/mach hr, Finishing $7.75/lab hr
parts.working: B1 each pair.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Job 52 needs 5 machine hours in Assembly and 6 labour hours in Finishing. Calculate the overhead charged to the job under each method.
parts.answer: Floor area $118.50; volume $115.50
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain which basis is more appropriate for heating costs.
parts.answer: Volume, because heating warms the air in a room; Assembly has a much higher ceiling and needs more heat per square metre, so floor area under-charges Assembly and over-charges Finishing.
parts.working: 1 mark: volume; 1 mark: reason linked to ceiling height / space heated.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A labour-intensive department has budgeted overheads of $96,000, budgeted direct labour hours of 16,000 and budgeted machine hours of 6,400. What is the most appropriate overhead absorption rate?
A $6.00 per direct labour hour
B $15.00 per machine hour
C $4.29 per hour
D $0.17 per direct labour hour
parts.answer: A $6.00 per direct labour hour
parts.working: In a labour-intensive department overheads are driven mainly by labour time: 96,000 ÷ 16,000 = $6.00 per direct labour hour. B uses machine hours, which suit a machine-intensive department; D inverts the calculation.

practice.stem:
Budgeted figures for two production departments:
                        Machining   Assembly
Overheads ($)             148,500     86,400
Machine hours              13,500      2,100
Direct labour hours         3,200     19,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate a machine hour rate for Machining and a direct labour hour rate for Assembly.
parts.answer: Machining $11.00; Assembly $4.50
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Justify the choice of basis for each department.
parts.answer: Machining uses far more machine hours than labour hours, so overheads are mainly caused by machine time; Assembly is labour intensive, so labour hours best reflect how overheads are incurred.
parts.working: 1 mark each department.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A unit of product uses 1.5 machine hours in Machining and 2 direct labour hours in Assembly. Calculate the production overhead absorbed by one unit.

practice.stem:

Job J88 used direct materials of $1,960; 20 labour hours in Fabrication at $16 per hour; 34 labour hours in Assembly at $12 per hour; and 26 machine hours in Fabrication.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate a suitable overhead absorption rate for each department.
parts.answer: Fabrication $15.00 per machine hour; Assembly $5.10 per labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total production cost of Job J88.
parts.working: B1 labour 320 + 408 = 728; B1 Fabrication overhead 26 × 15 = 390; B1 Assembly overhead 34 × 5.10 = 173.40; B1 total 3,251.40.

practice.stem: A department's budget shows overheads of $75,000, direct labour cost of $150,000 and 12,500 direct labour hours. Job K uses 40 hours of senior staff paid $18 per hour; Job L uses 40 hours of trainees paid $8 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate as (i) a percentage of direct labour cost and (ii) a rate per direct labour hour.
parts.answer: (i) 50% of direct labour cost (ii) $6.00 per direct labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overheads charged to Job K and Job L using each rate.
parts.answer:
Percentage of labour cost: K $360, L $160
Labour hour rate: K $240, L $240
parts.working: 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which rate gives a fairer charge.
parts.answer: The labour hour rate: both jobs occupy the department for the same 40 hours, so they use the same amount of time-related overheads. The percentage method charges K more only because its workers are paid more.
parts.working: 1 mark: labour hour rate; 1 mark: overheads relate to time, not wage rates.

practice.stem:
Budgeted data for next year:
                                    Product A  Product B
Production (units)                      4,000      2,500
Machine hours per unit – Dept X             3          2
Labour hours per unit – Dept Y           1.50          4
Budgeted overheads: Dept X $289,000 (absorbed on machine hours); Dept Y $168,000 (absorbed on labour hours).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted machine hours in Dept X and the budgeted labour hours in Dept Y.
parts.answer: Dept X 17,000 machine hours; Dept Y 16,000 labour hours
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate for each department.
parts.answer: Dept X $17.00 per machine hour; Dept Y $10.50 per labour hour
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorbed by one unit of each product.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two reasons why absorption rates are calculated from budgeted figures rather than actual figures.
parts.answer: Any two: actual overheads and hours are not known until the end of the period, but costs are needed now for pricing and quotations; actual monthly rates would fluctuate with seasonal costs and activity, giving different costs for identical jobs; budgeted rates allow inventory to be valued during the year; differences can be controlled as under/over-absorption.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Overheads are absorbed at $9 per machine hour, based on budgeted overheads of $108,000 and 12,000 machine hours. Actual overheads were $104,000 and actual machine hours were 11,200. What was the under- or over-absorption?
A Under-absorbed $3,200
B Over-absorbed $3,200
C Over-absorbed $4,000
D Under-absorbed $7,200
parts.answer: A Under-absorbed $3,200
parts.working: Absorbed = 11,200 × 9 = 100,800; actual 104,000; actual exceeds absorbed by 3,200, so under-absorbed. C compares actual with budgeted overheads, which is not the absorption test.

Dept 1           Dept 2
Absorption rate         $14 per mach hr $7.20 per lab hr
Actual hours                      6,300            9,800
Actual overheads ($)             86,500           72,400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the under- or over-absorption in each department.
parts.answer:
Dept 1: absorbed 88,200, over-absorbed $1,700
Dept 2: absorbed 70,560, under-absorbed $1,840
parts.working: B1 each absorbed figure; B1 each conclusion with amount.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the net amount and how it is treated in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Net under-absorption $140; it is added to cost of sales (reduces profit).
parts.working: B1 140 under-absorbed; B1 added to cost of sales / reduces profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Budgeted overheads were $250,000 and budgeted direct labour hours 20,000. Actual overheads were $262,000 and actual direct labour hours 21,500. Which statement is correct?
A Under-absorbed $12,000; profit is reduced
B Under-absorbed $6,750; profit is reduced
C Over-absorbed $6,750; profit is increased
D Over-absorbed $6,750; profit is reduced
parts.answer: C Over-absorbed $6,750; profit is increased
parts.working: Rate 12.50; absorbed 21,500 × 12.50 = 268,750, more than actual 262,000, so over-absorbed by 6,750. Too much overhead was charged to production, so the adjustment increases profit. A compares actual with budget.

practice.stem: A factory budgeted overheads of $192,000 and 16,000 machine hours for the year. Actual overheads were $201,300 and actual machine hours were 16,450.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorption rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the under- or over-absorption of overheads.
parts.answer: Under-absorbed $3,900
parts.working: B1 absorbed 16,450 × 12 = 197,400; M1 compare with 201,300; A1 under-absorbed 3,900.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that this amount is made up of a difference in spending and a difference in activity.
parts.answer: Spending: 201,300 − 192,000 = $9,300 more than budget (under). Activity: 450 extra hours × 12 = $5,400 extra absorbed (over). Net 9,300 − 5,400 = 3,900 under-absorbed.
parts.working: B1 spending 9,300; B1 activity 5,400 and net 3,900.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons for the overspending on overheads.
parts.answer: Any two: price rises (e.g. electricity tariffs) not foreseen in the budget; unplanned machine breakdown and repairs; extra supervision or overtime premium; poor control of indirect materials; an unrealistic budget.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A batch of 400 units uses materials of $2,600 and 30 direct labour hours at $14 per hour. Machine set-up for the batch costs $260. Overheads are absorbed at $9 per direct labour hour. What is the cost per unit?
A $7.55
B $8.23
C $9.53

On average 4% of the cupcakes in each batch are spoilt and have no value.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by absorption costing.
parts.answer: A costing method in which all production costs – direct costs plus a share of fixed and variable production overheads – are charged to each unit, using overhead absorption rates.
parts.working: 1 mark: all production costs including fixed overheads; 1 mark: charged to units / cost units via absorption rates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why a business uses absorption costing.
parts.answer: Any two: IAS 2 requires inventory in the financial statements to include production overheads; it helps set prices that cover all costs; it recognises that fixed overheads are needed to produce output; it shows the full cost of jobs for quotations.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between absorption costing and marginal costing.
parts.answer: Any two: absorption costing includes fixed production overheads in unit cost, marginal costing charges them as period costs; inventory is valued higher under absorption costing; profits differ when inventory levels change; marginal costing shows contribution, absorption costing does not.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing
practice.stem: In its first year Kestrel Ltd made 10,000 units and sold 8,500 units at $40 each. Variable production cost was $18 per unit. Fixed production overheads were $80,000, absorbed on the normal output of 10,000 units. Fixed selling and administration costs were $45,000. There was no opening inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit using absorption costing.
parts.working: B1 full cost 26 per unit; B1 cost of sales 221,000; B1 profit 74,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit using marginal costing.
parts.working: B1 contribution 187,000; B1 profit 62,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two profits are different.
parts.answer: Under absorption costing 1,500 units of closing inventory carry $8 each of fixed overhead ($12,000) forward to next year; under marginal costing all $80,000 is charged this year. So absorption profit is $12,000 higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: fixed overhead in closing inventory; 1 mark: 1,500 × 8 = 12,000.

practice.subtopic: Purpose and features of absorption costing
practice.stem:
Zephyr Ltd sells one product at $55. Variable production cost is $25 per unit. Fixed production overheads are $60,000 each period, absorbed on normal output of 6,000 units. Fixed non-production costs are $20,000 each period.
                        Period 1  Period 2
Production (units)         6,000     5,000
Sales (units)              5,000     6,000
There was no inventory at the start of Period 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each period using absorption costing.
parts.answer: Period 1 $80,000; Period 2 $90,000
parts.working: B1 full cost 35 per unit; B1 Period 1 profit 80,000; B1 Period 2 under-absorption 10,000 (5,000 × 10 absorbed against 60,000); B1 Period 2 profit 90,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each period using marginal costing.
parts.answer: Period 1 $70,000; Period 2 $100,000
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why total profit over the two periods is the same under both methods.
parts.answer: Both total $170,000. Inventory is zero at the start and end of the two periods, so all fixed production overhead has been charged under both methods; absorption costing only moved $10,000 of overhead from Period 1 to Period 2 through the inventory built up and then sold.
parts.working: 1 mark: same total 170,000; 1 mark: no opening/closing inventory over the two periods so timing difference reverses.

practice.stem: The new treasurer of Al-Huda Community Sports Club, Quetta, has prepared only a receipts and payments account. Members have asked for an income and expenditure account instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three differences between a receipts and payments account and an income and expenditure account.
parts.answer: R&P is a summary of the cash book; I&E follows the accruals basis. R&P includes capital items such as buying equipment; I&E has revenue items only. R&P ends with a cash/bank balance (an asset); I&E ends with a surplus or deficit. I&E includes non-cash items such as depreciation.
parts.working: For each of three differences: 1 mark identifying, 1 mark developing. Accept: cash v accruals basis; capital and revenue items v revenue only; closing balance v surplus/deficit; no depreciation/accruals in R&P; R&P covers all years' amounts received (e.g. arrears) v I&E for the current year only.

parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected surplus for the year.

$

parts.working: B1 start 6,300; B1 add 4,000; B1 deduct 900; B1 deduct 1,250; B1 corrected surplus $8,150.

practice.stem: Summit Hockey Club values its sports equipment each year. At 1 January 2025 it was valued at $8,400. During 2025 new equipment was bought for $2,600 and old equipment with a value of $450 was sold for $300. At 31 December 2025 the equipment was valued at $9,100.

parts.working: 1 mark depreciation as expenditure; 1 mark loss as expenditure; 1 mark equipment at valuation 9,100 under non-current assets.

practice.stem: A group of residents in Abbottabad are forming a hiking club and ask how its accounts will differ from those of a business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a non-profit-making organisation.
parts.answer: An organisation run to provide a service or facilities for its members, not to make profit for owners; any surplus is used for the members' benefit.
parts.working: 1 mark purpose is to provide a service to members; 1 mark surplus not distributed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the terms a club uses instead of (i) profit and (ii) capital.
parts.answer: (i) surplus (excess of income over expenditure) (ii) accumulated fund.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a club still needs to keep proper accounting records.
parts.answer: To show members how their money has been used (stewardship) and to plan subscriptions and spending; also to control cash and prevent fraud.

practice.stem: Members of Sapphire Drama Society, Colombo, will discuss the year's accounts at their annual general meeting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the stewardship role of a club treasurer.
parts.answer: The treasurer looks after the club's money and assets on behalf of the members and reports how they have been used.
parts.working: 1 mark looks after funds for members; 1 mark accounts/reports to members (e.g. at the AGM).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why members find an income and expenditure account more useful than a receipts and payments account.
parts.answer: It shows whether the year's income covered the year's running costs (surplus or deficit), which helps members decide on subscription levels.
parts.working: 1 mark shows surplus/deficit on accruals basis; 1 mark helps decide subscriptions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two items in a club's statement of financial position that would not appear in a receipts and payments account.
parts.answer: Subscriptions in arrears (or in advance); accumulated depreciation of equipment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: subscriptions in arrears/advance; accruals/prepayments; depreciation; accumulated fund; life membership balance; non-current assets at carrying amount.

practice.stem: Blue Ridge Golf Club's bar, run by volunteers, made a profit of $9,800 last year; profits have varied between $4,000 and $11,000 over five years and two volunteers have resigned. A catering company offers to run the bar for 3 years and pay the club a fixed fee of $8,500 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in annual income to the club between running the bar itself and accepting the franchise.
parts.answer: The club would receive $1,300 a year less from the franchise.
parts.working: Current bar profit 9,800 − franchise fee 8,500 (M1) = $1,300 less (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the committee whether to accept the franchise offer. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Although the club loses $1,300 a year, the franchise gives a guaranteed income and removes risks and the workload on volunteers; a justified decision.
parts.working: For franchise: fixed, certain income; no inventory, theft or wage risk; volunteers freed; professional service. Against: $1,300 less; club loses control of prices and opening hours; profit could grow if run well; tied for 3 years. 1 mark per point (max 4, both sides), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem:
Palm Grove Gymnasium Club, Jeddah, has 300 members and needs $18,000 for new fitness equipment.
Option 1: increase the annual subscription for 3 years and buy the equipment when enough is collected.
Option 2: a one-off levy of $60 per member now.
Option 3: a bank loan of $18,000 at 8% simple interest per annum, repaid after 3 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate: (i) the extra amount per member per year under option 1, (ii) the total interest under option 3, (iii) the interest cost per member.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the committee which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 1 or 2 avoids interest of $4,320; option 1 spreads the cost so members are less likely to leave; the loan gives the equipment now but costs more; a justified decision.
parts.working: Option 1: no interest, affordable $20 a year, but equipment not bought for 3 years unless cash saved first. Option 2: fastest, no interest, but $60 at once may make some members leave. Option 3: equipment now, members not asked for money, but interest $4,320, repayments are a commitment, risk if membership falls. 1 mark per point (max 4), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Willowbank Bridge Club's membership has fallen from 150 to 100 in three years. The treasurer's draft surplus of $5,750 includes $2,400 of subscriptions in arrears for the current year, and many of these members have stopped attending.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the going concern concept applies to the club.
parts.answer: Accounts assume the club will continue; with membership falling by a third, if the club might close, assets would need to be shown at what they would sell for instead of their carrying amounts.
parts.working: 1 mark assumption of continuing; 1 mark consequence for asset valuation if in doubt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the surplus if the treasurer follows the prudence concept for subscriptions in arrears.
parts.working: 5,750 − 2,400 arrears not yet received (M1) = $3,350 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the club should apply its policy on subscriptions in arrears consistently.
parts.answer: So that surpluses can be compared fairly from year to year; changing the policy could make the club look better or worse without any real change.
parts.working: 1 mark comparability; 1 mark avoids manipulation/misleading members.

practice.stem: Sunset Tennis Club charges an annual subscription of $200. To raise cash for new courts, the committee proposes a life membership fee of $2,400. Life membership fees would be transferred to the income and expenditure account over 10 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of years of annual subscriptions that the life membership fee represents.
parts.answer: 12 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount credited to the income and expenditure account each year for one life member, and compare it with the annual subscription.
parts.answer: $240 a year, which is $40 more than the annual subscription of $200.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the committee whether to introduce life membership. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Life membership brings in cash now for the new courts and secures members, but the club loses income from long-serving members (after 12 years they pay nothing) and must still provide services; a justified decision.
parts.working: For: immediate cash; loyal members; less collection effort/arrears; income spread $240 a year for 10 years. Against: members staying more than 12 years cost the club income; costs rise with inflation but the fee is fixed; club still serves them after the fee has been fully transferred. 1 mark per point (max 4), 1 decision.

practice.stem: Crescent Moon Cricket Club's café had takings of $18,000, food costs of $9,500 and wages of $7,200. The treasurer also charged the café $2,400 as its share of the clubhouse rent and insurance, which the club will pay whether or not the café stays open.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss of the café after charging its share of general overheads.
parts.answer: Loss $1,100

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on the club's surplus if the café is closed.
parts.answer: The surplus would fall by $1,300.
parts.working: The 2,400 overheads would still be paid (M1); the club would lose the café's $1,300 surplus over its own costs (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the committee whether to close the café. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Keep the café: it covers its own costs and contributes $1,300 towards overheads, and it attracts members; but look at raising prices or cutting wages.
parts.working: For keeping: contributes 1,300; service to members helps retain them; may raise prices. For closing: shown as a loss; volunteer/staff effort; could use space for something more profitable (e.g. rent to a caterer). 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision consistent with (b).

practice.stem: Highland Golf Society was formed on 1 January 2022. Life membership fees are credited to a life membership account and transferred to the income and expenditure account in equal amounts over 10 years, starting in the year the fee is received. practice.stem: Lakeside Rowing Club's year ends on 31 March. At 31 March 2026 its accumulated fund was $158,400. The surplus for the year was $12,600. During the year the club received a legacy (a gift in a former member's will) of $20,000, which was credited directly to the accumulated fund.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the accumulated fund at 1 April 2025.
parts.working: Closing fund = opening fund + surplus + legacy (M1). Opening = 158,400 − 12,600 − 20,000 (M1) = $125,800 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the legacy was credited directly to the accumulated fund rather than to the income and expenditure account.
parts.answer: It is a one-off capital receipt, not a regular revenue income; including it would overstate the surplus from normal activities and mislead members about whether subscriptions cover running costs.
parts.working: 1 mark capital/non-recurring receipt; 1 mark would distort the year's surplus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one item, other than a deficit, that would reduce the accumulated fund.
parts.answer: A decrease in the value of assets with no change in liabilities, e.g. a downward revaluation of the clubhouse charged to the fund.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid item (e.g. downward revaluation; loss of an uninsured asset).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is recorded on the credit side of a sales ledger control account?
A credit sales for the month
B a customer's cheque that has been dishonoured
C an irrecoverable debt written off
D interest charged to a customer on an overdue account
parts.answer: C an irrecoverable debt written off
parts.working: Irrecoverable debts reduce the amount owed by customers, so they are credited. A dishonoured cheque (B) is debited because the customer owes the money again.

parts.answer: A business that both buys from and sells to the same firm sets off the amount it owes against the amount owed to it, so only the net balance is settled in cash.

parts.answer: Any two explained: it gives a quick total of trade receivables for the statement of financial position; it helps to locate errors to the sales ledger; it acts as a check on the work of the sales ledger clerk / helps detect fraud; it allows a trial balance to be drawn up without listing every customer.

practice.stem:
At 31 August 2026 the sales ledger control account of Margalla Office Supplies showed a debit balance of $84,620. The total of the list of balances extracted from the sales ledger was $82,585. The following errors were found.
1 The sales journal was undercast by $900.
2 A credit note for $340 was entered in the customer's account but was omitted from the sales returns journal.
3 A discount allowed of $125 was credited to a customer's account twice.
4 An irrecoverable debt of $760 was written off in the customer's account but not in the control account.
5 A customer's balance of $1,280 was omitted from the list of balances.
6 A contra of $430 was recorded in the customer's account but not in the control account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected sales ledger control account balance.
parts.answer:
Balance per control account                            84,620
Add (1) sales journal undercast                           900
Less (2) credit note omitted from returns journal       (340)
Less (4) irrecoverable debt not entered                 (760)
Less (6) contra not entered                             (430)
Corrected balance                                      83,990
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 1, 2, 4 and 6 correctly adjusted; own figure total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected total of the list of sales ledger balances.
parts.answer:
Total of list                                          82,585
Add (3) discount credited twice                           125
Add (5) balance omitted                                 1,280
Corrected total                                        83,990
The corrected totals agree.
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 3 and 5; 1 mark corrected total $83,990 agreeing with (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one type of error that would not be revealed by comparing the control account with the list of balances.
parts.answer: For example an error of commission: an invoice posted to the wrong customer's account.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid error.

practice.stem:
At 30 June 2026 the purchases ledger control account of Lagos Fresh Foods showed a credit balance of $63,410. The total of the list of purchases ledger balances was $65,435. The following errors were discovered.
1 The purchases journal was overcast by $1,000.
2 Goods returned to a supplier, $560, were debited to the supplier's account as $650.
3 Discounts received of $215 were recorded in the suppliers' accounts but not in the control account.
4 A supplier's credit balance of $2,140 was entered in the list as $1,240.
5 A payment of $1,780 to a supplier was entered on the credit side of the supplier's account.
6 A contra of $670 was entered in the control account twice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected purchases ledger control account balance.
parts.answer:
Balance per control account (credit)                   63,410
Less (1) purchases journal overcast                   (1,000)
Less (3) discounts received not entered                 (215)
Add (6) contra debited twice                              670
Corrected balance                                      62,865
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 1, 3 and 6 (direction must be right: a credit balance is reduced by debits); 1 mark own figure total. Items 2, 4 and 5 do not affect the control account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected total of the list of purchases ledger balances.
parts.answer:
Total of list                                                65,435
Add (2) returns overstated by $90                                90
Add (4) balance listed as $1,240 instead of $2,140              900
Less (5) payment credited instead of debited (2 × $1,780)    (3,560)
Corrected total                                              62,865
parts.working: 1 mark each for items 2, 4 and 5 (item 5 must be doubled); 1 mark total agreeing with (a).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader finds two errors in her sales ledger records.
1 The sales journal was overcast by $500.
2 An invoice for $120 was credited to the customer's account instead of being debited.
What adjustments are needed to the sales ledger control account balance and to the total of the list of customers' balances?
A control account: decrease $500; list: increase $240
B control account: decrease $500; list: increase $120
C control account: increase $500; list: decrease $240
D control account: no change; list: increase $740
parts.answer: A control account: decrease $500; list: increase $240
parts.working: The overcast journal total is posted only to the control account, so its debit balance is $500 too high. The individual invoices were posted correctly except the $120 invoice, which was credited instead of debited, so the customer's balance is understated by 2 × $120 = $240. B forgets to double the reversal.

practice.stem: Farah runs a dressmaking business in Multan. She records all receipts and payments in a cash book.

parts.text: Explain two reasons why the balance on the bank statement may differ from the bank balance in the cash book.
parts.answer: Any two explained: timing differences such as unpresented cheques (entered in the cash book but not yet paid by the bank) or lodgements not yet credited; items the bank has entered that the business does not yet know about, such as bank charges, interest, standing orders, direct debits, credit transfers or dishonoured cheques; errors in the cash book or by the bank.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason, 1 mark for each explanation (2 × 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits of preparing a bank reconciliation statement regularly.
parts.answer: Any two: errors in the cash book or by the bank are found quickly; the cash book is brought up to date; fraud is more likely to be detected; stale (old unpresented) cheques can be identified; it confirms the bank balance shown in the statement of financial position.

3 A standing order of $600 for rent had not been entered in the cash book.

practice.stem:
On 31 January 2026 the bank statement of Tamarind Catering, Chennai, showed an overdraft of $2,380. The following items explain the difference from the cash book.
1 Cheques of $4,120 paid to suppliers had not been presented.
2 A lodgement of $3,560 had not been credited by the bank.
3 Bank charges of $140 had not been entered in the cash book.
4 A credit transfer of $920 from a customer had not been entered in the cash book.
5 A cheque payment of $715 had been recorded in the cash book as $175.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the updated (correct) cash book balance at 31 January 2026.

parts.working: Work back from the bank statement: −2,380 − 4,120 + 3,560 = (2,940). M1 unpresented cheques deducted; M1 lodgement added; A1 overdraft 2,940.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash book balance before the corrections were made.
parts.answer: Overdraft $3,180
parts.working: Updated = original − 140 + 920 − 540, so original = −2,940 + 140 − 920 + 540 = (3,180). M1 reversing the three items; M1 the error of $540 (715 − 175) treated correctly; A1 overdraft 3,180.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an overdraft is shown as a debit balance on the bank statement but as a credit balance in the cash book.
parts.answer: The bank statement is prepared from the bank's point of view: the customer owes the bank, so the customer is a debtor (debit). In the business's cash book the overdraft is money owed to the bank, a liability (credit).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

Dr                                  $ | Cr                                  $
Sales                           1,800 | Difference in trial balance       870
Rent                              360 | Discount allowed                  770
                                      | Repairs                           520
                                2,160 |                                 2,160
parts.working: 1 mark debit entries; 1 mark credit entries; 1 mark opening credit balance $870.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account
practice.stem:
Kamran owns an electrical goods shop in Quetta. His draft profit for the year ended 30 April 2026 was $48,360. The following errors and omissions were then found.
1 Closing inventory had been overvalued by $1,250.
2 A delivery van bought for $9,500 on 1 May 2025 had been debited to motor expenses. Vans are depreciated at 20% per annum on cost.
3 Discount received of $430 was credited to the discount allowed account.
4 An electricity bill of $680 for April 2026 had not been accrued.
5 Goods costing $1,100 taken by Kamran for his own use had not been recorded.
6 Insurance of $360 paid in advance had not been adjusted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 30 April 2026.
parts.answer:
Draft profit for the year                          48,360
Less inventory overvalued                         (1,250)
Add van wrongly charged to motor expenses           9,500
Less depreciation on van (20% × 9,500)            (1,900)
Discount error                                          0
Less electricity accrued                            (680)
Add goods taken by owner                            1,100
Add insurance prepaid                                 360
Corrected profit for the year                      55,490
parts.working: 1 mark each: inventory; van; depreciation; accrual; drawings of goods (reduce cost of sales); prepayment. Own figure total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on profit of error 3.
parts.answer: None. Discount allowed (an expense) was reduced by $430 instead of discount received (an income) being increased by $430; either way profit is $430 higher, so the profit figure is correct even though both accounts are wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark: no effect on profit; 1 mark: explanation.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account
practice.stem:
The draft profit of Coral Reef Electronics, Colombo, Sri Lanka, for the year ended 31 July 2026 was $72,900. The trial balance did not agree, and a suspense account was opened with a debit balance of $1,340. The following errors were found.
1 Returns inwards of $680 were posted to the credit side of the returns outwards account.
2 Commission received of $450 was entered in the bank account but not posted to the commission received account.
3 Machinery bought for $3,200 was debited to the machinery repairs account. (No depreciation is charged in the year of purchase.)
4 The wages account was undercast by $430.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the suspense account.
parts.answer:
Suspense account
Dr                                  $ | Cr                                  $
Difference in trial balance     1,340 | Returns inwards                   680
Commission received               450 | Returns outwards                  680
                                      | Wages                             430
                                1,790 |                                 1,790
parts.working: 1 mark opening debit balance; 1 mark returns entries (680 + 680); 1 mark commission and wages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 July 2026.
parts.answer:
Draft profit                                     72,900
Less returns inwards understated                  (680)
Less returns outwards overstated                  (680)
Add commission received                             450
Add machinery charged to repairs                  3,200
Less wages undercast                              (430)
Corrected profit                                 74,760
parts.working: 1 mark returns (−1,360 in total); 1 mark commission; 1 mark machinery; 1 mark wages and total $74,760.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of correcting error 3 on the non-current assets in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Non-current assets (machinery) increase by $3,200.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense account
practice.stem:
The trial balance of Hunza Apricot Traders at 31 December 2025 did not agree, and a suspense account was opened with a credit balance of $2,460. The draft profit was $31,250. Three errors were found, after which the suspense account was closed.
1 Insurance paid of $760 was credited to the insurance account.
2 Interest received of $290 was entered in the bank account but not posted to the interest received account.
3 The sales account was undercast by an amount not yet known.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the suspense account, showing the amount by which the sales account was undercast as the balancing figure.
parts.answer:
Suspense account
Dr                                  $ | Cr                                  $
Interest received                 290 | Difference in trial balance     2,460
Sales                           3,690 | Insurance                       1,520
                                3,980 |                                 3,980
parts.working: 1 mark opening credit balance; 1 mark insurance 2 × 760 = 1,520 credit; 1 mark interest 290 debit; 1 mark sales undercast $3,690.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 31,250 − 1,520 + 290 + 3,690 = 33,710. 1 mark insurance; 1 mark interest and sales; 1 mark answer.

practice.stem: Ayesha has just started work as an accounts assistant at a pharmacy chain in Islamabad. She believes that because her trial balance agrees, her ledger accounts must be correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two purposes of preparing a trial balance.
parts.answer: Any two: to check the arithmetical accuracy of double entry (debits = credits); to provide a summary of balances from which the financial statements are prepared; to help locate errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain three types of error that a trial balance will not reveal. Give an example of each.
parts.answer: Any three with an example: omission (a transaction not recorded at all); commission (posted to the wrong account of the same type); principle (posted to the wrong class of account, e.g. capital expenditure as revenue); original entry (wrong amount in the book of prime entry); complete reversal; compensating errors.
parts.working: 1 mark per error type with a correct example.
