topics.name: Company financial statements and IAS adjustments

practice.stem:
The draft profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 of Ravi Valley Cement plc was $286,400. The following matters have not been dealt with correctly.
1 Inventory with a cost of $24,000 has a net realisable value of $17,500.
2 Machinery bought on 1 January 2025 for $60,000 has not been depreciated. The policy is 10% per annum straight-line.
3 The company has $200,000 6% debentures. Interest for the second half of the year has not been paid or accrued.
4 An interim dividend of $15,000 was debited to administrative expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Draft profit for the year                                   286,400
Less inventory written down to NRV (24,000 − 17,500)        (6,500)
Less depreciation on new machinery (10% × 60,000)           (6,000)
Less debenture interest accrued (200,000 × 6% × 6/12)       (6,000)
Add interim dividend wrongly charged as an expense           15,000
Corrected profit for the year                               282,900
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment, total own figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an interim dividend paid must not be included in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: A dividend is a distribution (appropriation) of profit to the owners, not an expense of earning profit. It is deducted from retained earnings in the statement of changes in equity.
parts.working: 1 mark: appropriation/distribution to shareholders; 1 mark: shown in the SOCE / retained earnings.

practice.stem:
Lyallpur Fabrics plc had the following equity at 1 January 2025: ordinary shares of $1 each $500,000; share premium $80,000; retained earnings $214,000.
During the year ended 31 December 2025:
• in March a final dividend for 2024 of $0.06 per share was paid
• in May 100,000 ordinary shares were issued at $1.60 each, fully paid
• in August land was revalued upwards by $45,000
• in October an interim dividend of $0.04 per share was paid on all shares then in issue
• the profit for the year was $96,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the statement of changes in equity for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Statement of changes in equity for the year ended 31 December 2025
                            Share cap    Sh prem  Reval res   Ret earn      Total
Balance 1 January 2025        500,000     80,000          0    214,000    794,000
Share issue                   100,000     60,000                          160,000
Revaluation of land                                  45,000                45,000
Profit for the year                                             96,500     96,500
Dividends paid                                                (54,000)   (54,000)
Balance 31 December 2025      600,000    140,000     45,000    256,500  1,041,500
parts.working: Dividends: final 500,000 × 0.06 = 30,000; interim 600,000 × 0.04 = 24,000. 1 mark opening balances; 1 mark share capital 100,000; 1 mark premium 60,000; 1 mark revaluation; 1 mark profit and dividends 54,000; 1 mark closing balances.

practice.stem: Kohat Builders plc issued $250,000 9% debentures on 1 July 2025. It also had a 7% bank loan of $80,000 outstanding for the whole of the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why debenture interest is charged in the statement of profit or loss but ordinary dividends are not.
parts.answer: Debenture holders are lenders: interest is a contractual cost of borrowing that must be paid whether or not profits are made, so it is an expense. Dividends are a distribution of profit to the owners and are shown in the statement of changes in equity.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the finance costs for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Debentures 250,000 × 9% × 6/12 = 11,250; loan 80,000 × 7% = 5,600; total 16,850. M1 time-apportioning; M1 loan interest; A1.

practice.stem: Jhelum Packaging plc is preparing its financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each transaction state its effect on (i) the profit for the year and (ii) the statement of financial position.
1 a bonus issue of shares using the share premium account
2 accruing debenture interest owing at the year end
3 an upward revaluation of land
4 paying an ordinary dividend
parts.answer:
1 Profit: no effect; SOFP: share capital up, share premium down, total equity unchanged.
2 Profit: decreases; SOFP: current liabilities up, retained earnings down.
3 Profit: no effect; SOFP: non-current assets up, revaluation reserve up.
4 Profit: no effect; SOFP: cash down, retained earnings down.
parts.working: 1 mark per transaction, both effects correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the gain on revaluation of land is reported in the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income.
parts.answer: Under other comprehensive income (not in the profit for the year).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Oasis Hotels plc, Dubai, has a draft profit of $418,700 for the year ended 30 September 2026. The following items need attention.
1 The company has an 8% bank loan of $150,000, outstanding all year. Only $7,500 of the interest has been paid and recorded.
2 An ordinary dividend paid of $42,000 was debited to finance costs.
3 A customer's debt of $3,800 is irrecoverable and must be written off.
4 Trade receivables before the write-off were $193,800. The allowance for doubtful debts, currently $2,900, is to be 2% of trade receivables after the write-off.
5 Insurance of $2,600 paid for October 2026 was charged as an expense.
6 Kitchen equipment (cost $24,000, accumulated depreciation $20,500) was sold for $5,000 cash. The proceeds were credited to revenue and no other entries were made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 30 September 2026.
parts.answer:
Draft profit                                          418,700
Less loan interest accrued (12,000 − 7,500)           (4,500)
Add dividend wrongly charged to finance costs          42,000
Less irrecoverable debt                               (3,800)
Less increase in allowance (3,800 − 2,900)              (900)
Add insurance prepaid                                   2,600
Less disposal proceeds wrongly in revenue             (5,000)
Add gain on disposal (5,000 − 3,500)                    1,500
Corrected profit                                      450,600
parts.working: 1 mark each: interest (12,000 − 7,500 = 4,500); dividend; irrecoverable debt; allowance (2% × 190,000 = 3,800, increase 900); prepayment; disposal (remove 5,000 from revenue, add gain 5,000 − 3,500 = 1,500: net −3,500). Corrected profit $450,600.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the gain on disposal of the equipment is shown in the financial statements.
parts.answer: In the statement of profit or loss, as other income (or deducted from expenses).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
On 1 April 2025 the equity of Bolan Minerals plc was: ordinary shares of $0.50 each $400,000; share premium $120,000; general reserve $50,000; retained earnings $310,000.
During the year ended 31 March 2026:
1 a rights issue of 1 share for every 4 held was made at $0.90 per share, fully taken up
2 after the rights issue, a bonus issue of 1 share for every 5 held was made, using the share premium account
3 profit for the year was $128,000
4 $20,000 was transferred to the general reserve
5 a dividend of $0.05 per share was paid on all shares in issue after the bonus issue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of ordinary shares in issue at 31 March 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the equity section of the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026.
parts.answer:
Equity
Ordinary shares of $0.50 each (1,200,000 shares)    600,000
Share premium                                       100,000
General reserve (50,000 + 20,000)                    70,000
Retained earnings                                   358,000
Total equity                                      1,128,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the bonus issue does not change the total equity of the company.
parts.answer: A bonus issue only transfers an amount from a reserve (share premium) to share capital. No cash is received, so total equity is unchanged; only its make-up changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: transfer between equity accounts; 1 mark: no cash/resources received.

practice.stem:
Coastal Fisheries plc, Gwadar, has a draft profit of $164,000 for the year ended 30 June 2026. The following errors have been found.
1 Closing inventory of frozen fish was included at cost, $12,400; its net realisable value is $9,100.
2 Proceeds of $50,000 from an issue of ordinary shares at par were credited to revenue.
3 A new boat engine costing $18,000, bought at the start of the year, was charged to repairs. Engines are depreciated at 25% per annum reducing balance.
4 Debenture interest of $3,600 owing at the year end has not been recorded.
5 The final dividend for the previous year, $25,000, was charged to administrative expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a table showing the effect (increase, decrease or no effect, with the amount) of correcting each item on (i) the profit for the year and (ii) the net assets.
parts.answer:
Item     Profit for the year          Net assets
1            decrease $3,300     decrease $3,300
2           decrease $50,000           no effect
3           increase $13,500    increase $13,500
4            decrease $3,600     decrease $3,600
5           increase $25,000           no effect
parts.working: 1 mark per item, both columns correct. Item 3: capitalise 18,000 less depreciation 25% × 18,000 = 4,500. Item 2: share issue proceeds move from profit to share capital; net assets unchanged. Item 5: dividend moves to retained earnings; net assets unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

practice.stem: Mirpur Ceramics plc had a profit before tax of $340,000 for the year ended 31 March 2026. Income tax on this year's profit is estimated at $78,000. Last year's financial statements included a tax liability of $61,000, but $64,500 was paid in settlement during this year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income tax expense for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.working: Current estimate 78,000 + under-provision for the previous year (64,500 − 61,000) 3,500. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the amount of the current tax liability in the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026.
parts.working: 1 mark. The previous year's liability has been settled.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an under-provision for tax and how it is treated.
parts.answer: The tax actually agreed and paid for the previous year was more than the amount estimated in last year's financial statements. The shortfall is added to this year's tax expense.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark treatment.

practice.stem:
Nile Valley Textiles plc, Egypt, has a draft profit of $127,800 for the year ended 31 December 2025. These errors have been found.
1 A rights issue of 40,000 ordinary shares of $1 each at $1.75 per share was recorded as Dr Bank $70,000, Cr Share capital $70,000.
2 Repairs to the factory roof of $8,600 were debited to the buildings account. (Ignore depreciation.)
3 Rent of $2,400 owed by a tenant at the year end has not been recorded.
4 Goods sent to a customer on sale or return at a selling price of $6,000 (cost $4,500) were recorded as a credit sale. The customer has not yet accepted the goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare journal entries to correct items 1–4. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $     Cr $
1 Share capital                  30,000
   Share premium                          30,000
2 Repairs (profit or loss)        8,600
   Buildings                               8,600
3 Other receivables               2,400
   Rent receivable (income)                2,400
4 Revenue                         6,000
   Trade receivables                       6,000
  Inventory                       4,500
   Cost of sales                           4,500
parts.working: 1 mark each for 1–3; 2 marks for 4. Item 1: premium 40,000 × 0.75 = 30,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year.
parts.working: 127,800 − 8,600 + 2,400 − 6,000 + 4,500 = 120,100. 1 mark repairs; 1 mark rent; 1 mark sale or return (net −1,500) and answer.

practice.stem:
Extracts from the equity of Thar Coal Services plc (ordinary shares of $1 each):
                            1 Jan 2025 $ 31 Dec 2025 $
Ordinary share capital           400,000       520,000
Share premium                     60,000       132,000
Retained earnings                233,000       301,400
During the year there was one issue of shares for cash. A final dividend of $0.07 per share for 2024 was paid before the share issue, and an interim dividend of $0.05 per share was paid after it. There were no other changes in equity apart from the profit for the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of shares issued during the year and the issue price per share.
parts.answer: 120,000 shares at $1.60

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash received from the share issue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.

practice.stem:
The draft statement of financial position of Shalimar Paper plc at 31 March 2026 showed: ordinary shares of $1 each $300,000; share premium $40,000; retained earnings $406,000 (opening balance $94,000 plus draft profit for the year $312,000); trade payables $48,000. There were no other equity or liability balances. The following have been found.
1 On 1 October 2025 the company issued $120,000 7% debentures 2032 at par. The cash received was credited to revenue. No interest has been paid.
2 On 31 March 2026 a building with a carrying amount of $410,000 was revalued at $520,000. The gain was credited to the statement of profit or loss.
3 Inventory costing $15,600 has a net realisable value of $11,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.answer:
Draft profit                                                312,000
Less debenture proceeds wrongly credited to revenue       (120,000)
Less debenture interest accrued (120,000 × 7% × 6/12)       (4,200)
Less revaluation gain wrongly credited to profit          (110,000)
Less inventory written down (15,600 − 11,200)               (4,400)
Corrected profit for the year                                73,400
parts.working: 1 mark each adjustment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the equity and liabilities section of the statement of financial position at 31 March 2026, after the corrections.
parts.answer:
Equity and liabilities
Ordinary shares of $1 each                            300,000
Share premium                                          40,000
Revaluation reserve                                   110,000
Retained earnings (94,000 + 73,400)                   167,400
Total equity                                          617,400
Non-current liabilities: 7% debentures 2032           120,000
Current liabilities: trade payables                    48,000
                    other payables (interest)           4,200
Total equity and liabilities                          789,600
parts.working: 1 mark revaluation reserve; 1 mark retained earnings; 1 mark debentures as non-current liability; 1 mark accrued interest as current liability with correct total.

practice.stem:
The following balances were extracted from the books of Saffron Foods plc at 30 June 2026.
                                                    $
Revenue                                     1,840,000
Cost of sales                               1,104,000
Distribution costs                            186,000
Administrative expenses                       212,000
Debenture interest paid                         9,000
6% debentures                                 300,000
Delivery vans at cost                         160,000
Delivery vans: accumulated depreciation        40,000
Office equipment at cost                       90,000
Additional information
1 Administrative expenses include ordinary dividends paid of $60,000.
2 Depreciation for the year has not been charged: delivery vans 25% reducing balance (distribution costs); office equipment 10% on cost (administrative expenses).
3 Inventory included in cost of sales must be written down by a further $7,000.
4 The debentures were in issue all year.
5 Tax for the year is estimated at $82,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distribution costs and the administrative expenses for the year.
parts.answer: Distribution costs $216,000; administrative expenses $161,000
parts.working: Vans 25% × (160,000 − 40,000) = 30,000 added to distribution (1); dividend 60,000 removed from admin (1); office equipment 10% × 90,000 = 9,000 added (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2026.
parts.answer:
Saffron Foods plc — Statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2026
Revenue                                                 1,840,000
Cost of sales (1,104,000 + 7,000)                     (1,111,000)
Gross profit                                              729,000
Distribution costs (186,000 + 30,000)                   (216,000)
Administrative expenses (212,000 − 60,000 + 9,000)      (161,000)
Profit from operations                                    352,000
Finance costs                                            (18,000)
Profit before tax                                         334,000
Tax                                                      (82,000)
Profit for the year                                       252,000
parts.working: 1 cost of sales and gross profit; 1 expenses (own figures from (a)) and profit from operations; 1 finance costs 18,000 (full year, not 9,000 paid); 1 tax; 1 profit for the year.

practice.stem:
The draft statement of financial position of Highland Tea plc, Kandy, at 30 June 2026 shows current assets of inventory $84,000, trade receivables $66,000 and cash $12,000, and current liabilities of trade payables $58,000, accruals $4,000 and tax payable $28,000. The draft profit for the year is $98,000. The following matters have been found.
1 Damaged inventory costing $9,000 has a net realisable value of $3,500.
2 A customer owing $4,800 went into liquidation before the year end; the debt should be written off.
3 An electricity accrual of $1,700 was omitted.
4 A payment of $6,000 to a supplier was entered in the cash book but not in the trade payables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year.
parts.working: 98,000 − 5,500 − 4,800 − 1,700 = 86,000. Item 4 does not affect profit. 1 mark each adjustment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio before and after the corrections. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Before 1.80 : 1; after 1.77 : 1
parts.working: Before 162,000 ÷ 90,000 = 1.80. After: current assets 162,000 − 5,500 − 4,800 = 151,700; current liabilities 90,000 + 1,700 − 6,000 = 85,700; ratio 1.77. 1 mark before; 1 mark CA; 1 mark CL; 1 mark after.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the change in the current ratio.
parts.answer: The ratio has fallen only slightly and remains comfortably above 1, so liquidity is still adequate; the draft figures overstated liquidity.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Pamir Outdoor Gear plc has a draft profit of $205,300 for the year ended 31 December 2025. Retained earnings at 1 January 2025 were $142,000.
1 An interim dividend of $18,000 paid in July 2025 was debited to administrative expenses.
2 A final dividend of $32,000 for 2025, proposed by the directors in February 2026, was charged as an expense and shown as a current liability.
3 Goods sent on sale or return at a selling price of $9,000 were included in revenue; the customer has not accepted them. The company sells at cost plus 50%.
4 Development costs of $14,000 meeting all the IAS 38 criteria for recognition were written off. Production of the new product starts in 2026.
5 The final dividend for 2024, $25,000, was paid in April 2025 and correctly recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Draft profit                                        205,300
Add interim dividend charged as an expense           18,000
Add proposed final dividend wrongly accrued          32,000
Less sale or return goods in revenue                (9,000)
Add those goods returned to inventory at cost         6,000
Add development costs to be capitalised              14,000
Corrected profit                                    266,300
parts.working: 1 mark interim dividend; 1 mark final dividend (IAS 10: proposed after the year end, so not a liability); 1 mark revenue; 1 mark inventory at cost 9,000 ÷ 1.5 = 6,000; 1 mark development costs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 142,000 + 266,300 − interim 18,000 − previous year's final 25,000 = 365,300. 1 mark profit; 1 mark both dividends; 1 mark answer.

practice.stem: At 31 December 2025 a printing machine owned by Urdu Press plc has a carrying amount of $84,000. Because of falling demand, its fair value less costs to sell is estimated at $61,000 and its value in use at $69,500. The machine has never been revalued.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the recoverable amount of the machine.
parts.working: Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs to sell (61,000) and value in use (69,500). M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the impairment loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the impairment loss is treated in the financial statements.
parts.answer: The machine's carrying amount is reduced to its recoverable amount. The loss is charged as an expense in the statement of profit or loss (because the asset has not been revalued, so there is no revaluation reserve to set it against).
parts.working: 1 mark carrying amount reduced; 1 mark expense in profit or loss.

practice.stem:
Zarghun Juices plc bought a bottling machine. The costs were:
                                                         $
List price                                         145,000
Trade discount on list price                            5%
Sales tax (recoverable from the tax authority)      12,000
Import duty                                          9,200
Delivery to the factory                              2,400
Installation                                         6,300
Testing before use                                   1,800
Training staff to operate the machine                3,000
One-year maintenance contract                        4,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the machine to be recognised as a non-current asset under IAS 16.
parts.working: List price less 5% trade discount 137,750; add import duty 9,200, delivery 2,400, installation 6,300, testing 1,800. Exclude recoverable sales tax, staff training and the maintenance contract. 1 mark discount; 1 mark duty and delivery; 1 mark installation and testing; 1 mark exclusions and total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the staff training and the maintenance contract are treated.
parts.answer: Both are revenue expenditure: they do not bring the asset to working condition, so they are charged as expenses in the statement of profit or loss (the maintenance contract over the year it covers).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Bukhara Carpets plc bought a building on 1 January 2016 for $600,000. It is depreciated at 2.5% per annum on cost (a 40-year life, no residual value). On 31 December 2025, after the depreciation for 2025 had been charged, the building was revalued at $690,000. The useful life is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revaluation gain.
parts.working: Accumulated depreciation 600,000 × 2.5% × 10 = 150,000; carrying amount 450,000; gain 690,000 − 450,000 = 240,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the revaluation. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $      Cr $
Accumulated depreciation: buildings      150,000
Buildings (690,000 − 600,000)             90,000
   Revaluation reserve                             240,000
parts.working: 1 mark eliminating accumulated depreciation; 1 mark building increased by 90,000; 1 mark revaluation reserve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge on the building for the year ending 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 690,000 ÷ remaining life 30 years = 23,000. M1 A1.

practice.stem:
Arabian Spice Traders plc holds four product lines at 31 May 2026.
Line     Cost $Notes
A        12,000Net realisable value $15,400
B         8,600Expected selling price $8,300; selling costs $1,200
C        21,000Net realisable value $26,500
D         5,400Selling price $4,800 after repackaging costing $600; selling costs $300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of inventory at 31 May 2026 in accordance with IAS 2.
parts.working: Lower of cost and NRV for each item: A 12,000; B NRV 8,300 − 1,200 = 7,100; C 21,000; D NRV 4,800 − 600 − 300 = 3,900. Total 44,000. 1 mark each item.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the comparison of cost and net realisable value is made item by item rather than for the inventory as a whole.
parts.answer: Comparing totals would let the profit expected on some items hide the losses on others (here total cost 47,000 is below total NRV 52,900, so no write-down would be made). Prudence requires each foreseeable loss to be recognised.
parts.working: 1 mark losses hidden/offset; 1 mark prudence.

practice.stem: Gilgit Hotels plc bought land for $300,000 in 2020. Land is not depreciated. In December 2023 the land was revalued to $380,000 and a revaluation reserve was created. At 31 December 2026 the land is revalued at $270,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much of the fall in value is charged against the revaluation reserve and how much is charged in the statement of profit or loss for 2026.
parts.answer: Revaluation reserve $80,000; profit or loss $30,000
parts.working: Total fall 380,000 − 270,000 = 110,000. The reserve for this asset is used first (80,000); the remaining 30,000 is an impairment loss in profit or loss. 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry for the fall in value. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $      Cr $
Revaluation reserve                   80,000
Impairment loss (profit or loss)      30,000
   Land                                        110,000
parts.working: 1 mark each line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the carrying amount of the land at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Hala Ajrak Printers plc bought a machine on 1 January 2022 for $240,000. It was depreciated straight-line over 10 years with a residual value of $20,000. On 1 January 2026 the directors decided that the machine has only 4 more years of useful life and a residual value of $12,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine at 1 January 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2026 and the carrying amount at that date.
parts.answer: Depreciation $35,000; carrying amount $117,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the change is not applied to the depreciation charged in earlier years.
parts.answer: It is a change in an accounting estimate (IAS 8), not an error or a change of policy. It is applied prospectively, to the current and future years only; past figures were based on the best information available at the time.
parts.working: 1 mark change in estimate; 1 mark prospective treatment.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem: The directors of Kalash Mountain Resorts plc are preparing the financial statements and are unsure how to deal with a number of uncertain items.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the following terms as used in IAS 37: (i) a provision, (ii) a contingent liability.
parts.answer: (i) A liability of uncertain timing or amount. (ii) A possible obligation whose existence depends on uncertain future events, or a present obligation that is not probable or cannot be measured reliably.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the three conditions that must be met before a provision is recognised.
parts.answer: There is a present obligation (legal or constructive) from a past event; an outflow of resources to settle it is probable; a reliable estimate of the amount can be made.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how a probable contingent asset is treated.
parts.answer: It is disclosed in a note but not recognised in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
Indus Ferries plc has the following matters at 31 March 2026.
1 A passenger is suing the company for injuries suffered on one of its ferries in January 2026. The lawyers say the company will probably lose, and estimate damages of $85,000.
2 The company has guaranteed a $200,000 bank loan of a supplier. The supplier has had some cash-flow difficulties; the company's advisers consider a default possible but not probable.
3 The company is claiming $40,000 compensation from a shipyard for late delivery of a ferry. The lawyers think the claim will probably succeed, but the shipyard has not agreed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each matter, state how it should be treated in the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026. Give reasons.
parts.answer:
1 Recognise a provision of $85,000: present obligation from a past event, outflow probable, reliable estimate. Charge to profit or loss; show as a liability.
2 Disclose as a contingent liability in a note only: an outflow is possible, not probable.
3 Do not recognise; disclose as a contingent asset in a note because the inflow is probable but not virtually certain.
parts.working: 1 mark treatment and 1 mark reason for each matter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The draft profit before dealing with these matters was $520,000. Calculate the revised profit.
parts.working: Only the provision affects profit.

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
The draft profit of Saddar Electronics plc for the year ended 31 March 2026 is $310,000. The financial statements will be authorised for issue on 30 June 2026. These events occurred after the year end.
1 20 April 2026: a customer who owed $18,000 at 31 March 2026 was declared bankrupt; nothing will be received.
2 5 May 2026: a fire destroyed inventory worth $60,000 in the warehouse.
3 12 May 2026: goods held in inventory at 31 March 2026 at a cost of $25,000 were sold for $19,000, with selling costs of $1,000.
4 1 June 2026: the directors proposed a final dividend of $40,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each event as adjusting or non-adjusting and state how each should be treated.
parts.answer:
1 Adjusting: confirms the customer could not pay at the year end; write off $18,000.
2 Non-adjusting: the condition (fire) arose after the year end; disclose in a note if material.
3 Adjusting: gives evidence of NRV at the year end; write inventory down to 18,000.
4 Non-adjusting: no obligation existed at the year end; disclose in a note, no liability.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.working: 310,000 − 18,000 − (25,000 − 18,000) = 285,000. 1 mark each adjustment, 1 mark answer (non-adjusting events ignored).

practice.subtopic: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period
practice.stem:
Crescent Appliances plc sold 12,000 washing machines in 2025 with a one-year warranty. Past experience shows that 80% need no repairs, 15% need minor repairs costing $40 each and 5% need major repairs costing $250 each. The warranty provision brought forward from 2024 is $180,000. At 31 December 2025 the provision should equal the expected cost of repairs on the machines sold in 2025. The draft profit is $960,000. In addition:
• a former employee is suing the company for $70,000; lawyers believe the claim will possibly, but not probably, succeed
• the company's insurer has confirmed in writing that it will pay $15,000 for flood damage costs already charged as an expense in 2025; nothing has been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the warranty provision required at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 12,000 × (15% × 40 + 5% × 250) = 12,000 × 18.50. M1 expected value; M1 both outcomes; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the amount to be charged in the statement of profit or loss for the warranty provision.
parts.answer: $42,000 (increase in the provision)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the lawsuit and the insurance claim should be treated.
parts.answer: Lawsuit: an outflow is only possible, so it is disclosed as a contingent liability, not provided for. Insurance: the inflow is virtually certain (written confirmation), so it is no longer contingent and is recognised as a receivable and income of $15,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the revised profit for the year.

practice.stem: Neelum Mineral Water plc has 2,000,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each. Profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 was $380,000 and retained earnings at that date are $1,150,000. An interim dividend of $0.04 per share has been paid. The directors propose a final dividend of $0.12 per share. The company has cash of $90,000 and plans to extend its factory next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the proposed final dividend.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the dividend cover for the year if the final dividend is paid. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 1.19 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should pay the proposed final dividend. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For: retained earnings of $1,150,000 mean the dividend is legally possible; shareholders expect a return and the share price may fall if it is cut; a stable dividend signals confidence.
Against: cash is only $90,000, so the company would need to borrow about $150,000, adding interest; dividend cover of 1.19 is low, so most of this year's profit is paid out; the factory extension planned for next year needs funds.
Decision: pay a reduced final dividend (for example $0.05 per share, $100,000) or delay payment until cash allows.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for, up to 2 marks for points against (using figures), 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem:
Tarbela Engineering plc has 1,500,000 ordinary shares of $1 each, share premium of $400,000, retained earnings of $900,000 and cash of $260,000. The directors are considering two options.
Option A: pay a cash dividend of $0.15 per share.
Option B: make a bonus issue of 1 share for every 5 held, using the share premium account, and pay no cash dividend.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show the effect of each option on share capital, share premium, retained earnings, total equity and cash.
parts.answer:
Cash dividend   Bonus issue
Ordinary share capital        no change     +$300,000
Share premium                 no change     −$300,000
Retained earnings             −$225,000     no change
Total equity                  −$225,000     no change
Cash                          −$225,000     no change
parts.working: Option A: 1,500,000 × 0.15 = 225,000. Option B: 1,500,000 ÷ 5 = 300,000 shares × $1 = $300,000 from share premium. 1 mark each correct column pair (share capital/premium; retained earnings; total equity; cash).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors which option they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Cash dividend: rewards shareholders with cash and meets their income expectations, but leaves only $35,000 cash, which may cause liquidity problems. Bonus issue: no cash leaves the company and reserves are kept for growth; shareholders receive more shares, but the share price will fall in proportion, so they gain no real wealth and may be disappointed. Decision: e.g. a bonus issue (or a smaller cash dividend) because cash is needed for operations.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two relevant points, 1 mark use of figures, 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: While preparing the financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025, the accountant of Kirthar Foods plc discovered that closing inventory at 31 December 2024 had been overstated by $36,000 because of a counting error. This is a material error. Retained earnings at 1 January 2025, as previously reported, were $512,000. The draft profit for 2025, calculated using the incorrect opening inventory, is $148,000. Dividends of $50,000 were paid in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2025.
parts.working: 512,000 − 36,000: the 2024 profit was overstated by the overstatement of closing inventory. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for 2025.
parts.working: Opening inventory for 2025 was overstated, so cost of sales was too high: 148,000 + 36,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 December 2025.
parts.working: 476,000 + 184,000 − 50,000 = 610,000. The error has reversed itself by the end of 2025. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how IAS 8 requires a material prior period error to be corrected.
parts.answer: It is corrected retrospectively: the comparative figures for the prior period are restated and the opening balance of retained earnings is adjusted in the statement of changes in equity, rather than putting the correction through the current year's profit.
parts.working: 1 mark retrospective/restate comparatives; 1 mark adjust opening retained earnings.

practice.stem: In 2026 the auditors of Swat Marble plc found that a machine bought on 1 July 2024 for $80,000 had been debited to repairs in 2024. The company depreciates machinery at 20% per annum straight-line, with a time apportionment in the year of purchase. The error is material. The year end is 31 December. Retained earnings at 1 January 2026, as previously reported, were $645,000. The draft profit for 2026 is $210,000 (no depreciation has been charged on the machine).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2026.
parts.working: 2024: profit understated by 80,000 − depreciation 8,000 (6 months) = 72,000; 2025: depreciation 16,000 omitted. 645,000 + 72,000 − 16,000 = 701,000. 1 mark each step.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the correction for 2024 and 2025 is not included in the profit for 2026.
parts.answer: Including it would distort the 2026 profit and make comparison with earlier years misleading. IAS 8 requires material prior period errors to be corrected retrospectively through opening retained earnings, with comparatives restated.
parts.working: 1 mark distortion/comparability; 1 mark IAS 8 retrospective treatment.

practice.stem:
Solaris Devices plc, Islamabad, spent the following in the year ended 30 June 2026.
1 Salaries of scientists investigating new battery materials, with no particular product in view: $42,000
2 Testing a prototype of a new solar phone charger (all IAS 38 development criteria are met): $68,000
3 Market research carried out before the charger project was approved: $9,000
4 Designing tools for production of the new charger (criteria met): $25,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be charged as an expense and the amount to be recognised as an intangible asset for the year.
parts.answer: Expense $51,000; intangible asset $93,000
parts.working: Research (1) and market research before approval (3) are expensed: 51,000. Development meeting all criteria (2) and (4) is capitalised: 93,000. 1 mark per item correctly treated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two of the criteria that development expenditure must meet before it can be recognised as an asset under IAS 38.
parts.answer: Any two: technically feasible to complete; intention to complete and use or sell; ability to use or sell; probable future economic benefits (a market exists); adequate technical, financial and other resources to complete; expenditure can be measured reliably.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Medisonic plc capitalised development costs of $180,000 for a new ultrasound scanner in 2024. Commercial production began on 1 January 2025 and the costs are amortised straight-line over the expected sales life of 5 years. At 31 December 2026 a competitor launched a cheaper scanner, and the recoverable amount of the development costs was estimated at $90,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amortisation charge for 2026.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the development costs at 31 December 2026 before any impairment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the impairment loss at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: 108,000 − recoverable amount 90,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the total charge in the statement of profit or loss for 2026 relating to the development costs.
parts.working: Amortisation plus impairment.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why capitalised development costs are amortised.
parts.answer: Matching: the costs are spread over the periods that benefit from sales of the product; the asset has a limited useful life, so its carrying amount should fall as the benefits are used up.
parts.working: 1 mark matching; 1 mark finite life/benefits consumed.

subtopics.name: Provisions, contingencies and events after the reporting period

practice.stem: A rice mill in Larkana is thinking of replacing an old husking machine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two non-financial factors a business should consider before replacing a machine.
parts.answer: Any two: effect on employees (training, job losses, morale); quality of output; environmental impact; reliability and after-sales service of the supplier; flexibility of the new machine.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of net present value over the payback method.
parts.answer: NPV considers all cash flows over the project's life and the time value of money, whereas payback ignores cash flows after the payback point.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: The manager of a cinema in Karachi has been told that a new projector has a positive net present value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a positive net present value.
parts.answer: The present value of the future net cash inflows is greater than the initial cost; the project earns more than the cost of capital and increases the value of the business.
parts.working: 1 mark PV of inflows > cost; 1 mark return above cost of capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of the net present value method.
parts.answer: Any two: cash flows are hard to forecast; choosing the right discount rate is difficult; ignores non-financial factors; harder to understand than payback; assumes the cost of capital stays the same.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The finance director of a cement company is appraising a new kiln.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a business uses its cost of capital as the discount rate.
parts.answer: It is the return the business must pay to its providers of finance; a project must earn at least this return to add value.
parts.working: 1 mark cost of finance; 1 mark minimum required return.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by sensitivity analysis.
parts.answer: Testing how much one estimate (e.g. sales volume, cost, discount rate) can change before the NPV becomes zero, to show which estimates the decision depends on most.
parts.working: 1 mark change one variable; 1 mark effect on NPV/decision.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of sensitivity analysis.
parts.answer: Changes one variable at a time, whereas in reality several change together / gives no probability of the change happening.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Khan Engineering can afford only one of two projects. Its cost of capital is 10%. Results:
                             Project Canal  Project Bridge
Net present value                  $24,000         $19,500
Payback period                   3.2 years       2.1 years
Accounting rate of return              18%             22%
Internal rate of return                15%             17%
The company has a large bank overdraft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors which project they should choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Either project may be recommended with justification; a strong answer recommends Project Canal on NPV (it adds the most value) unless liquidity is a priority.
parts.working: Canal (max 3): higher NPV ($24,000 v $19,500) so adds more to shareholder value; NPV is the most reliable method; both IRRs exceed the 10% cost of capital. Bridge (max 3): faster payback (2.1 v 3.2 years), less risk and better for cash flow; higher ARR and IRR; later cash flows of Canal are harder to forecast. Other points: non-financial factors such as staff, customers, environment; forecasts are estimates. Clear decision (1).

practice.stem: A project costing $100,000 is expected to give net cash inflows of $32,000 a year for five years. The cost of capital is 12% and the sum of the discount factors for years 1–5 at 12% is 3.605.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the annual cash inflow could fall before the project became unprofitable, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 NPV ÷ PV of the inflows; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what your answer to (b) shows.
parts.answer: If annual inflows fall by more than 13.31% (below about $27,739), the NPV becomes negative; a small margin means the project is risky.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Saba Textiles may install a dyeing plant costing $180,000. Net cash inflows are forecast at $55,000, $65,000, $70,000 and $45,000 in years 1–4. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value.
parts.working: M1 discounting; M1 less cost; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the initial cost that would make the NPV zero, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on your answer to (b).
parts.answer: The project is very sensitive to the initial cost: an overspend of under 4% would make it unprofitable, so cost control/fixed-price quotes are important.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Zainab runs a packaging factory in Lahore. Her old machine breaks down often and three customers complained about late orders last month. A new machine would cost $95,000, financed by a bank loan at 9% interest. Its NPV at the 10% cost of capital is $8,400 and its payback period is 3.8 years over a 5-year life. It uses 15% less electricity. Staff would need two weeks of training, during which output would fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Zainab whether she should buy the new machine. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A justified recommendation, e.g. buy: positive NPV, solves the reliability problem and saves energy, but she should plan the training and loan carefully.
parts.working: For (max 4): NPV positive ($8,400) at the 10% cost of capital; breakdowns of the old machine have caused late orders and lost customers; 15% energy saving and lower emissions; better quality may win new contracts. Against (max 4): payback of 3.8 years in a 5-year life leaves little margin; NPV small compared with $95,000 cost so sensitive to forecasts; staff need two weeks of training and output will fall; loan increases gearing and interest at 9%. Decision (1).

practice.stem: A company may launch a water pump. It needs a machine costing $110,000 with a four-year life and no residual value. It expects to sell 5,000 pumps a year at a contribution of $12 each. Extra fixed cash costs are $20,000 a year. The cost of capital is 10%; the sum of the discount factors for years 1–4 is 3.169.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which sales volume could fall before the NPV becomes zero, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 only contribution varies with volume; M1 NPV ÷ PV of contribution; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum annual sales volume needed, in whole units.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Hassan Foods has $300,000 to invest and a cost of capital of 12%. It is considering two projects:
                                              Project Tulip  Project Lotus
Initial cost                                       $300,000       $150,000
Life                                                6 years        4 years
Net present value                                   $42,000        $31,000
Internal rate of return                                 18%            21%
Payback period                                    3.5 years      2.4 years
Fall in annual inflows that makes NPV zero               7%            16%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors which project, if either, they should invest in. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Either may be chosen with justification; e.g. Lotus: lower risk, faster payback and higher IRR, and leaves $150,000 for other uses, although Tulip has the higher NPV.
parts.working: Tulip (max 3): higher NPV $42,000 adds most value; uses all available funds productively; longer life gives returns for six years. Lotus (max 3): higher IRR 21% v 18%; payback 2.4 v 3.5 years; NPV only falls to zero if inflows drop 16% (Tulip only 7%) so far less risky; half the investment, leaving $150,000 for another project, which could make total NPV higher. Other: forecasts over six years less reliable; non-financial factors. Decision (1).

practice.stem:
An engineering firm in Sialkot appraised a project costing $160,000 with net cash inflows of $45,000 a year for five years and no residual value. The finance manager now believes the inflows will be 10% lower, but the equipment could be sold for $12,000 at the end of year 5. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683; year 5 0.621

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the original net present value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revised net present value.
parts.working: M1 inflows reduced by 10%; M1 residual at year 5; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on what the revision shows about the project.
parts.answer: The NPV falls to only $947: the project is still just acceptable but is very sensitive to the sales forecast.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A school in Abbottabad may install solar panels costing $85,000. Electricity savings are expected to be $23,500 a year for five years, with no residual value. The cost of capital is 8%.
Discount factors at 8%: year 1 0.926; year 2 0.857; year 3 0.794; year 4 0.735; year 5 0.681

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sum of the discount factors for years 1 to 5.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum annual net cash inflow needed for the project to be worthwhile, to the nearest dollar.
parts.working: M1 NPV = 0; M1 cost ÷ annuity factor; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the expected inflow of $23,500 could fall before the project is rejected, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

practice.stem:
A dairy in Okara is considering a new bottling machine costing $80,000. It would give net cash inflows of $26,000 at the end of each of the next four years. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the machine.
parts.working: M1 present values of inflows; M1 less cost; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the machine should be bought, based on your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Yes: the NPV of $2,394 is positive.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A private school in Islamabad plans to build a science laboratory costing $150,000. Extra fee income less extra running costs is expected to be $40,000, $55,000, $60,000 and $35,000 in years 1 to 4. The cost of capital is 12%.
Discount factors at 12%: year 1 0.893; year 2 0.797; year 3 0.712; year 4 0.636

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the project.
parts.working: M1 each year discounted; M1 total present value; M1 less cost; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what your answer to (a) shows.
parts.answer: The NPV is negative (−$5,465): the project does not earn the 12% cost of capital, so on financial grounds it should not go ahead.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A courier firm in Peshawar may buy an electric van for $36,000. Fuel and repair savings are expected to be $11,000, $12,000, $12,000 and $9,000 in years 1 to 4, and the van will be sold for $4,000 at the end of year 4. The cost of capital is 14%.
Discount factors at 14%: year 1 0.877; year 2 0.769; year 3 0.675; year 4 0.592

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of buying the van.
parts.working: M1 cash flow for year 4 includes sale proceeds; M1 discounting; M1 total; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the van should be bought on financial grounds.
parts.answer: No: the NPV is negative (−$1,329), so the savings do not cover the cost at a 14% cost of capital.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A food processor in Multan is considering a new production line costing $200,000. It needs extra working capital of $25,000 at the start, which will be released at the end of year 5. Net operating cash inflows will be $52,000 a year for five years and the line will be sold for $30,000 at the end of year 5. The cost of capital is 8%.
Discount factors at 8%: year 1 0.926; year 2 0.857; year 3 0.794; year 4 0.735; year 5 0.681

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for year 0 and for year 5.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the project.
parts.working: M1 years 1–4 discounted; M1 year 5 discounted; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the working capital is shown as an inflow in year 5.
parts.answer: The extra inventory and receivables are no longer needed when the project ends, so the cash tied up is released.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A transport company in Karachi may buy a bus for $120,000. It will be used for four years and then sold for $20,000. Depreciation is straight-line. Forecast profits after depreciation are: year 1 $18,000; year 2 $22,000; year 3 $27,000; year 4 $15,000. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each of years 1 to 4.
parts.working: M1 add back depreciation; A1 including residual value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value.
parts.working: M1 discounting; M1 less cost; A1 OF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the project should be accepted.
parts.answer: Accept: NPV is positive.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A company in Hyderabad can afford only one of two projects, each costing $60,000 now. Net cash inflows:
Year    Project Indus $  Project Ravi $
1                25,000          10,000
2                25,000          20,000
3                20,000          30,000
4                10,000          35,000
The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of each project.
parts.working: M1 discounting A; A1; M1 discounting B; A1; 1 mark presentation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which project should be chosen on financial grounds and give one reason why the result may be less certain for the other project.
parts.answer: Project Ravi (higher NPV). Ravi's cash flows come later, so they are harder to forecast and riskier.
parts.working: 1 mark for both points.

practice.stem:
Sharif Ltd may make a new juicer. A machine costing $190,000 and a launch campaign costing $15,000 would both be paid now. The juicer would sell 6,000 units a year for five years at $45 each, with a variable cost of $27 per unit. Extra fixed cash costs would be $48,000 a year. The machine would be scrapped for $10,000 at the end of year 5. The cost of capital is 12%.
Discount factors at 12%: year 1 0.893; year 2 0.797; year 3 0.712; year 4 0.636; year 5 0.567

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual net cash flow from operating the machine.
parts.working: M1 contribution less fixed cash costs; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the project.
parts.working: Year 0 includes launch costs: 190,000 + 15,000 (1); scrap in year 5 (1); discounting (1); A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the net present value may not be reliable.
parts.answer: Any one: sales volume, price or costs are estimates; the cost of capital may change; the machine's life or scrap value may differ.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A private hospital in Lahore may buy a scanner costing $250,000. It would bring net cash inflows of $70,000 a year for six years. A major overhaul costing $40,000 would be needed at the end of year 3, and the scanner could be sold for $15,000 at the end of year 6. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683; year 5 0.621; year 6 0.564

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the present value of the annual cash inflows, using the sum of the discount factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value of the project.
parts.working: M1 overhaul discounted at year 3; M1 residual at year 6; M1 less cost; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one non-financial factor the hospital board should consider.
parts.answer: Any one: patient waiting times/quality of care; staff training; reliability of the supplier; space needed.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A printing firm in Faisalabad forecasts for a new press:
Year    Revenue $  Total costs $
1          90,000         67,000
2         105,000         73,000
3         120,000         81,000
Total costs include depreciation of $15,000 a year on the press.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each year.
parts.working: M1 depreciation removed from costs; A1 A1 (all three for 2 marks).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why depreciation is not included in the net cash flows.
parts.answer: Depreciation is not a payment of cash; the cash outflow is the purchase cost at the start.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Fatima Foods is considering a new snack line for four years. Information:
1 Market research already paid: $8,000
2 New machine, paid now: $70,000 (no residual value)
3 Extra supervisor: $14,000 a year
4 Share of head office costs charged to the line: $6,000 a year
5 Contribution from sales: $40,000 a year

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the items 1 to 5, state whether it is a relevant cash flow for the decision and give a reason for items 1 and 4.
parts.answer: 1 not relevant: market research is a sunk cost (already paid). 2 relevant. 3 relevant. 4 not relevant: apportioned head office cost will be paid whether or not the project goes ahead. 5 relevant.
parts.working: 1 mark for all five classifications; 1 mark each reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for year 0 and for each of years 1 to 4.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Amir runs a car-wash in Sukkur. New equipment would cost $66,000, last three years and be sold for $6,000. Forecast profits after straight-line depreciation are $14,000, $19,000 and $11,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why profit is not used directly in net present value calculations.
parts.answer: Profit includes non-cash items such as depreciation and is based on accruals; NPV discounts the timing of actual cash receipts and payments.
parts.working: 1 mark non-cash/accruals; 1 mark timing of cash.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each of years 1 to 3.
parts.working: M1 depreciation; M1 added back; A1 including residual.

practice.stem: A laundry in Dubai plans to buy machinery for $120,000, to be used for four years and then sold for $12,000. Extra working capital of $18,000 is needed at the start and will be recovered at the end of year 4. Revenue is forecast at $100,000, $110,000, $95,000 and $80,000 in years 1–4. Variable costs are 40% of revenue. Fixed cash costs are $22,000 a year, and depreciation will be $27,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for year 0.
parts.answer: Machine 120,000 + working capital 18,000 = ($138,000)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow for each of years 1 to 4.
parts.working: M1 contribution = 60% of revenue; M1 fixed cash costs deducted; M1 depreciation (27,000) not deducted; M1 working capital released year 4; A1 residual value year 4.

practice.stem: A solar-panel project has an NPV of $4,500 at 8% and −$3,000 at 12%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the internal rate of return.
parts.answer: The discount rate at which the net present value of a project is zero; the project should be accepted if it is higher than the cost of capital.
parts.working: 1 mark NPV = 0; 1 mark decision rule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the answer to (b) is only an estimate.
parts.answer: Interpolation assumes NPV changes in a straight line between the two rates, but the real relationship is curved.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A project has a net present value of $18,400 at a discount rate of 10% and −$6,200 at 18%. The company's cost of capital is 14%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1 interpolation formula; M1 correct substitution; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the project should be accepted.
parts.answer: Accept: the IRR of 15.98% is above the 14% cost of capital.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem:
A clinic in Karachi may buy dental equipment for $90,000. Net cash inflows are expected to be $25,000, $35,000, $40,000 and $30,000 in years 1–4.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683
Discount factors at 16%: year 1 0.862; year 2 0.743; year 3 0.641; year 4 0.552

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 10%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net present value at 16%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the internal rate of return, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1; A1 OF.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The cost of capital is 12%. State whether the project should go ahead and give one advantage of the IRR method.
parts.answer: Go ahead: IRR 15.88% exceeds 12%. Advantage: a percentage is easy to compare with the cost of capital / takes account of the time value of money.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark advantage.

practice.stem: A furniture maker in Chiniot may buy a CNC router for $60,000. It will last five years with no residual value. Total profit after depreciation over the five years is forecast at $45,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return based on the average investment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the project meets the target return of 25%.
parts.answer: Yes: 30% is above 25%.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem: Haroon Builders may buy a crane for $140,000. It will produce net cash inflows of $50,000 a year for four years and then be sold for $20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual profit.
parts.answer: Total cash inflows 200,000 − depreciation 120,000 = 80,000; ÷ 4 = $20,000
parts.working: M1 depreciation deducted; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the accounting rate of return on (i) the average investment and (ii) the initial investment, correct to two decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of the accounting rate of return.
parts.answer: Any one: ignores the time value of money; uses profit not cash flow; different formulas give different answers; ignores the timing of profits.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A school in Lahore must choose between two projects, each costing $48,000. Project X returns $12,000 a year for six years. Project Y returns $20,000, $18,000, $15,000 and $10,000 in years 1–4. Cash flows arise evenly through each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period for Project X.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the payback period for Project Y in years and months.
parts.answer: After 2 years 38,000 recovered; 10,000 of year 3's 15,000 needed = 0.67 of a year ≈ 8 months. Payback = 2 years 8 months.
parts.working: M1 cumulative; M1 fraction; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of the payback method.
parts.answer: Ignores cash flows after payback / ignores the time value of money (unless discounted).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A bakery chain in Islamabad may open a new outlet costing $75,000. Net cash inflows are $28,000, $30,000, $26,000 and $20,000 in years 1–4, arising evenly through each year. The cost of capital is 10%.
Discount factors at 10%: year 1 0.909; year 2 0.826; year 3 0.751; year 4 0.683

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the simple payback period, correct to two decimal places of a year.
parts.answer: After 2 years 58,000; 17,000 ÷ 26,000 = 0.65; payback = 2.65 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the discounted payback period, correct to two decimal places of a year.
parts.answer: Present values: 25,452, 24,780, 19,526, 13,660. Cumulative after year 3: 69,758; still to recover 5,242; 5,242 ÷ 13,660 = 0.38. Discounted payback = 3.38 years
parts.working: M1 present values; M1 cumulative; M1 fraction of year 4; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the discounted payback period is longer than the simple payback period.
parts.answer: Discounting reduces the value of each future inflow, so it takes longer to recover the cost.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A bakery in Lahore makes cakes. The standard is 3 kg of flour mix per batch at $4 per kg. In March it made 2,000 batches, using 6,300 kg that cost $24,570.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance.
parts.working: M1 AQ × SP − actual cost; A1 with F/A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material usage variance.
parts.answer: Standard quantity 2,000 × 3 = 6,000 kg; (6,000 − 6,300) × 4 = $1,200 adverse
parts.working: M1 (SQ − AQ) × SP; A1 with F/A.

practice.stem: A garment factory in Faisalabad sets a standard of 1.5 labour hours per shirt at $12 per hour. Last month 4,000 shirts were made using 5,800 hours, and wages paid were $72,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance.

practice.stem: A company in Karachi budgeted to sell 5,000 electric irons at $40 each, giving a standard profit of $9 per iron. It actually sold 4,600 irons at $42 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price variance.
parts.working: M1 actual units × price difference; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sales volume variance, using standard profit.

practice.stem: A furniture company in Chiniot budgeted to sell 2,000 dining tables at $250 each. The standard cost of a table is $190. It actually sold 2,150 tables at $240 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sales volume variance, using standard profit.
parts.answer: Standard profit 250 − 190 = 60; (2,150 − 2,000) × 60 = $9,000 favourable

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the net effect of the two variances on profit.
parts.answer: Net $12,500 adverse
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem: A workshop in Jaipur makes brass lamps. Each lamp needs 2.5 kg of brass at $8 per kg and 45 minutes of labour at $16 per hour. Variable overhead is absorbed at $4 per labour hour and fixed overhead at $20 per labour hour. Each lamp sells for $65.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the standard cost card for one lamp.
parts.answer:
Standard cost card: one lamp
                                                              $
Direct materials (2.5 kg × $8)                            20.00
Direct labour (45 minutes × $16 per hour)                 12.00
Variable overhead (0.75 hours × $4)                        3.00
Fixed overhead (0.75 hours × $20)                         15.00
Standard cost per unit                                    50.00
parts.working: Labour time converted to 0.75 hours (1); overheads on labour hours (1); total $50.00 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard profit per lamp.
parts.working: 1 mark OF.

practice.stem: Each valve made by a factory in Gujranwala should take 2 machine hours; variable overhead is absorbed at $3 per machine hour. The standard material cost is $15 per valve. In June 3,500 valves were made. Machine hours were 7,400, variable overhead was $21,460 and material cost $54,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the variable overhead expenditure and efficiency variances.
parts.working: M1 A1 for each variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total material cost variance.
parts.working: M1 standard cost of actual output − actual cost; A1.

practice.stem: A firm in Sialkot budgeted fixed production overhead of $96,000 for an output of 12,000 cricket bats. Actual output was 11,400 bats and actual fixed overhead was $98,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead absorption rate per unit.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead expenditure variance and the fixed overhead volume variance.
parts.working: M1 A1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total under- or over-absorbed fixed overhead.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A paint maker in Rawalpindi uses 0.8 litres of resin per tin at a standard price of $6.50 per litre. In May it made 9,000 tins and bought and used 7,050 litres of resin costing $47,235.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual price paid per litre.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material price variance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the material usage variance.

practice.stem: A call-centre in Islamabad measures output in 'cases handled'. The standard is 30 minutes per case at $16 per hour. In April 8,400 cases were handled; staff worked and were paid for 4,350 hours at $15.60 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard hours for the actual output.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the labour efficiency variance and the total labour variance.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A company in Peshawar budgeted to make 10,000 units. Budgeted costs: materials $80,000; labour $60,000; variable overhead $20,000; fixed overhead $45,000. Actual output was 9,000 units. Actual costs: materials $73,500; labour $52,900; variable overhead $18,600; fixed overhead $46,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a flexed budget for an output of 9,000 units.
parts.answer: Materials $72,000; Labour $54,000; Variable overhead $18,000; Fixed overhead $45,000
parts.working: 1 mark variable costs × 90%; 1 mark fixed overhead unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the variance for each cost and the total cost variance.
parts.answer: Materials $1,500 adverse; Labour $1,100 favourable; Variable overhead $600 adverse; Fixed overhead $1,200 adverse; total $2,200 adverse
parts.working: 2 marks all four (1 mark for two or three); 1 mark total.

practice.stem: Budgeted fixed overhead for a pharmaceutical packaging plant was $180,000, based on 36,000 standard labour hours. Each pack has a standard time of 1.5 labour hours. Actual output was 23,000 packs and actual fixed overhead was $176,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead absorption rate per labour hour.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead absorbed and the amount under- or over-absorbed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fixed overhead expenditure and volume variances.
parts.answer: Expenditure 180,000 − 176,400 = $3,600 favourable; volume (34,500 − 36,000) × 5 = $7,500 adverse
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Shah Appliances makes one model of water heater. Standard cost card per heater: materials 4 kg × $5 = $20; labour 2 hours × $14 = $28; variable overhead 2 hours × $3 = $6; fixed overhead 2 hours × $10 = $20. Standard cost $74; selling price $100; standard profit $26. Budgeted output and sales: 3,000 heaters (budgeted fixed overhead $60,000).
Actual results for the month: 3,200 heaters made and sold at $97 each; materials 13,100 kg costing $64,190; labour 6,250 hours costing $89,375; variable overhead $19,500; fixed overhead $61,800.
The following variances have already been calculated: material price $1,310 favourable; material usage $1,500 adverse; labour rate $1,875 adverse; labour efficiency $2,100 favourable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sales price and sales volume variances.
parts.answer: Price: 3,200 × (97 − 100) = $9,600 adverse. Volume: 200 × 26 = $5,200 favourable.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the variable overhead expenditure and efficiency variances, and the fixed overhead expenditure and volume variances.
parts.answer: VOH expenditure 6,250 × 3 − 19,500 = $750 adverse; VOH efficiency (6,400 − 6,250) × 3 = $450 favourable; FOH expenditure 60,000 − 61,800 = $1,800 adverse; FOH volume (3,200 − 3,000) × 20 = $4,000 favourable.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare a statement reconciling the budgeted profit with the actual profit.
parts.answer:
Reconciliation of budgeted profit with actual profit
                                    Fav $     Adv $         $

Sales price                                   9,600
Sales volume                        5,200

Labour rate                                   1,875
Labour efficiency                   2,100
Variable overhead expenditure                   750
Variable overhead efficiency          450
Fixed overhead expenditure                    1,800
Fixed overhead volume               4,000
Totals                             13,060    15,525   (2,465)
Actual profit                                          75,535
parts.working: Budgeted profit 78,000 with all ten variances correctly signed (1); actual profit $75,535 (1).

practice.stem: A soap factory in Karachi has a standard of 5 kg of oil per carton at $2.40 per kg. Last month it made 1,800 cartons. The material usage variance was $1,080 adverse and the material price variance was $920 favourable. All material bought was used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual quantity of material used.
parts.answer: Standard quantity 1,800 × 5 = 9,000 kg; extra kg = 1,080 ÷ 2.40 = 450; actual = 9,450 kg
parts.working: M1 SQ; M1 variance ÷ standard price; A1 (adverse, so add).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual total cost of the material and the actual price per kg, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: AQ × SP = 9,450 × 2.40 = 22,680; favourable price variance so actual cost = 22,680 − 920 = $21,760; price = 21,760 ÷ 9,450 = $2.30 per kg
parts.working: M1 AQ × SP; M1 less favourable variance; A1.

practice.stem:
Rizvi Garden Products uses standard marginal costing. Standard per planter: price $60; materials 5 kg × $4 = $20; labour 1 hour × $12 = $12; variable overhead 1 hour × $6 = $6; standard contribution $22. Budget: 10,000 planters; fixed costs $150,000.
Actual: 9,400 planters made and sold at $62; materials 48,000 kg costing $187,200; labour 9,700 hours costing $119,310; variable overhead $56,000; fixed costs $153,000.

practice.stem: A shoe factory in Kasur has a standard of 3 labour hours per pair of boots at $11 per hour. In May it made 2,500 pairs. The labour efficiency variance was $1,650 favourable and the labour rate variance was $2,205 adverse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual labour hours worked.

parts.working: M1 SH; M1 favourable so fewer hours; A1.

parts.working: M1; M1 add adverse variance; A1.

practice.stem: Standard variable cost of one bicycle frame made in Lahore: materials 6 kg × $3.50 = $21.00; labour 1.25 hours × $18 = $22.50; variable overhead 1.25 hours × $4 = $5.00. In July 4,000 frames were made. Actual costs: materials 24,600 kg costing $84,870; labour 4,900 hours costing $90,650; variable overhead $20,090.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the material price and usage variances.

parts.label: b
