practice.stem: A furniture factory in Karachi reports an adverse material price variance and a favourable material usage variance for timber last month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible reasons for an adverse material price variance.
parts.answer: Any two: supplier raised prices / inflation; higher-quality material bought; loss of bulk discount; urgent purchase from a dearer supplier; exchange-rate changes on imports; standard set unrealistically low.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible reasons for a favourable material usage variance.
parts.answer: Any two: better-quality material with less waste; more skilled or careful workers; new or better-maintained machinery; improved production methods; standard set too loosely.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A clothing factory in Faisalabad bought cheaper fabric from a new supplier. Its variance report shows a favourable material price variance, an adverse material usage variance and an adverse labour efficiency variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the decision to buy cheaper fabric could cause each of these three variances.
parts.answer: Cheaper fabric lowers the price paid → favourable material price variance (1). Lower quality causes more cutting waste and rejects → adverse material usage variance (1). Workers take longer handling poor fabric and re-cutting → adverse labour efficiency variance (1). The variances are interrelated, so the purchasing decision should be judged on the net effect (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: The owner of a biscuit factory in Lahore is considering introducing standard costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to a business of using standard costing.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: it gives targets for planning and budgeting; variances show where performance differs from plan so managers can act (management by exception); it helps control costs and motivate staff; it makes inventory valuation and pricing easier.
parts.working: 1 mark benefit; 1 mark explanation, × 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of standard costing.
parts.answer: Any two: standards are costly and time-consuming to set; they quickly become out of date; less suitable for one-off or service work; may demotivate if unrealistic; focus on cost may harm quality.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The production manager of a shoe factory in Sialkot is setting new labour standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an ideal standard and an attainable standard.
parts.answer: An ideal standard assumes perfect conditions with no waste, idle time or breakdowns; an attainable standard allows for normal waste and inefficiency and can be achieved with reasonable effort.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which type of standard is more likely to motivate employees.
parts.answer: Attainable: workers can reach it with effort, so it is a realistic target; ideal standards are almost never met, so constant adverse variances demotivate.
parts.working: 1 mark choice; 1 mark reason.

practice.stem: A manager in a printing company in Lahore is pleased that his department has a large favourable labour rate variance because cheaper trainee staff were used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a favourable variance is not always good for the business.
parts.answer: A favourable variance may result from poor decisions elsewhere, e.g. cheaper materials (favourable price) causing waste and returns (1); it may mean the standard was set too loosely, hiding inefficiency (1); cost savings such as cutting maintenance or training may harm quality or future performance (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each point, max 3.

practice.stem: Three months ago Ahmed Electricals switched to a cheaper supplier of copper wire. Quarterly variances since the change: material price $6,400 favourable; material usage $4,100 adverse; labour efficiency $3,200 adverse. Customer returns of faulty cables have risen from 1% to 4% of sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the production director whether the company should continue to buy from the new supplier. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Net effect of the three variances = 6,400 − 4,100 − 3,200 = $900 adverse each quarter, plus higher returns, so the company should probably return to the old supplier or renegotiate quality. Either decision accepted if justified.
parts.working: Calculation (max 2): net variance 6,400 F − 4,100 A − 3,200 A = 900 adverse. Continue (max 3): lower price saves $6,400; waste may fall as workers get used to the material; supplier might improve quality; standards could be revised. Return (max 3): extra waste and labour time outweigh the saving; customer returns up from 1% to 4% damage reputation and future sales; overtime and morale problems. Decision (1).

practice.stem: A company selling school shoes in Quetta raised its price from the standard $40 to $45. Its variance report shows a favourable sales price variance of $27,000 and an adverse sales volume variance of $33,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the sales price variance and the sales volume variance might be linked.
parts.answer: Raising the price to $45 gives a favourable price variance on each unit sold (1). Customers are price-sensitive, so fewer units are sold than budgeted (1), causing an adverse sales volume variance (1). Other reasons for the volume fall, e.g. a competitor's new product, should also be considered before judging the sales manager (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: A company that makes ceiling fans in Gujrat uses standard costing and wants to hold managers responsible only for costs they control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of these variances, state the manager most likely to be responsible and give a reason: material price, material usage, labour rate, sales volume.
parts.answer: Material price – purchasing manager (chooses suppliers and negotiates prices). Material usage – production manager (controls waste in the factory). Labour rate – HR/personnel manager (sets pay and grades of staff). Sales volume – sales/marketing manager (responsible for the number of units sold).
parts.working: 1 mark each (manager with reason).

practice.stem: A juice factory in Multan had delays in fruit deliveries in August. Its variance report shows an adverse labour efficiency variance and an adverse fixed overhead volume variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a problem with materials could cause an adverse labour efficiency variance.
parts.answer: Poor-quality or late material (1) means workers waste time waiting, re-working or handling rejects (1), so more hours are worked than the standard allows for the output (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each step.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what an adverse fixed overhead volume variance shows.
parts.answer: Actual output was lower than budgeted output (1), so less fixed overhead was absorbed than budgeted — the fixed costs were spread over fewer units (1).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A textile mill in Karachi had an adverse labour rate variance of $1,800 last month; the standard labour cost of actual output was $45,000. The new manager wants employees to help set next year's standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour rate variance as a percentage of the standard labour cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which involving employees in setting standards may affect their behaviour.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: staff feel ownership so are more motivated to meet the standard; standards are more realistic because staff know the work; but staff may build in slack (easy standards) to earn bonuses; discussions take time and may cause conflict.
parts.working: 1 mark point; 1 mark explanation, × 2.

practice.stem: Siddiqui Tools makes 10,000 drills a year. Skilled workers are paid $18 per hour and take 2 hours per drill. Semi-skilled workers would be paid $14 per hour but would take 2.4 hours per drill, and material waste would rise by 3% of the $30 standard material cost per drill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should replace the skilled workers with semi-skilled workers. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Relevant cost per drill (labour plus extra material): skilled 2 × 18 = $36.00; semi-skilled 2.4 × 14 = $33.60 plus extra material 3% × 30 = $0.90 = $34.50. Saving $1.50 per drill, $15,000 a year. A justified decision either way.
parts.working: Calculations (max 3): skilled 36.00; semi-skilled 34.50; annual saving 15,000. For (max 2): lower costs improve profit; trained over time the semi-skilled workers may reach the standard time. Against (max 3): 20% more labour hours are needed per drill (2.4 v 2), so the same hours give about 17% less output (an extra 4,000 hours a year for 10,000 drills) – may not meet demand; quality and reputation risk; redundancy costs and staff morale; adverse labour efficiency and material usage variances against the current standards. Decision (1).

practice.stem: A factory in Gujrat makes 12,000 ceramic sinks a year. Each sink currently uses 4 kg of clay at $6.00 per kg and 1.5 labour hours at $15 per hour. A cheaper clay costs $5.20 per kg, but each sink would need 4.5 kg and 1.6 labour hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the material and labour cost per unit using (i) the current material and (ii) the cheaper material.
parts.working: M1 current; M1 new; A1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: If the standards are not changed, calculate the material price, material usage and labour efficiency variances that the cheaper material would cause for 12,000 units.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the company should change to the cheaper material.
parts.answer: No: the net effect is $10,800 adverse a year (= 12,000 × $0.90), so costs rise despite the lower price.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark reason using figures.

practice.stem:
Yousaf Plastics investigates any variance greater than 5% of the standard cost to which it relates. Last month's variances:
Variance                      Amount $  F/A  Standard cost $
Material price                   2,300    F           40,000
Material usage                     900    A           40,000
Labour rate                      3,100    A           62,000
Labour efficiency                4,400    A           62,000
Fixed overhead expenditure       1,200    F           30,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the management accountant which variances should be investigated. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Percentages of standard cost: Material price 5.75%; Material usage 2.25%; Labour rate 5.00%; Labour efficiency 7.10%; Fixed overhead expenditure 4.00%. Under the 5% rule investigate material price (5.75%) and labour efficiency (7.10%); labour rate is exactly 5% so borderline.
parts.working: Calculations (max 3): percentages as shown. Points (max 3): material price is favourable but large — may be linked to cheaper material, and to the adverse labour efficiency (poor material slows workers); labour rate at 5% and adverse — check if it is a trend; small variances such as material usage cost more to investigate than they would save; consider trends over several months, controllability and cost of investigation versus benefit. Clear conclusion (1).

practice.stem: Malik Packaging installed a new cutting machine seven months ago. Since then the material usage variance has been adverse by about 8% of standard material cost every month. Production staff say the machine design wastes more card than the old one and complain that their bonus, which depends on meeting the standard, is never paid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether the material usage standard should be revised. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A justified recommendation, e.g. revise the standard to an attainable level, because the adverse variance is permanent (caused by the new machine) and is demotivating staff, while keeping a target that encourages improvement.
parts.working: Revise (max 4): adverse usage variance of about 8% every month for six months shows the standard is out of date; the cause (new machine design) is outside workers' control; unrealistic standards demotivate and make variance reports useless; budgets and prices based on the old standard understate costs. Do not revise (max 3): the machine may be adjusted or staff trained to reduce waste; revising too easily builds in inefficiency; cost and time of setting new standards; supplier may be responsible. Decision (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The partners of Hilltop Traders, Quetta, agree to value goodwill at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years. Profits were: year 1 $84,000; year 2 $96,000; year 3 $105,000.
What is the value of goodwill?
A $95,000
B $190,000
C $210,000
D $285,000
parts.working: Average profit = (84,000 + 96,000 + 105,000) ÷ 3 = $95,000; × 2 years = $190,000. A is the average only; C uses the latest year; D is the total of three years.

practice.stem:
Jabbar and Sons, a partnership of opticians in Peshawar, made these profits:
Year  Profit $  Weight
2023    72,000       1
2024    81,000       2
2025    90,000       3
The partners agree to value goodwill at three years' purchase of the weighted average profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weighted average profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of goodwill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two factors that may give a business goodwill.
parts.answer: For example: a good reputation; a loyal customer base.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: reputation; loyal customers; good location; skilled staff; brand name; good supplier relationships.

practice.stem: Usman, Vania and Waleed are partners sharing profits 2:2:1. Waleed retires on 30 June 2026. Goodwill is valued at $45,000. The partners decide that a goodwill account will be opened and kept in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the goodwill. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $    Cr $
Goodwill          45,000
Capital – Usman           18,000
Capital – Vania           18,000
Capital – Waleed           9,000
parts.working: Dr goodwill 45,000 (B1); Cr capitals in the old ratio 2:2:1 (M1): 18,000, 18,000, 9,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many businesses do not keep a goodwill account in the books after a change of partners.
parts.answer: Goodwill generated inside the business cannot be measured reliably, so IAS 38 does not allow internally generated goodwill to be recognised as an asset; it is written off to the partners' capital accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark: value is subjective / cannot be measured reliably / can change quickly. 1 mark: accounting standards (IAS 38) / prudence do not allow internally generated goodwill to be shown.

practice.stem: Kamran and Laila run a bakery in Islamabad, sharing profits equally. On 1 April 2026 Mehwish is admitted for a one-quarter share of profits; Kamran and Laila will share the remaining three-quarters equally. Goodwill is valued at $72,000 and is not to be recorded in the books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an adjustment for goodwill is needed when a new partner is admitted.
parts.answer: The old partners built up the goodwill; without an adjustment the new partner would share in the value they created, so the old partners must be compensated for the share they give up.
parts.working: 1 mark: goodwill was created by the existing partners. 1 mark: new partner gains a share of it / old partners lose part of their share and must be compensated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net amount credited or debited to each partner's capital account for goodwill.
parts.answer: Kamran credit $9,000; Laila credit $9,000; Mehwish debit $18,000.
parts.working: New ratio K:L:M = 3/8 : 3/8 : 2/8. Kamran: +36,000 created − 27,000 written off = +9,000 (B1). Laila: same, +9,000 (B1). Mehwish: −72,000 × 1/4 = −18,000 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prepare a single journal entry to record the net goodwill adjustment. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $   Cr $
Capital – Mehwish  18,000
Capital – Kamran           9,000
Capital – Laila            9,000
parts.working: Dr Mehwish 18,000 (1); Cr Kamran 9,000 and Laila 9,000 (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ali and Bilal share profits 3:2. Chand is admitted and the new ratio is Ali 2, Bilal 2, Chand 1. Goodwill is valued at $60,000 but no goodwill account is to remain in the books.
What is the net effect of the goodwill adjustment on Ali's capital account?
A credit $12,000
B debit $12,000
C credit $36,000
D no change
parts.answer: A credit $12,000
parts.working: Goodwill created in old ratio: Ali credited 3/5 × 60,000 = 36,000. Written off in new ratio: Ali debited 2/5 × 60,000 = 24,000. Net credit $12,000. D is Bilal's position (24,000 − 24,000 = 0), not Ali's.

practice.stem:
Sana and Tariq run a furniture business in Faisalabad, sharing profits and losses 3:2. Their capital account balances on 31 December 2025 were Sana $80,000 and Tariq $60,000.
On 1 January 2026 Umar was admitted as a partner and paid $50,000 into the business bank account as his capital. It was agreed that:
1 land would be revalued from $120,000 to $150,000
2 inventory would be written down by $4,000
3 goodwill would be valued at $45,000; no goodwill account would be kept in the books
4 the new profit sharing ratio would be Sana 2, Tariq 2, Umar 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the revaluation account.
parts.answer:
Revaluation account                      $
Dr
Inventory                            4,000
Profit on revaluation: Sana (3/5)   15,600
                       Tariq (2/5)  10,400
                                    30,000
Cr
Land                                30,000
                                    30,000
parts.working: Dr inventory 4,000 (1); Cr land 30,000 and profit 26,000 shared 3:2, Sana 15,600 and Tariq 10,400 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the partners' capital accounts in columnar form, showing the balances carried down on 1 January 2026.
parts.answer:
Capital accounts                 Sana   Tariq    Umar
Dr
Goodwill written off (2:2:1)   18,000  18,000   9,000
Balance c/d                   104,600  70,400  41,000
                              122,600  88,400  50,000
Cr
Balance b/d                    80,000  60,000
Bank                                           50,000
Revaluation profit             15,600  10,400
Goodwill created (3:2)         27,000  18,000
                              122,600  88,400  50,000
parts.working: B1 opening balances and bank; B1 revaluation profit 15,600/10,400; B1 goodwill created 27,000/18,000; B1 goodwill written off 18,000/18,000/9,000; B1 each correct closing balance (max 2): Sana 104,600, Tariq 70,400, Umar 41,000.

practice.stem: Rafay, Saad and Zoya are partners in a software firm in Lahore, sharing profits 4:3:3. Saad retires on 31 August 2026. Rafay and Zoya will continue, sharing profits equally. Goodwill is valued at $90,000. No goodwill account is to appear in the books; the adjustment is to be made through the capital accounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net goodwill adjustment for each partner, stating whether it is a debit or a credit.
parts.answer: Rafay debit $9,000; Zoya debit $18,000; Saad credit $27,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the adjustment, including a narrative.
parts.answer:
Dr $    Cr $
Capital – Rafay   9,000
Capital – Zoya   18,000
Capital – Saad           27,000
Narrative: adjustment for Saad's share of goodwill on his retirement; no goodwill account kept.
parts.working: Debits (1); credit (1); narrative (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Xavier and Yusra share profits 3:2. Zain is admitted and the new ratio is Xavier 2, Yusra 1, Zain 1. On admission the building is revalued upwards by $40,000 and machinery downwards by $15,000.
What is the entry in Yusra's capital account for the revaluation?
A credit $6,250
B credit $10,000
C credit $16,000
D debit $6,000
parts.answer: B credit $10,000
parts.working: Net revaluation profit 25,000 belongs to the old partners in the old ratio: Yusra 2/5 × 25,000 = 10,000 credit. A wrongly uses the new ratio (1/4); C ignores the machinery loss.

practice.stem:
Farah, Gul and Hina are partners in a travel agency in Karachi, sharing profits and losses 2:2:1. Hina retired on 31 December 2025. On that date the balances were:
Capital accounts: Farah $70,000; Gul $60,000; Hina $40,000
Current accounts: Farah $5,000 credit; Gul $3,000 debit; Hina $6,500 credit
It was agreed that:
1 premises would be revalued upwards by $25,000 and office equipment downwards by $5,000
2 goodwill was valued at $50,000; no goodwill account would remain in the books
3 Hina's current account would be transferred to her capital account
4 Hina would receive $20,000 in cash immediately and the rest of the amount due to her would be transferred to a loan account
5 Farah and Gul would share profits equally in future.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the capital accounts of Farah, Gul and Hina in columnar form on 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Capital accounts             Farah     Gul    Hina
Dr
Goodwill written off (1:1)  25,000  25,000
Bank                                        20,000
Hina loan account                           40,500
Balance c/d                 73,000  63,000
                            98,000  88,000  60,500
Cr
Balance b/d                 70,000  60,000  40,000
Current account                              6,500
Revaluation profit (2:2:1)   8,000   8,000   4,000
Goodwill created (2:2:1)    20,000  20,000  10,000
                            98,000  88,000  60,500
parts.working: Revaluation profit = 25,000 − 5,000 = 20,000 shared 2:2:1 (B1). Goodwill created 20,000/20,000/10,000 (B1); written off 25,000/25,000 (B1). Current account transfer 6,500 (B1). Bank 20,000 and loan 40,500 (B1). Closing balances Farah 73,000 and Gul 63,000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the balance on Hina's loan account.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the partners agreed to transfer part of the amount due to Hina to a loan account.
parts.answer: Paying the full amount in cash at once would leave the business short of working capital.
parts.working: Any one: protects the bank balance / liquidity; avoids selling assets; gives time to raise finance.

practice.stem:
Nadia and Omar own a wholesale rice business in Hyderabad, sharing profits 3:1. Their capitals on 31 March 2026 were Nadia $90,000 and Omar $50,000.
On 1 April 2026 Pervez was admitted. He brought in $30,000 cash and a delivery vehicle valued at $18,000 as his capital. It was agreed that:
1 premises would be revalued from $160,000 to $200,000
2 inventory, shown at $42,000, would be reduced to its net realisable value of $38,500
3 a provision for doubtful debts of 5% would be created on trade receivables of $30,000
4 goodwill was valued at $64,000; it would not be kept in the books
5 the new profit sharing ratio would be Nadia 2, Omar 1, Pervez 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the revaluation account.
parts.answer:

Inventory                      3,500
Provision for doubtful debts   1,500
Profit: Nadia (3/4)           26,250
        Omar (1/4)             8,750
                              40,000
Cr
Premises                      40,000
                              40,000
parts.working: Dr inventory 3,500 and provision 1,500 (1); Cr premises 40,000 (1); profit 35,000 shared 3:1, Nadia 26,250, Omar 8,750 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the capital accounts of all three partners in columnar form on 1 April 2026.
parts.answer:
Capital accounts                Nadia    Omar  Pervez
Dr
Goodwill written off (2:1:1)   32,000  16,000  16,000
Balance c/d                   132,250  58,750  32,000

                              164,250  74,750  48,000
parts.working: B1 Pervez's cash and vehicle; B1 revaluation profit; B1 goodwill created 48,000/16,000; B1 goodwill written off 32,000/16,000/16,000; B1 closing balances Nadia 132,250, Omar 58,750, Pervez 32,000.

practice.stem:
Daud and Esha have shared profits equally in their pharmacy in Multan. From 1 July 2026 they agree to share profits Daud 3, Esha 2, because Daud will work full time. Capital balances on 30 June 2026: Daud $50,000; Esha $45,000.
It is agreed that goodwill is worth $80,000 (not to be kept in the books) and that the shop property is revalued upwards by $20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a goodwill adjustment is needed even though no partner is joining or leaving.
parts.answer: Daud gains an extra 1/10 share of future profits, including profits from goodwill built up jointly; Esha gives up that share and must be compensated by Daud.
parts.working: 1 mark: change in ratio transfers a share of goodwill. 1 mark: the gaining partner compensates the losing partner.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance on each partner's capital account after the adjustments.

practice.stem: Imran retired from a partnership of engineers in Rawalpindi on 31 December 2025. The amount due to him was $84,000. He received $24,000 in cash on that date. The balance became a loan, repaid in three equal annual instalments starting on 31 December 2026. Interest at 8% per annum on the balance outstanding during each year is paid with each instalment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of each loan instalment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total amount (instalment plus interest) paid to Imran on 31 December 2026, 2027 and 2028.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage, for the continuing partners, of this arrangement compared with paying Imran in full immediately.
parts.answer: Advantage: cash outflow is spread, protecting liquidity. Disadvantage: interest of $9,600 in total is payable and reduces profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for an advantage (liquidity / no need to borrow from a bank / no need to sell assets); 1 mark for a disadvantage (interest cost / fixed commitment / Imran remains a creditor).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Jamil and Kiran share residual profits equally. Profit for the year was $96,000. Jamil receives a salary of $12,000. Interest on capital is 6% per annum; capitals are Jamil $50,000 and Kiran $70,000.
What is Kiran's total share of the profit?
A $38,400
B $42,600
C $48,000
D $48,600
parts.working: Interest on capital: Jamil 3,000, Kiran 4,200. Residual = 96,000 − 12,000 − 7,200 = 76,800; half = 38,400. Kiran's total = 4,200 + 38,400 = 42,600. A omits interest on capital; D forgets to deduct Jamil's salary.

practice.stem:
Waqas and Yasmin run a printing business in Karachi, sharing residual profits 2:1. For the year ended 30 June 2026 the profit for the year was $65,000. The partnership agreement provides for:
• interest on capital at 5% per annum: capitals Waqas $80,000 and Yasmin $40,000
• a salary for Yasmin of $9,000 a year
• interest on drawings: Waqas $600 and Yasmin $400 for the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the appropriation account for the year ended 30 June 2026.
parts.answer:
Appropriation account                   $         $
Profit for the year                          65,000
Add interest on drawings: Waqas       600
                           Yasmin     400     1,000
                                             66,000
Less interest on capital: Waqas     4,000
                          Yasmin    2,000
Less salary: Yasmin                 9,000  (15,000)
Residual profit                              51,000
Share of profit: Waqas (2/3)       34,000
                 Yasmin (1/3)      17,000    51,000
parts.working: B1 interest on drawings added; B1 interest on capital 4,000/2,000; B1 salary 9,000; B1 residual 51,000; B1 shares 34,000/17,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Yasmin's salary is shown in the appropriation account and not in the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: A partner is an owner, not an employee; her salary is a way of sharing profit, so it is an appropriation of profit rather than an expense of earning it.
parts.working: 1 mark: partner is an owner / not an employee. 1 mark: salary is a division of profit, not a cost of running the business.

practice.stem: Laraib is a partner in a beauty salon in Islamabad. For the year ended 31 December 2025: current account balance 1 January 2025 $1,400 debit; interest on capital $2,500; salary $8,000; share of residual profit $21,300; cash drawings $30,000; interest on drawings $750; goods taken for own use $1,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare Laraib's current account for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer:
Current account – Laraib       $
Dr
Balance b/d                1,400
Drawings – cash           30,000
Drawings – goods           1,600
Interest on drawings         750
                          33,750
Cr
Interest on capital        2,500
Salary                     8,000
Share of profit           21,300
Balance c/d                1,950
                          33,750
Balance b/d 1 January 2026: $1,950 debit
parts.working: B1 opening debit balance; B1 drawings, goods and interest on drawings on debit side; B1 credits; B1 closing debit balance 1,950 b/d.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a debit balance on a partner's current account shows.
parts.answer: The partner has withdrawn more than her share of profits and other entitlements, so she owes the partnership money.
parts.working: 1 mark: drawings exceed profit entitlement. 1 mark: partner owes the business / reduces capital employed.

practice.stem: A partnership keeps fixed capital accounts and separate current accounts for each partner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two items that are credited to a partner's current account.
parts.answer: Interest on capital; share of residual profit.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: interest on capital; partner's salary; share of profit; commission to partner.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items that are debited to a partner's current account.
parts.answer: Drawings; interest on drawings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: cash drawings; goods taken for own use; interest on drawings; share of a loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage of keeping fixed capital accounts with separate current accounts.
parts.answer: Fixed capitals show the long-term investment agreed in the agreement, while the current account shows clearly how profit entitlements compare with drawings each year.
parts.working: 1 mark: capital stays at the agreed amount / used for interest on capital. 1 mark: current account shows profit share versus drawings / easy to see overdrawing.

practice.stem:
Nabeel is a partner in a clothing shop in Sialkot. The partnership agreement charges interest on drawings at 10% per annum. The financial year ends on 31 December 2025. Nabeel's drawings were:
1 March 2025  $6,000
1 September 2025  $9,000
1 December 2025  $12,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest on Nabeel's drawings for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a partnership agreement may charge interest on drawings.
parts.answer: It discourages partners from withdrawing cash early or excessively, and it is fair to partners who leave their money in the business, because those who draw early benefit from the use of business funds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two points: discourages drawings / protects working capital; fairness between partners who draw different amounts or at different times.

practice.stem: Hamid and Iqra share profits 3:2 in a mobile phone repair business in Gujranwala. Hamid also lent the business $30,000 at 6% per annum interest for the whole year. No interest has been paid. A trainee bookkeeper calculated the profit for the year as $48,600 and then showed the loan interest in the appropriation account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why interest on Hamid's loan should not be shown in the appropriation account.
parts.answer: The loan is not part of Hamid's capital; the business owes it as a lender would be owed, so the interest is an expense charged in the statement of profit or loss before profit is calculated.
parts.working: 1 mark: loan is a liability / Hamid acts as a lender. 1 mark: interest is an expense in the statement of profit or loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the correct profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the correct profit.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate Hamid's total income from the business for the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a partnership, which change would reduce the residual profit shared between the partners?
A an increase in the rate of interest charged on drawings
B an increase in the salaries paid to partners
C repayment of a loan made to the business by a partner
D a decrease in the rate of interest allowed on capital
parts.answer: B an increase in the salaries paid to partners
parts.working: Salaries are deducted before residual profit, so higher salaries reduce it. A and D increase residual profit; C removes loan interest expense, raising profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Parvez, Qasim and Rubina share profits 3:2:1. Rubina is guaranteed a minimum share of $15,000; any shortfall is borne by Parvez and Qasim in their profit sharing ratio. The residual profit for the year is $72,000.
What is Parvez's final share of the residual profit?
A $34,200
B $34,500
C $36,000
D $33,000
parts.working: Rubina's share = 72,000 × 1/6 = 12,000; shortfall 3,000 borne 3:2, Parvez 1,800. Parvez = 72,000 × 3/6 − 1,800 = 34,200. B shares the shortfall equally; D charges it all to Parvez.

practice.stem:
Ella, Faisal and Ghazala run a catering business in Dubai, sharing residual profits equally. Interest on capital is 5% per annum on capitals of Ella $60,000, Faisal $40,000 and Ghazala $20,000. Faisal receives a salary of $6,000. Ghazala, a new partner, is guaranteed that her total income from the partnership (interest on capital plus share of profit) will be at least $20,000; any shortfall is borne by Ella and Faisal in the ratio 3:2.
Profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 was $54,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the appropriation account for the year ended 31 March 2026.
parts.answer:
Appropriation account                           $         $
Profit for the year                                  54,000
Interest on capital: Ella                   3,000
                     Faisal                 2,000
                     Ghazala                1,000
Salary: Faisal                              6,000  (12,000)

Share of profit: Ella (14,000 − 3,000)     11,000
                 Faisal (14,000 − 2,000)   12,000
                 Ghazala (14,000 + 5,000)  19,000    42,000
parts.working: B1 interest on capital; B1 salary; B1 residual 42,000 and equal shares 14,000; M1 Ghazala's total 1,000 + 14,000 = 15,000, shortfall 5,000; A1 shortfall split Ella 3,000, Faisal 2,000; A1 final shares 11,000/12,000/19,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why a partner might be offered a guaranteed minimum income.
parts.answer: To attract a new partner with skills or contacts to join; to give a junior partner a secure income while the business grows.
parts.working: 1 mark each: attract/keep a partner with valuable skills; security of income for a new or junior partner; compensation for giving up a salaried job; reward for bringing customers.

practice.stem:
Junaid and Khadija share residual profits 3:2. After interest on capital (Junaid $3,000, Khadija $2,000) the draft profit for the year ended 30 September 2026 of $72,000 had been appropriated, giving residual shares of Junaid $40,200 and Khadija $26,800. The following errors were then found:
1 closing inventory had been overstated by $4,500
2 electricity owing of $1,200 had not been recorded
3 goods costing $2,000 taken by Khadija for her own use had not been recorded
4 depreciation of $3,000 on a vehicle had been omitted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
$
Draft profit                                    72,000
Less inventory overstated                      (4,500)
Less electricity accrued                       (1,200)
Add goods taken by Khadija (reduce purchases)    2,000
Less depreciation                              (3,000)
Corrected profit                                65,300
parts.working: 1 mark each for correct direction of items 1–4 with total 65,300 (max 4; deduct if total wrong).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected residual profit shares.
parts.answer: Junaid $36,180; Khadija $24,120.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overall effect of the corrections on Khadija's current account balance.
parts.answer: Reduced by $4,680.
parts.working: Share of profit falls 26,800 − 24,120 = 2,680 (M1); drawings rise 2,000; total reduction 4,680 (A1).

practice.stem:
Mansoor and Nida share residual profits equally in a courier business in Peshawar. For the year ended 31 March 2026:
                              Mansoor $    Nida $
Interest on capital               3,600     2,400
Salary                                     10,000
Interest on drawings                500       300
Current account 1 April 2025   2,000 Cr  1,500 Dr
Drawings                         28,000    35,000
Mansoor's current account balance on 31 March 2026 was $4,100 credit. The profit for the year was mislaid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Mansoor's share of the residual profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.
parts.working: Residual = 2 × 27,000 = 54,000 (B1); profit = 54,000 + 6,000 interest on capital + 10,000 salary (M1) − 800 interest on drawings = 69,200 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Nida's current account balance on 31 March 2026.
parts.answer: $2,600 credit

practice.subtopic: Partnership statement of profit or loss
practice.stem:
The draft profit for the year of a partnership running a tuition centre in Lahore was $58,400. The following items were then discovered:
1 rent of $1,200 paid in advance had been charged as an expense of this year
2 wages of $900 owing at the year end had been omitted
3 interest of $1,500 on a partner's loan had been shown in the appropriation account
4 depreciation of $4,000 on furniture had not been charged.

$
Draft profit                      58,400
Add rent prepaid                   1,200
Less wages accrued                 (900)
Less interest on partner's loan  (1,500)
Less depreciation                (4,000)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items that appear in a partnership appropriation account but not in a sole trader's statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Interest on capital; partners' salaries.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: interest on capital; partners' salaries; interest on drawings; share of residual profit.

practice.subtopic: Partnership statement of profit or loss

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is charged in a partnership's statement of profit or loss rather than in its appropriation account?
A interest on partners' capital
B interest on a loan made to the business by a partner
C salary paid to a partner
D interest charged on partners' drawings
parts.answer: B interest on a loan made to the business by a partner
parts.working: A partner's loan is a liability of the business, so its interest is an expense. A, C and D are ways of dividing profit between the owners and belong in the appropriation account.

practice.stem: Asma and Bushra started a partnership without a written partnership agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four provisions of the Partnership Act 1890 that will apply to their partnership.
parts.answer: Profits and losses are shared equally; no interest is allowed on capital; no interest is charged on drawings; no salaries are paid to partners; interest of 5% per annum is paid on partners' loans.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the five provisions listed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the partners should draw up a written partnership agreement.
parts.answer: So that terms such as profit sharing, salaries and interest suit their different capital and work contributions, and to avoid disputes later.
parts.working: 1 mark: tailor terms to contributions (capital, time, skills). 1 mark: reduce disputes / clear rules for admission, retirement, dissolution.

practice.stem: Shoaib and Tahira formed a partnership without any agreement. Shoaib contributed capital of $60,000 and also lent the business $20,000 at the start of the year. Tahira contributed capital of $40,000 and works full time in the business; Shoaib works part time. The profit for the year before any interest on Shoaib's loan was $50,000. Shoaib claims profits should be shared in the ratio of capitals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the profit as required by the Partnership Act 1890.
parts.answer: Shoaib $24,500; Tahira $24,500.
parts.working: Loan interest 5% × 20,000 = 1,000 is an expense (M1); profit 49,000 (A1) shared equally 24,500 each (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Shoaib's total income from the business for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether Shoaib's claim is valid.
parts.answer: No. Without an agreement the Act requires equal sharing of profits, whatever the capital contributed.
parts.working: 1 mark: claim not valid. 1 mark: the Act applies when there is no agreement – equal shares, no interest on capital.

practice.stem: Ittehad Steel Fabricators, Lahore, makes gates, railings and window grilles in batches. It is introducing activity based costing (ABC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a cost driver.
parts.answer: The factor that causes the cost of an activity to be incurred, so that the cost changes with the level of that factor.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Suggest a suitable cost driver for each of the following activities.
(i) setting up machines for a new batch
(ii) buying materials from suppliers
(iii) inspecting finished goods
(iv) despatching goods to customers
parts.answer: (i) number of set-ups (ii) number of purchase orders (iii) number of inspections (iv) number of despatches/deliveries
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Mehran Pharmaceuticals has identified the following activities for the coming year.
Activity                  Cost $  Expected driver volume
Machine set-ups           84,000             120 set-ups
Quality inspection        56,000       1,400 inspections
Material handling         37,500         2,500 movements

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Machine set-ups $700 per set-up; quality inspection $40 per inspection; material handling $15 per movement

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a cost pool.
parts.answer: The total of all the overhead costs caused by one activity, collected together before being charged to products using the cost driver rate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A company uses these cost driver rates: $700 per set-up, $40 per inspection and $15 per material movement. Product K needs 18 set-ups, 260 inspections and 400 material movements to make 5,000 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total overhead charged to product K using ABC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of product K.

practice.stem: The purchasing department of Faisalabad Garments has annual costs of: staff salaries $38,000; stationery and postage $2,400; purchasing software $5,600. It expects to place 920 purchase orders in the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for the purchasing activity.
parts.answer: $50 per purchase order

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the purchasing cost charged to the hospital uniforms product line, which needed 140 purchase orders.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the number of purchase orders is a more suitable basis than direct labour hours for charging purchasing costs.
parts.answer: Purchasing cost is caused by the number of orders placed, not by how long workers spend making the products.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A commercial bank in Lahore wants to find the cost of each service it provides to customers.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Suggest a suitable cost driver for each of the following activities in the bank.
(i) processing loan applications
(ii) operating cash machines (ATMs)
(iii) handling customer complaints
parts.answer: (i) number of loan applications (ii) number of ATM transactions/withdrawals (iii) number of complaints received
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why activity based costing is useful to a service business such as a bank.
parts.answer: Most of its costs are overheads, so ABC gives a more accurate cost of each service or customer, helping to set fees.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Al-Rawdah Printing, Riyadh, is pricing a job for a customer. Direct costs are $2,400. The job needs 2 press set-ups (rate $180 per set-up), 6 hours of design (rate $45 per design hour) and 3 deliveries (rate $60 per delivery).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead charged to the job using activity based costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the job and the price charged using a mark-up of 30%.
parts.answer: Total cost $3,210; price $4,173.00
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The owner of a spice-grinding and packing business in Hyderabad has heard about activity based costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of activity based costing.
parts.answer: Any two: overheads are collected in cost pools by activity; each pool has its own cost driver; costs are charged to products according to their use of each activity; recognises that some costs are driven by batches or complexity, not volume.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of a business for which activity based costing is likely to be most useful.
parts.answer: Any two: overheads are a large part of total cost; many different products or services; products differ greatly in complexity, batch size or support needed; a competitive market where accurate prices matter.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Medicare Tablets makes a vitamin product in batches of 250 packs. Each batch needs one set-up (rate $500) and two inspections (rate $40 each). Each pack needs 0.2 machine hours (rate $30 per hour).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ABC overhead cost per unit.
parts.working: Batch costs (500 + 2 × 40) ÷ 250 = 2.32; machine 0.2 × 30 = 6.00; total 8.32. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the batch-related overhead per unit would fall if batches of 500 units were made.
parts.answer: Set-up and inspection costs are incurred per batch, so they are spread over more units.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Karachi Sweets makes boxes of mithai (20,000 boxes a year) and celebration cakes (6,000 cakes a year). Its overheads have been analysed as follows.
Activity           Cost $  Cost driver           Mithai    Cakes
Batch set-ups      45,000  Number of set-ups         40      110
Quality checks     30,000  Number of checks         200      400
Packing            27,000  Packing hours          1,500    1,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Batch set-ups 45,000 ÷ 150 = $300 per set-up; Quality checks 30,000 ÷ 600 = $50 per check; Packing 27,000 ÷ 2,700 = $10 per packing hour
parts.working: 1 mark each rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per box of mithai and per cake.
parts.working: 1 mark each product total, 1 mark each cost per unit (to 2 decimal places).

practice.stem:
Chiniot Woodcraft makes 4,000 chairs and 1,000 tables a year. Direct costs per unit are: chair materials $22, labour $15; table materials $95, labour $48. Each chair takes 0.5 machine hours and each table 2 machine hours. Overheads are:
Activity              Cost $  Cost driver           Chairs   Tables
Machine operation     96,000  Machine hours          2,000    2,000
Machine set-ups       36,000  Number of set-ups         20       40
Order processing      18,000  Number of orders         100       50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per chair and per table using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Machine operation 96,000 ÷ 4,000 = $24 per machine hour; Machine set-ups 36,000 ÷ 60 = $600 per set-up; Order processing 18,000 ÷ 150 = $120 per order
Chairs: 2,000 × 24 + 20 × 600 + 100 × 120 = $72,000; ÷ 4,000 units = $18.00 per unit
Tables: 2,000 × 24 + 40 × 600 + 50 × 120 = $78,000; ÷ 1,000 units = $78.00 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark chairs total; 1 mark tables total; 1 mark per-unit figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost per chair and per table.
parts.answer: Chair $55; table $221
parts.working: Chair 22 + 15 + 18; table 95 + 48 + 78. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each product if the business adds a mark-up of 40% on total cost.
parts.answer: Chair $77.00; table $309.40
parts.working: Total cost × 1.4. 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Margalla Medical Centre, Islamabad, treats 6,000 outpatients and 1,200 day-surgery patients a year. It has analysed its support costs as follows.
Activity       Cost $  Cost driver             Outpatient  Day surgery
Admissions     72,000  Number of admissions         6,000        1,200
Theatre       240,000  Theatre hours                    0        1,600
