parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Admissions 72,000 ÷ 7,200 = $10 per admission; Theatre 240,000 ÷ 1,600 = $150 per theatre hour; Laboratory 54,000 ÷ 6,000 = $9 per test
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per patient for each type of patient.
parts.working: 1 mark each total, 1 mark each cost per patient.

practice.stem: Gulf Signs, Muscat, receives an order for 600 aluminium signs. Direct costs are $14.20 per sign. The order will need 3 set-ups, 12 inspections and 80 machine hours. ABC cost driver rates are $450 per set-up, $35 per inspection and $28 per machine hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost of the order using activity based costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the order.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the price to quote for the order, in total and per unit, using a mark-up of 25% on cost. Give the price per unit to the nearest cent.
parts.answer: $15,662.50 in total; $26.10 per unit
parts.working: M1 × 1.25; A1 both figures.

practice.stem: The set-up cost pool of Bolan Plastics is $63,000 and the cost driver rate is $350 per set-up. Product P used 48 set-ups. The total ABC overhead charged to product P was $41,300, made up of set-up costs, inspection costs at $25 per inspection, and machine-related costs of $15,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of set-ups expected in the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the set-up cost charged to product P.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of inspections used by product P.

practice.stem:
Sunrise Distributors, Peshawar, supplies two customers. Customer A is a supermarket chain; customer B is a group of small shops. Activity costs are $40 per order processed, $85 per delivery and $25 per return handled.
                Customer A  Customer B
Revenue $           60,000      40,000
Gross margin           25%         40%
Orders                  50         120
Deliveries              50         100
Returns                 10          30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total activity cost of serving each customer.
parts.answer: Customer A $6,500; customer B $14,050

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit earned from each customer after activity costs.
parts.answer: Customer A $8,500; customer B $1,950

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions the business could take to improve the profit from customer B.
parts.answer: Any two: set a minimum order size; charge for deliveries or for small orders; combine orders into fewer deliveries; reduce returns (better quality/packing); encourage online ordering.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Nairobi Business College runs a full-time course (300 students) and a weekend course (600 students). Fees are $900 per full-time student and $260 per weekend student. Tutor costs are $280 and $110 per student respectively. Other costs are:
Activity       Cost $  Cost driver             Full-time  Weekend
Enrolment      36,000  Number of enrolments          300      600
Classrooms    180,000  Room hours                  8,000    4,000
Assessment     42,000  Scripts marked              2,400    1,800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per student for each course using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Enrolment 36,000 ÷ 900 = $40 per enrolment; Classrooms 180,000 ÷ 12,000 = $15 per room hour; Assessment 42,000 ÷ 4,200 = $10 per script
Full-time: 300 × 40 + 8,000 × 15 + 2,400 × 10 = $156,000; ÷ 300 students = $520.00 per student
Weekend: 600 × 40 + 4,000 × 15 + 1,800 × 10 = $102,000; ÷ 600 students = $170.00 per student
parts.working: 1 mark each rate (3); 1 mark each cost per student (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss per student for each course.
parts.answer: Full-time $100 profit; weekend $20 loss
parts.working: Full-time 900 − 280 − 520; weekend 260 − 110 − 170. 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Pine View Hotel, Murree, sold 9,000 standard room-nights and 2,000 suite room-nights last year. Its support costs were:
Activity         Cost $  Cost driver            Standard    Suite
Housekeeping     96,000  Cleaning hours            6,000    2,000
Laundry          28,000  Kilograms washed         20,000   15,000
Reception        18,000  Number of check-ins       2,800      800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Housekeeping 96,000 ÷ 8,000 = $12 per cleaning hour; Laundry 28,000 ÷ 35,000 = $0.80 per kg; Reception 18,000 ÷ 3,600 = $5 per check-in
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per room-night for each type of room.
parts.working: 1 mark each total; 1 mark each cost per room-night.

practice.stem:
An online homeware retailer in Karachi has these activity cost rates: picking $0.40 per item, packing $1.20 per parcel, returns $3.50 per return, customer calls $2.00 per call. Monthly data:
                    Small orders  Large orders
Parcels (orders)          20,000         2,500
Items picked              20,000        20,000
Returns                      800           300
Customer calls             3,000         1,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total monthly activity cost of small orders and of large orders.
parts.answer: Small $40,800; large $15,050

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity cost per order for each type.
parts.answer: Small $2.04; large $6.02
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The retailer currently adds a flat handling charge of $3 to every order. Explain why this is unfair.
parts.answer: Large orders cost about three times as much to handle as small orders, so small-order customers pay more than their cost and large-order customers pay less than their cost (cross-subsidy).
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem:
Shahrah Motors, Lahore, assembles 10,000 City motorcycles (1.5 machine hours each, direct cost $410) and 3,000 Sport motorcycles (3 machine hours each, direct cost $690) a year. Overheads:
Activity                Cost $  Cost driver                     City    Sport
Purchasing             210,000  Number of purchase orders      1,200    1,800
Engineering changes     96,000  Number of changes                  8       24
Assembly line          480,000  Machine hours                 15,000    9,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ABC overhead cost per motorcycle for each model.
parts.answer:
Purchasing 210,000 ÷ 3,000 = $70 per order; Engineering changes 96,000 ÷ 32 = $3,000 per change; Assembly line 480,000 ÷ 24,000 = $20 per machine hour
City: 1,200 × 70 + 8 × 3,000 + 15,000 × 20 = $408,000; ÷ 10,000 units = $40.80 per unit
Sport: 1,800 × 70 + 24 × 3,000 + 9,000 × 20 = $378,000; ÷ 3,000 units = $126.00 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark each rate (3); 1 mark each per-unit figure (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each model using a mark-up of 25% on total cost.

practice.stem:
Lahore Leather makes 8,000 standard bags and 1,500 designer bags a year. Direct costs are $24.45 per standard bag and $89.60 per designer bag. Overheads are:
Activity            Cost $  Cost driver              Standard  Designer
Design              60,000  Design hours                  100       400
Cutting set-ups     42,000  Number of set-ups              30        70
Inspection          33,000  Number of inspections         900       600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each bag using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Design 60,000 ÷ 500 = $120 per design hour; Cutting set-ups 42,000 ÷ 100 = $420 per set-up; Inspection 33,000 ÷ 1,500 = $22 per inspection
Standard: 100 × 120 + 30 × 420 + 900 × 22 = $44,400; ÷ 8,000 units = $5.55 per unit
Designer: 400 × 120 + 70 × 420 + 600 × 22 = $90,600; ÷ 1,500 units = $60.40 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark product totals; 1 mark per-unit figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each bag needed to give a profit margin of 20% of selling price.
parts.answer: Standard $37.50; designer $187.50
parts.working: Total cost: standard 24.45 + 5.55 = 30.00; designer 89.60 + 60.40 = 150.00; divide by 0.8. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A competitor sells a similar designer bag for $175. Advise Lahore Leather whether it should reduce the price of its designer bag to $175. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: At $175 the margin would fall to (175 − 150) ÷ 175 = 14.29%, still a profit of $25 per bag. For: keeps market share; ABC shows the true cost is $150, so the bag is still profitable. Against: lower margin; the brand may justify a higher price (quality, design); other customers may expect discounts. Decision e.g. match the price only if volumes rise, or keep $187.50 and stress quality.
parts.working: 1 mark revised margin/profit; 1 mark points for and against; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem:
Penang Circuits makes three electronic modules. Annual data:
                                  X        Y        Z
Output (units)               10,000    5,000    2,000
Selling price per unit $         30       48      120
Direct costs per unit $          16       22       31
Overheads:
Activity               Cost $  Cost driver                 X        Y        Z
Set-ups               150,000  Number of set-ups          10       30       60
Component handling     90,000  Components handled      6,000    9,000   15,000
Testing               120,000  Test hours                500      700    1,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark each product (3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss per unit of each product.
parts.working: Price − direct cost − ABC overhead. 2 marks all correct, 1 mark for two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors what action they should take on product Z. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Z makes a loss of $8.50 per unit because it uses a large share of set-ups and testing for low output. Options: raise the price above $128.50 (break-even cost), make Z in larger batches to cut set-ups, or redesign to reduce testing. Before dropping Z, check which overheads would actually be saved and whether customers buy Z with X and Y. Decision: e.g. raise price/reduce set-ups rather than drop at once.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures and action(s); 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Swift Filters, Gujranwala, makes 24,000 oil filters a year in batches of 400. Each batch needs one machine set-up costing $600 and four inspections costing $45 each. Each filter costs $40 to make, and inventory holding costs are 15% a year of the average value held.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the batch-related cost per unit with the current batch size of 400 units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the batch-related cost per unit if the batch size is increased to 1,000 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving from the larger batch size, after allowing for higher inventory holding costs.
parts.working: Saving 46,800 − 18,720 = 28,080; extra holding cost: average inventory rises by (1,000 − 400) ÷ 2 = 300 units × $40 × 15% = 1,800; net 26,280. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the managers whether to increase the batch size. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes on cost grounds: a large net saving. But larger batches mean more finished inventory, a risk of obsolescence, less flexibility to meet changing customer orders and more storage space. Decision: increase, perhaps to an intermediate size, if demand is steady.
parts.working: 1 mark point(s) using figures/qualitative; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Ravi Valves wants to win a contract to supply 3,000 valves a year at a market price of $64 each, with a profit margin of at least 10% of selling price. Direct costs are $41 per valve. Production uses 24 set-ups at $900 each, 300 inspections at $30 each and 1,500 machine hours at $20 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current total cost per unit of the valve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum cost per unit that allows a 10% margin at a price of $64.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many set-ups must be eliminated if the cost reduction is to come entirely from set-ups.
parts.answer: 12 set-ups (from 24 to 12)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Discuss whether this reduction is realistic.
parts.answer: Halving set-ups means producing in batches twice as large, which increases inventory and holding costs and may not suit customer delivery schedules; set-up time might instead be cut by better tooling, or savings found in inspections.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: Seaside Snacks, Gwadar, uses ABC. Product Z has annual revenue of $180,000 and direct costs of $102,000. ABC charges it with set-up costs $36,000, inspection costs $18,000 and facility costs $40,000 (factory rent and insurance, shared on floor area). If Z were discontinued, all its set-up and inspection costs would be saved, but the facility costs would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit or loss of product Z using activity based costing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on the company's total profit if product Z is discontinued.
parts.answer: Profit falls by $24,000
parts.working: Lost revenue 180,000; saved direct costs 102,000, set-ups 36,000 and inspections 18,000; facility costs continue. 180,000 − 156,000 = 24,000 reduction. M1 avoidable costs; M1 facility cost excluded; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to discontinue product Z. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Do not discontinue on these figures: Z contributes $24,000 towards facility costs that would still be paid. Consider raising its price or reducing set-ups. Also consider whether the space could be used for a more profitable product and the effect on customers who buy other products.
parts.working: 1 mark use of the figure; 1 mark other factor; 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Zamzam Bottling budgeted set-up costs of $120,000 for 200 set-ups and inspection costs of $60,000 for 1,500 inspections. Actual results were: 215 set-ups costing $126,500; 1,420 inspections costing $61,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted cost driver rate for each activity.
parts.answer: Set-ups $600; inspections $40
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead absorbed and the amount over- or under-absorbed for each activity.
parts.answer: Set-ups: absorbed $129,000, over-absorbed $2,500. Inspections: absorbed $56,800, under-absorbed $4,200
parts.working: 215 × 600; 1,420 × 40. 1 mark each figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net effect on profit of the over- and under-absorption.
parts.answer: Net under-absorption $1,700, reducing profit

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the under-absorption of inspection costs.
parts.answer: Actual inspection costs were higher than budgeted (e.g. higher inspector wages) while fewer inspections were carried out than budgeted.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Kohinoor Paints sells 12,000 tins a year at $18 each to a hardware chain, delivered in 12 monthly deliveries. The chain now wants weekly deliveries (52 a year) with no change in total volume or price. ABC rates: delivery $140 per delivery; order processing $35 per order (one order per delivery); quality certificate $20 per delivery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual activity cost of supplying the customer under the present arrangement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual activity cost if the customer's request is accepted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the increase in price per unit needed to keep the profit from this customer unchanged.
parts.answer: $0.65 per unit (price rises to $18.65)
parts.working: Extra cost 7,800 ÷ 12,000 units. M1 A1.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the company how to respond to the customer's request.
parts.answer: Accept only if the price rises by about $0.65 a unit (or a delivery charge of $195 per extra delivery is made); otherwise profit falls by $7,800. Consider the value of keeping a large customer and whether deliveries can be combined with other customers' routes.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures; 1 mark justified advice.

practice.stem: Quetta Woollens absorbs all its production overheads using a single rate per direct labour hour. The finance director suggests changing to activity based costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of activity based costing compared with traditional absorption costing.
parts.answer: Any two explained: more accurate product costs because overheads are charged according to what causes them; better pricing decisions, avoiding over-pricing high-volume and under-pricing low-volume products; identifies costly activities that can be controlled or reduced; better information for decisions about products and customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each advantage, 1 mark each explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one limitation of activity based costing.
parts.answer: Any one: expensive and time-consuming to set up and run; choice of cost drivers can be subjective; some costs (e.g. factory rent) have no clear driver and still have to be apportioned; still based on historical/budgeted data.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Sargodha Agro Tools makes Alpha (20,000 units, 1 direct labour hour each) and Beta (2,000 units, 2 direct labour hours each). Total overheads are $240,000, analysed as:
Activity           Cost $  Cost driver            Alpha     Beta
Set-ups           100,000  Number of set-ups         10       40
Order handling     60,000  Number of orders          50      100
Machining          80,000  Machine hours         15,000    5,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using a single absorption rate per direct labour hour.
parts.answer: Alpha $10.00; Beta $20.00
parts.working: 240,000 ÷ 24,000 hours = $10 per hour; Alpha 1 hour, Beta 2 hours. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using activity based costing.
parts.working: 1 mark set-up and order rates; 1 mark machining rate; 1 mark each per-unit figure (2).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two methods give such different results.
parts.answer: Beta is made in small batches with many set-ups and orders, but uses few labour hours. Absorption on labour hours ignores this, so Beta is under-costed and high-volume Alpha over-costed.
parts.working: 1 mark: low-volume/complex product uses more batch-level activities; 1 mark: labour hours do not reflect this.

practice.stem: Tulip Cosmetics produced 10,000 units of a face cream and sold 8,000 units in its first year. There was no opening inventory. Production overhead per unit is $12 under traditional absorption costing and $9 under activity based costing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead included in the closing inventory under each method.
parts.answer: Absorption $24,000; ABC $18,000
parts.working: Closing inventory 10,000 − 8,000 = 2,000 units; × $12 and × $9. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on reported profit for the year of using ABC instead of absorption costing.
parts.answer: Profit is $6,000 lower under ABC, because $3 less overhead per unit is carried forward in closing inventory, so more of the year's overhead is charged against this year's profit.
parts.working: 1 mark amount; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State when the two methods would give the same profit.
parts.answer: When there is no change in the level of inventory (production equals sales), since total overhead charged is the same.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Spice Route, Karachi, sells 50,000 packs of ground spices (direct cost $2.00 each, 0.1 machine hours each) and 4,000 gift hampers (direct cost $30.00 each, 0.25 machine hours each). Overheads of $180,000 are currently absorbed on machine hours. An ABC analysis shows:
Activity             Cost $  Cost driver            Packs  Hampers
Set-ups              72,000  Number of set-ups         12       36
Packaging design     48,000  Design hours              20       60
Machining            60,000  Machine hours          5,000    1,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using the current machine-hour rate.
parts.answer: Packs $3.00; hampers $7.50
parts.working: 180,000 ÷ 6,000 hours = $30; packs 0.1 hours, hampers 0.25 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overhead cost per unit of each product using activity based costing.
parts.answer:
Set-ups 72,000 ÷ 48 = $1,500 per set-up; Packaging design 48,000 ÷ 80 = $600 per design hour; Machining 60,000 ÷ 6,000 = $10 per machine hour
Packs: 12 × 1,500 + 20 × 600 + 5,000 × 10 = $80,000; ÷ 50,000 units = $1.60 per unit
Hampers: 36 × 1,500 + 60 × 600 + 1,000 × 10 = $100,000; ÷ 4,000 units = $25.00 per unit
parts.working: 1 mark rates; 1 mark each per-unit figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each product under each method, using a mark-up of 30% on total cost.
parts.answer: Machine-hour rate: packs $6.50, hampers $48.75. ABC: packs $4.68, hampers $71.50
parts.working: 1 mark each method.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Discuss the consequences for the business of continuing to price using the machine-hour rate.
parts.answer: Packs are over-priced ($6.50 against an ABC-based $4.68), so the business may lose sales of its main product to competitors. Hampers are under-priced ($48.75 against $71.50), so they may sell well but could be making a loss. Overall profit may fall and wrong products be promoted.
parts.working: 1 mark packs over-priced/lost sales; 1 mark hampers under-priced/possible losses.

practice.stem: Indus Packaging plc makes 40 product lines, from high-volume standard cartons to small custom orders that need special design and many machine set-ups. Overheads are 60% of total cost and are absorbed using a single direct labour hour rate. The company has recently lost two large contracts for standard cartons to competitors that charged lower prices, while custom orders have increased. A new ABC system would cost $45,000 to install.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should replace absorption costing with activity based costing. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For ABC: overheads are 60% of total cost, so how they are charged matters; the 40 product lines vary greatly in batch size and the custom orders need many set-ups and design hours, so labour-hour absorption is likely to distort costs; recent loss of high-volume contracts suggests these are over-priced; ABC would give better pricing and show which customers and products are profitable.
Against ABC: the $45,000 system cost and staff time; drivers must be chosen and data collected continually; some costs (rent) still have to be apportioned; staff may resist change; benefits are not certain.
Decision: introduce ABC (perhaps first in the custom-order area) because the potential to correct pricing outweighs the cost.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 2 marks for points against (in context); 1 mark use of case data; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Jade River Toys transfers completed goods from its factory to its warehouse at production cost plus 20%. The production cost of goods completed for the year was $300,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the transfer price of goods completed and the factory profit.
parts.answer: Transfer price $360,000; factory profit $60,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a manufacturer may transfer goods to its trading account at a price above production cost.
parts.answer: To compare the factory's cost with the price of buying the goods from outside, so the factory's efficiency (and the trading section's) can be judged separately; it can also be used to reward factory managers.
parts.working: 1 mark compare with market/outside price; 1 mark measure factory performance separately/manager bonus.

practice.stem: Falcon Paints transfers goods to its trading account at production cost plus 20%. Finished goods inventory at the year end, valued at transfer price, was $48,000. The provision for unrealised profit brought forward was $6,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for unrealised profit at the year end.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the adjustment to the provision for the year and state its effect on profit.
parts.answer: Increase of $1,500, which reduces profit.
parts.working: 8,000 − 6,500 = 1,500 increase (M1); charged against profit (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the value of finished goods inventory in the statement of financial position.

practice.stem: Orchid Soaps, Ipoh, transfers its products from its factory to its shop at production cost plus a mark-up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'unrealised profit' in a manufacturing business.
parts.answer: The factory profit added to goods that are still in finished goods inventory at the year end; it has not been earned because the goods have not been sold to customers.
parts.working: 1 mark factory profit/mark-up in closing inventory; 1 mark not yet sold outside the business.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a provision for unrealised profit is needed.
parts.answer: Without it, inventory would be shown above cost and profit would include profit the business has made from 'selling to itself', so profit and assets would be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark inventory must be at cost (not above); 1 mark profit/assets would be overstated (realisation/prudence).

practice.stem: Sundarbans Honey processes and bottles honey in its own factory and sells it from its own warehouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define (i) production cost of goods completed and (ii) transfer price.
parts.answer: (i) The total factory cost (prime cost plus factory overheads, adjusted for work in progress) of goods finished in the period. (ii) The value at which finished goods are passed from the factory to the trading account (production cost plus factory profit, or market value).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where (i) the factory profit and (ii) the provision for unrealised profit are shown in the financial statements.
parts.answer: (i) Added to the gross profit in the statement of profit or loss (transferred from the manufacturing account). (ii) The change is charged/credited in the statement of profit or loss; the balance is deducted from finished goods inventory in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Tulip Bakeware transfers goods to its shop at production cost plus 25%. Finished goods at transfer price at the year end were $40,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for unrealised profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the provision is shown in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Deducted from finished goods inventory (shown at $32,000).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the accounting concept that says inventory should not be valued above cost, and explain it.
parts.answer: Prudence: assets and profits should not be overstated, so inventory is shown at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
parts.working: 1 mark prudence (accept realisation: profit is not recognised until goods are sold); 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem:
Indus Steel Fabricators transfers goods from its factory at production cost plus 20%. For the year:
                                                         $
Revenue                                            620,000
Goods transferred from factory at transfer price   480,000
Finished goods at start (at transfer price)         36,000
Finished goods at end (at transfer price)           42,000
Administration and selling expenses                 61,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the trading section of the statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer:
$         $
Revenue                                          620,000
Opening inventory of finished goods     36,000
Transfer from manufacturing account    480,000
                                       516,000
Closing inventory of finished goods   (42,000)
Cost of sales                                    474,000
Gross profit                                     146,000
parts.working: B1 opening inventory; B1 transfer 480,000; B1 cost of sales 474,000; B1 gross profit 146,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year of the business as a whole.

practice.stem: Andromeda Electronics transfers goods to its trading account at production cost plus 25%. At 31 December 2025, finished goods at transfer price were $62,500. The provision for unrealised profit at 1 January 2025 was $9,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for unrealised profit required at 31 December 2025 and the adjustment for the year.
parts.answer: Provision $12,500; increase $2,700

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the journal entry to record the adjustment. A narrative is required.
parts.answer:
Debit $   Credit $
Statement of profit or loss                                       2,700
  Provision for unrealised profit                                            2,700
Increase in provision for unrealised profit on finished goods
parts.working: B1 correct sides; B1 amount with narrative.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which accounting concept requires the provision.
parts.answer: Realisation: the factory profit included in the inventory has not been earned until the goods are sold to an outside customer, so it is removed (also prudence).
parts.working: 1 mark realisation (or prudence); 1 mark profit not realised until sold outside the business.

practice.stem: Finished goods held by Galaxy Shoes at the year end are valued at a transfer price of $75,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for unrealised profit if the factory profit is 25% of production cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the provision if the factory profit is 25% of the transfer price.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two answers are different.
parts.answer: A 25% margin on transfer price is the same as a 33⅓% mark-up on cost, so more of the transfer price is unrealised profit; in (a) profit is one-fifth of transfer price, in (b) one-quarter.
parts.working: 1 mark mark-up based on cost v margin based on transfer price; 1 mark fraction 25/125 v 25/100.

practice.stem: At 31 March 2026, Kalahari Leather had inventories of raw materials $23,400 and work in progress $17,800 (both at cost) and finished goods of $57,600 at transfer price. Goods are transferred at production cost plus 20%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for unrealised profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the inventory section of the current assets in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer:
$        $
Inventories:
  Raw materials                                    23,400
  Work in progress                                 17,800
  Finished goods                          57,600
  Less provision for unrealised profit   (9,600)   48,000
                                                   89,200
parts.working: B1 raw materials and WIP; B1 finished goods less provision; B1 total 89,200.

practice.stem: Highveld Bricks transfers completed goods to its trading account at market value. This year the production cost of goods completed was $360,000 and their market value was $432,000. There was no opening inventory of finished goods; closing finished goods at transfer price were $21,600.

parts.label: a

practice.stem: Mosaic Tiles transfers goods from its factory at production cost plus 15% (the same rate as last year). parts.answer: Factory profit is only an internal transfer; the provision removes the part still in unsold inventory, so the only profit recognised is that realised by selling to customers.

practice.stem: The factory manager of Nile Valley Juices receives a bonus of 5% of factory profit. Goods produced this year cost $450,000 and would have cost $540,000 to buy from another manufacturer. The manager proposes that goods should be transferred at production cost plus 30% instead of at market price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the factory profit (i) using the market price, (ii) using the proposed 30% mark-up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a market-price transfer is a better measure of the factory's performance.
parts.answer: It shows what the business would have paid an outside supplier, so the factory profit shows how much the factory saves by making the goods; a fixed mark-up gives a profit even if the factory is inefficient.
parts.working: 1 mark comparison with buying in; 1 mark mark-up hides inefficiency/rewards cost increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors which basis to use for the factory manager's bonus. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Market price: the 30% mark-up would raise the bonus by $2,250 (5% of $45,000) without any improvement, and rises automatically if costs rise; market price rewards real cost savings, though market prices can be hard to find and may change.
parts.working: For market price: fair, motivates cost control, comparable with outside. Against: market price may be hard to obtain/volatile; manager cannot control it. For mark-up: simple, certain; but rewards higher costs. 1 mark per point (max 3), 1 mark decision.

practice.stem: Orbit Bicycles makes 12,000 gear units a year. The production cost of goods completed is $504,000, which includes $96,000 of fixed factory overheads that would still be paid if the gear units were bought in. An outside supplier offers to sell identical units for $39 each.

parts.answer: Keep making it: buying at $39 costs $5 a unit more than the $34 that would be saved, i.e. $60,000 a year worse, even though $39 is below the full cost of $42.

parts.working: B1 11,400 − 9,000 debenture interest.

parts.answer: Interest paid may be shown either as an operating cash flow (it is a cost that enters profit) or as a financing cash flow (it is a cost of obtaining finance). The company must choose one and apply it consistently from year to year.

parts.working: B1 profit added; B1 transfer to reserve deducted; A1 30,000.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Financing activities

practice.stem: At 31 December 2026 Onyx Ltd had: cash at bank $14,200; cash in hand $650; a deposit of $20,000 made on 15 December 2026 that matures on 15 February 2027; a one-year deposit of $50,000 made on 1 October 2026; and an overdraft of $6,300 at another bank, repayable on demand and used for day-to-day cash management.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'cash and cash equivalents' as used in IAS 7.
parts.answer: Cash on hand and demand deposits, plus short-term highly liquid investments readily convertible to known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value (normally maturing within three months of acquisition); bank overdrafts repayable on demand that form part of cash management are deducted.
parts.working: 1 mark: cash and demand deposits; 1 mark: short-term liquid investments (≤ 3 months) / overdrafts included.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cash and cash equivalents at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: B1 2-month deposit included, overdraft deducted; B1 28,550.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the one-year deposit is treated.
parts.answer: It is not a cash equivalent because its maturity is more than three months from acquisition. Placing the $50,000 on deposit is an investing cash outflow.
parts.working: 1 mark: excluded – maturity over three months; 1 mark: investing outflow.

Redemption of 10% debentures ($200,000)

parts.working: B1 each line.

practice.stem: At 1 January 2026 Slate Ltd's statement of financial position showed tax payable of $30,000, the estimated tax for 2025. The tax actually paid for 2025 during 2026 was $32,500. The estimated tax for 2026 is $27,000; this is payable in 2027.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the opening and closing tax liabilities and the tax charge to calculate the tax paid in 2026.
parts.working: M1 30,000 + 29,500 − 27,000; A1 32,500 (agrees with the amount paid).

parts.label: c

During the year the company bought property, plant and equipment for $70,000 and sold investments for $12,000 (their carrying amount). The company classifies interest paid and tax paid as operating cash flows, interest and dividends received as investing cash flows, and dividends paid as financing cash flows.

parts.label: b

practice.stem:
Summary statements of cash flows of Marble Furniture Ltd:
                                             2026       2025
                                                $          $
Net cash from operating activities         38,000     92,000
Net cash used in investing activities   (145,000)   (30,000)
Issue of debentures                       100,000          –
Dividends paid                           (40,000)   (40,000)
At 31 December 2026 the company had a bank overdraft of $21,000. Profit for the year rose by 15% in 2026. Inventories and trade receivables both rose sharply during 2026, and the investing outflow was for a new factory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in cash and cash equivalents for 2026 and the balance at 1 January 2026.
parts.answer: Decrease of $47,000; balance at 1 January 2026 $26,000 (in hand)
parts.working: B1 net decrease 47,000; B1 opening 26,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the shareholders whether they should be concerned about the company's cash position. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Concerns: operating cash flow fell from $92,000 to $38,000 although profit rose 15% – profit is tied up in inventories and receivables (poor working-capital control); cash moved from $26,000 in hand to a $21,000 overdraft; dividends of $40,000 were paid that exceed operating cash; the new debentures add interest costs and must be repaid.
Reassurance: the outflow was mainly a one-off investment in a new factory, financed largely by long-term debentures (matching long-term finance to long-term assets); the factory should raise future profits and cash; the company is still profitable.
Decision: some concern – the investment is sensible, but management must improve credit control and inventory levels and may need to cut the dividend until operating cash flow recovers.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for concerns using figures; up to 2 marks for reassuring points; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three uses of a statement of cash flows to the shareholders and managers of a company.
parts.answer: Any three: shows how cash was generated and used; shows whether operating activities generate enough cash to pay interest, tax and dividends; helps assess liquidity and the ability to pay debts; shows how investment was financed; helps forecast future cash flows; cash figures are hard to manipulate and easy to compare.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a statement of cash flows is useful in addition to a statement of profit or loss.
parts.answer: Profit is based on the accruals concept and includes non-cash items such as depreciation and provisions, so a profitable business can still run out of cash. The statement of cash flows shows actual cash movements and liquidity.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit uses accruals/non-cash items; 1 mark: cash flows show liquidity/actual cash.

practice.stem: Ivory Ltd made a profit from operations of $120,000 for 2026, but its bank balance fell sharply. Its statement of cash flows shows: depreciation $26,000; increase in inventories $48,000; increase in trade receivables $61,000; decrease in trade payables $19,000; net cash from operating activities $18,000; net cash used in investing activities $200,000; net cash from financing activities $50,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in cash and cash equivalents for 2026.
parts.answer: Decrease of $132,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the figures, explain three reasons why Ivory Ltd's cash fell although it was profitable.
parts.answer:
1 Working capital absorbed cash: inventories rose by $48,000 and receivables by $61,000, so much of the profit is tied up in unsold goods and unpaid customer balances.
2 Suppliers were paid faster: payables fell by $19,000, another outflow not shown in profit.
3 Heavy investment: $200,000 was spent on non-current assets, only $50,000 of which was financed by long-term financing; the rest came from existing cash.
(Depreciation of $26,000 reduced profit without any cash outflow, which partly offset these.)
parts.working: For each of three reasons: 1 mark for identifying it and 1 mark for supporting it with figures from the question.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A delivery van was bought for $48,000. It is expected to be used for 6 years and then sold for $6,000. The straight-line method is used. What is the annual depreciation charge?
A $7,000
B $8,000
C $6,000
D $9,000
parts.working: (48,000 − 6,000) ÷ 6 = $7,000. $8,000 ignores the residual value; $9,000 wrongly adds the residual value to cost.

practice.stem: Hamza Printers, Lahore, bought a printing machine on 1 January 2024 for Rs 1,250,000. Installation cost Rs 50,000. The machine is expected to last 5 years and then be sold for Rs 100,000. The straight-line method is used and the financial year ends on 31 December.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual depreciation charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount of the machine at 31 December 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the accounting concept applied when depreciation is charged, and explain how it is applied.
parts.answer: Matching (accruals) concept: the cost of the machine is spread over the years in which it helps to earn revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming matching/accruals; 1 mark for explaining that the cost is charged against the revenue of the periods that benefit from the asset.

practice.stem: Rukhsana runs a tailoring workshop in Peshawar and owns sewing machines and a delivery motorcycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two causes of depreciation of non-current assets.
parts.answer: Wear and tear through use; obsolescence (also: passage of time, depletion).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: wear and tear; obsolescence (new technology/fashion); passage of time (e.g. lease); depletion (e.g. a quarry).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on the financial statements if a business does not provide for depreciation.
parts.answer: Expenses are understated so profit is overstated, and non-current assets are overstated in the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark profit overstated (expenses too low); 1 mark non-current assets/capital overstated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State three figures needed to calculate a straight-line depreciation charge.
parts.answer: Cost of the asset, expected residual value, expected useful life.
parts.working: All three for 2 marks; two correct for 1 mark.

practice.stem: A freelance designer in Dhaka buys a laptop for $2,400 and depreciates it at 30% per annum using the reducing balance method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for each of the first two years.
parts.answer: Year 1 $720; year 2 $504

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount at the end of year 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reducing balance method suits a laptop.
parts.answer: Laptops become obsolete quickly and lose most value in the first years, so a larger charge early matches the fall in value.
parts.working: 1 mark obsolescence/early loss of value; 1 mark matching charge with benefit/value.

practice.stem: Zainab Fashions, Faisalabad, bought shop fittings for Rs 360,000 on 1 July 2025. Its year ends on 31 December. Fittings are depreciated at 12.5% per annum on cost, calculated monthly.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.text: The owner says, 'Depreciation means I am saving money to replace the fittings.' Explain why this is not correct.
parts.answer: Depreciation is a non-cash expense: it reduces profit but no money is set aside, so cash is not saved unless the owner chooses to keep it in a separate fund.
parts.working: 1 mark non-cash/book entry; 1 mark no cash set aside/does not create a replacement fund.

C $15,000

parts.working: Year 1: 25% × 80,000 = 20,000 (CA 60,000). Year 2: 25% × 60,000 = 15,000 (CA 45,000). Year 3: 25% × 45,000 = $11,250. $20,000 is the straight-line style charge on cost; $33,750 is the carrying amount at the end of year 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business with a year end of 31 December bought equipment for $36,000 on 1 April 2025. Depreciation is charged at 20% per annum on cost, calculated on a monthly basis. What is the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2025?
A $5,400
B $7,200
C $1,800
D $6,000
parts.working: 20% × 36,000 = 7,200 per year; April to December = 9 months; 7,200 × 9/12 = $5,400. $7,200 charges a full year; $1,800 charges only 3 months.

practice.stem: SwiftDrop, a courier business in Nairobi, bought a delivery van for $40,000. It uses the reducing balance method at 40% per annum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for each of the four years using the reducing balance method.
parts.working: 40% × 40,000 = 16,000; 40% × 24,000 = 9,600; 40% × 14,400 = 5,760; 40% × 8,640 = 3,456. M1 for applying 40% to the carrying amount, A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The van will be worth $5,184 after four years. Calculate the annual charge if the straight-line method were used instead.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reducing balance method may be more suitable for the van.
parts.answer: A van loses more of its value in its early years, and repair costs rise as it gets older, so a high early charge gives a more even total cost each year.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: van loses most value early; carrying amount closer to resale value; maintenance rises with age so depreciation + repairs is more even; van used most heavily when new.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the effect on profit for year 1 of using the reducing balance method instead of the straight-line method.
parts.answer: Profit is $7,296 lower.
parts.working: 16,000 − 8,704 = 7,296 (M1); profit lower/decreases (A1).

parts.text: Calculate the depreciation charge for office equipment for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.working: Equipment held at year end at cost: 90,000 − 8,000 + 14,000 = 96,000 (M1 M1). 20% × 96,000 = $19,200 (A1). Full year on the new item, nothing on the item sold.

practice.stem: Lumière Bakery, in Montreal, bought an oven for $50,000 at the start of year 1. Its policy is to depreciate the oven at 20% per annum using the reducing balance method. Years 1 and 2 were correct, but in year 3 the bookkeeper charged 20% of the original cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the error on the profit for year 3.
parts.answer: Profit understated by $3,600
parts.working: Charged 10,000, should be 6,400; difference 3,600 (M1); profit understated (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of the error on the statement of financial position at the end of year 3.
parts.answer: Accumulated depreciation overstated by $3,600, so the carrying amount of non-current assets (and capital) is understated by the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark non-current assets/carrying amount understated by the amount; 1 mark capital (retained profit) understated.

practice.stem: Cloudline Data, a web-hosting company in Singapore, bought server equipment for $125,000. It expects to sell the equipment for $27,000 after three years.

parts.label: a

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the carrying amount at the end of year 2.

parts.label: d

parts.answer: The equipment (e.g. computer servers) becomes out of date quickly and loses most of its value early, so a higher charge in early years matches its fall in value and use.

parts.label: b

practice.stem: Farhan is opening a furniture workshop in Sialkot and will apply for a bank loan after his first year. He buys a CNC machine for $90,000, expected to last 5 years with a residual value of $10,000. He can use the straight-line method or the reducing balance method at 35% per annum. Profit before depreciation for year 1 is expected to be $60,000. He wants to choose the method that shows the higher profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for year 1 under each method.
parts.answer: Straight-line $44,000; reducing balance $28,500

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Farhan which method he should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Advice should favour the method that best reflects how the machine is used, applied consistently, rather than the one that flatters the loan application (e.g. reducing balance if the machine loses value fast).
parts.working: Points for SL: higher year-1 profit by $15,500; simple; suits even use. Points for RB: matches heavy early use/fall in value; more prudent; profits more even when repairs rise. Consistency concept: once chosen, the method must be kept, so a switch later to boost profit is not allowed; a bank will look at cash flow and security, not only profit; choosing a method only to impress the bank misleads users. Up to 4 marks for points (max 3 one side), 2 marks for a justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A machine cost $30,000. Accumulated depreciation on it was $18,000 when it was sold for $9,500 cash. What was the result of the disposal?
A Loss of $2,500
B Profit of $9,500
C Profit of $2,500
D Loss of $20,500
parts.answer: A Loss of $2,500

practice.stem: Takumi Textiles, Osaka, bought a machine on 1 January 2022 for $64,000. It is depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase and none in the year of sale. The machine was sold on 1 January 2025 at a loss of $3,800.

practice.stem: Aster Ltd owns land bought for $180,000. A professional valuer now values it at $260,000. The directors decide to show the land at the new value.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.working: 1 mark unrealised/realisation concept; 1 mark development (not available for dividends / would overstate profit).

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Rukhsana does not keep full accounting records. Her business net assets were $25,000 at the start of the year and $31,400 at the end. During the year she took drawings of $8,200 and paid $3,000 of her own savings into the business bank account. What was her profit for the year?
A $1,200
B $6,400
C $11,600
D $17,600
parts.working: Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings − capital introduced = 31,400 − 25,000 + 8,200 − 3,000 = $11,600. D adds the capital introduced instead of deducting it; the extra $3,000 came from Rukhsana's savings, not from trading.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An electronics wholesaler in Karachi keeps incomplete records. Trade receivables were $7,420 at the start of the year and $8,950 at the end. During the year it received $61,300 from credit customers, allowed cash discounts of $1,150 and wrote off irrecoverable debts of $480. What were the credit sales for the year?
A $59,770
B $62,830
C $64,460
D $61,400
parts.working: Credit sales = receipts + discounts allowed + irrecoverable debts + closing receivables − opening receivables = 61,300 + 1,150 + 480 + 8,950 − 7,420 = $64,460. B ignores discounts allowed and irrecoverable debts, which also reduce what customers owe.

What is the balancing figure for credit purchases in her total trade payables account?
A $50,035
B $50,215
C $50,805

parts.working: Debit side: bank 48,270 + discounts received 940 + returns 1,120 + contra 350 + balance c/d 6,105 = 56,785. Credit side: balance b/d 5,630 + purchases. Purchases = $51,155. A leaves out the returns; returns reduce the amount owed, so they must be added back to find the goods bought.

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

parts.label: a
parts.text:

practice.stem:

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records
practice.stem:
Nikhil runs a mobile food van in Colombo. His capital at 1 January 2025 was $27,400. For 2025 his profit was $18,250 and his drawings were $13,600. At 31 December 2025 his other balances were:

practice.subtopic: Missing figures and statements from incomplete records

Goods were stolen from a shoe shop in Peshawar shortly before the year end. Opening inventory was $14,200, purchases were $63,800 and revenue was $84,000. All goods are sold at a mark-up of 40% on cost. The inventory remaining at the year end cost $9,450. What was the cost of the goods stolen?

B $8,550
C $18,150

practice.stem:

parts.label: a

practice.stem: Tariq sells second-hand books from a small shop in Lahore. He keeps a cash book and files his invoices, but has no ledgers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a small trader might keep incomplete records rather than a full double-entry system.
parts.answer: Any two: lack of bookkeeping knowledge; saves time; saves the cost of a bookkeeper or software; the business is small with few transactions.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages to the trader of keeping incomplete records.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: (1) no trial balance, so arithmetical errors are hard to find; (2) no detailed statement of profit or loss, so the trader cannot see which expenses are rising; (3) theft or loss of cash or goods may go unnoticed; (4) harder to get a bank loan or satisfy tax authorities without reliable statements.
parts.working: 1 mark for each disadvantage and 1 mark for each explanation, max 2 disadvantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader keeps no books. At the start and end of each year she simply lists her business assets and liabilities. Which can be found from these two lists alone, with no other details?
A the gross profit for the year
B the owner's capital at each year end
C the profit for the year
D the cost of goods stolen during the year
parts.answer: B the owner's capital at each year end
parts.working: Capital = assets − liabilities, so a statement of affairs at each date gives the capital. C is wrong because profit from the change in capital also needs the drawings and any capital introduced, which the lists of assets and liabilities do not show.

practice.stem: Idris owns a furniture workshop in Chiniot. Five years ago he had four customers who paid in cash; now he has 35 credit customers and six employees. He keeps a cash book only, and an accountant prepares his statements from statements of affairs each year. Last year cash differences of $1,800 could not be explained. Idris wants a bank loan of $40,000 to buy a new machine. A part-time bookkeeper would cost $3,000 per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Idris whether he should change to a full double-entry bookkeeping system. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A reasoned recommendation, e.g. Idris should change to full double entry (or computerised accounts): the business has grown, a bank loan is wanted and the cost is small compared with the benefits. Either decision accepted if justified.
parts.working: For (max 4): bank needs reliable statements for the $40,000 loan; full detail of expenses lets him control costs; control accounts and trial balance help find errors and fraud (cash differences of $1,800 last year); detailed receivables records help chase the 35 credit customers; accounting software can automate entries. Against (max 4): cost of a bookkeeper ($3,000 per year) or software and training; time taken from running the workshop; incomplete records have produced a profit figure so far; an accountant could still prepare statements from his records at year end. Decision with justification linked to the figures (1). Max 7: at most 5 for one-sided answers.

1 K. Osei's debt of $1,400 is irrecoverable and is to be written off.
2 L. Tan owes $2,000. L. Tan is in financial difficulty, so a provision is to be made for the whole debt.
3 A general provision of 3% is to be made on the remaining receivables.
The provision for doubtful debts at 1 January 2026 was $2,950. During the year $300 was received from a customer whose debt had been written off in 2025; this had been correctly recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total provision for doubtful debts at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: B1 specific provision 2,000; B1 general 3% × (61,000 − 2,000) = 1,770; B1 total 3,770.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net effect of irrecoverable debts, debts recovered and the provision on the profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit reduced by $1,920 (irrecoverable debts 1,400 + increase in provision 820 − debts recovered 300)
parts.working: B1 increase in provision 820; B1 irrecoverable debt 1,400 and recovery 300 included; B1 net reduction 1,920.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the trade receivables figure shown in the statement of financial position.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why L. Tan's debt is provided for but not written off.
parts.answer: It is doubtful, not certainly irrecoverable: the debt may still be paid, so prudence requires a provision while the debt remains on the ledger.

practice.stem:
Yasmin's draft profit for the year ended 31 October 2026 was $31,600. The following were then discovered.
(i) Depreciation of $2,400 on the delivery van had not been charged.
(ii) Commission receivable of $650 for October 2026 had not been recorded.
(iii) Wages of $900 owing at 31 October 2026 had not been recorded.
(iv) Goods costing $400 taken by Yasmin for her own use had not been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year ended 31 October 2026.
parts.answer:
Statement of corrected profit
                                                     $
Draft profit                                    31,600
(i) Depreciation of van                        (2,400)
(ii) Commission receivable                         650
(iii) Wages accrued                              (900)
(iv) Goods for own use (purchases reduced)         400
Corrected profit                                29,350
parts.working: 1 mark for each adjustment with the correct sign (4); 1 mark corrected profit 29,350.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of item (iii) on current liabilities.
parts.answer: Current liabilities increase by $900.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A draft profit of $42,000 has been calculated. It is then found that:
• closing inventory was overstated by $1,500
• electricity of $800 owing was not accrued
• insurance of $600 paid for next year was charged as an expense.
What is the corrected profit?
A $39,100
B $41,900
C $43,300
D $40,300
parts.working: Overstated closing inventory overstated profit (−1,500); the accrual adds an expense (−800); the prepayment removes an expense (+600). 42,000 − 1,500 − 800 + 600 = 40,300. A treats the prepayment as an extra expense.

practice.stem:
Ibrahim's draft financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2026 show a profit of $48,250 and net current assets of $18,600. The following have not yet been taken into account.
(i) Closing inventory includes damaged goods that cost $2,300. They can be sold for $1,500 after repairs costing $200.
(ii) A customer owing $700 has been declared bankrupt. The debt has not been written off. The provision for doubtful debts of 2% was calculated on receivables that included this debt.
(iii) Rent of $1,800 paid for January–March 2027 was charged as an expense of 2026.
(iv) Repairs to the premises costing $1,600 were debited to the premises (non-current asset) account. No depreciation is charged on premises in the year of expenditure.
(v) Loan interest of $450 owing at 31 December 2026 has not been recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.answer:
Statement of corrected profit
                                                             $
Draft profit                                            48,250
(i) Inventory written down to NRV (2,300 − 1,300)      (1,000)
(ii) Irrecoverable debt written off                      (700)
(ii) Reduction in provision (2% × 700)                      14
(iii) Rent prepaid                                       1,800
(iv) Repairs charged as expense                        (1,600)
(v) Loan interest accrued                                (450)
Corrected profit                                        46,314
parts.working: B1 NRV 1,300 and write-down 1,000; B1 debt 700 deducted; B1 provision reduced by 14 added; B1 prepayment +1,800; B1 repairs −1,600; B1 interest −450 and corrected profit 46,314.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected net current assets at 31 December 2026.
parts.working: M1 18,600 − 1,000 − 700 + 14 + 1,800 − 450 (item (iv) affects non-current assets only); A1 18,264.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has three lines of inventory at its year end.
Line              Cost $ Selling price $ Selling costs $
X                  4,000           5,200               0
Y                  3,500           2,900               0
Z                  6,100           6,400             500
At what value should the inventory be shown in the statement of financial position?
A $13,600
B $13,000
C $12,800
D $14,000
parts.working: Each line at the lower of cost and net realisable value: X 4,000; Y 2,900; Z NRV 6,400 − 500 = 5,900 (below cost 6,100). Total 12,800. B ignores the selling costs of Z; A uses cost throughout.

practice.stem:
Grace owns a fashion shop. Her inventory at 31 December 2026 was counted and valued at cost: $54,800. The following were then found.
1 Forty jackets costing $45 each are out of fashion. They can be sold through an agent for $38 each; the agent charges 10% commission on the selling price.
2 Goods that cost $900 are damaged. After repairs costing $150 they can be sold for $1,000.
3 One box of goods costing $1,650 was counted twice.
4 Goods costing $2,400 have a net realisable value of $3,100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected value of inventory at 31 December 2026.
parts.answer:
Inventory
                                                 $
Value at cost                               54,800
Jackets: 40 × (45 − 34.20)                   (432)
Damaged goods: 900 − 850                      (50)
Box counted twice                          (1,650)
Goods with NRV above cost – no change            0
Corrected inventory                         52,668
parts.working: B1 jacket NRV 38 × 90% = 34.20 and write-down 432; B1 damaged goods write-down 50; B1 double count removed; B1 no change for item 4 and total 52,668.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the corrections on gross profit.
parts.answer: Gross profit decreases by $2,132.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
parts.answer: Prudence: losses are recognised as soon as they are foreseen, so assets and profit are not overstated. Unrealised profits (NRV above cost) are not recognised until goods are sold (realisation).
parts.working: 1 mark: prudence – avoid overstating assets/profit; 1 mark: profit not recognised until realised / IAS 2 requirement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature applies to a sole trader?
A The owner has limited liability.
B The business is a separate legal entity from its owner.
C The owner has unlimited liability for the business's debts.
D The business must publish audited financial statements.
parts.answer: C The owner has unlimited liability for the business's debts.
parts.working: A sole trader is not a separate legal person, so the owner is personally liable for all business debts (unlimited liability). A and B describe limited companies.

practice.stem: Areeba plans to open a small bakery in Multan as a sole trader.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of operating as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two: owner keeps all the profit; full control and quick decisions; easy and cheap to set up; financial affairs are private (no need to publish accounts).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of operating as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two: unlimited liability; limited capital (own savings and loans only); heavy workload / no one to share responsibility; business may end if the owner dies or is ill; harder to borrow.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term limited liability.
parts.answer: Shareholders can lose no more than the amount they have paid (or agreed to pay) for their shares; their personal assets cannot be used to pay the company's debts.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss limited to investment in shares; 1 mark: personal assets protected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by saying a limited company is a separate legal entity.
parts.answer: The company exists in law separately from its owners: it can own assets, enter contracts, sue and be sued in its own name, and it continues if shareholders change or die.
parts.working: 1 mark: separate person in law; 1 mark: example (contracts, own assets, continuity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between ownership and control in a limited company.
parts.answer: Shareholders own the company, but the directors (who may not be shareholders) manage and control it on their behalf.
parts.working: 1 mark owners = shareholders; 1 mark control = directors/managers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why limited companies must publish annual financial statements.
parts.answer: Because shareholders do not run the company, they need information to judge the directors' performance (stewardship); creditors and lenders need information because their claims are limited to the company's assets (limited liability).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about a public limited company are correct?
1 Its shares may be offered for sale to the general public.
2 Its shareholders have unlimited liability.
3 It is a separate legal entity from its shareholders.
4 It must have only one owner.
A 1 and 2
B 1 and 3
C 2 and 4
D 3 and 4
parts.answer: B 1 and 3
parts.working: A public limited company can offer shares to the public (1) and is a separate legal entity (3). Shareholders' liability is limited to the amount unpaid on their shares, so 2 is wrong; it can have many shareholders, so 4 is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between a private limited company and a public limited company.
parts.answer: Any two: a private company cannot offer its shares to the general public, a public company can (and may be listed on a stock exchange); private company shares are usually transferred only with the directors' agreement, public company shares are freely traded; a public company usually needs a minimum share capital and stricter disclosure; a private company name ends in 'Limited/(Private) Limited', a public one in 'plc' or equivalent.
parts.working: 2 marks per difference, comparing both types.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a family business might prefer to remain a private limited company.
parts.answer: The family keeps control because shares cannot be sold to outsiders without approval, so there is no risk of takeover; also fewer disclosure requirements and lower costs.
parts.working: 1 mark reason, 1 mark development.

practice.stem: Usman has run a computer accessories shop in Hyderabad as a sole trader for six years. He wants to open a second branch and start selling online. His brother, who has IT skills, offers to invest $40,000 and become a partner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Usman whether he should form a partnership with his brother. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: extra capital ($40,000) to open the second branch; brother's IT and online-sales skills add expertise; workload and decision-making shared; cover during illness or holidays. Against: profits must be shared; unlimited liability continues — Usman becomes liable for his brother's business decisions; disagreements may arise, especially in a family; slower decisions; partnership may end on death or retirement. Decision: e.g. form the partnership with a written partnership agreement covering profit sharing, interest on capital and salaries, because the capital and skills are needed for the expansion.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for advantages and up to 2 for disadvantages, applied to the case; 1 mark recommendation of a written agreement or other safeguard; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Fahad, a sole trader, has closed his furniture business. It owes creditors $85,000. The business assets were sold for $52,000. Fahad has personal assets (savings and a car) worth $60,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount that Fahad must pay from his personal assets.
parts.working: Debts 85,000 − business assets realised 52,000 = 33,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fahad's friend Nasir owned 30,000 $1 shares, fully paid at $1.20 each, in a limited company that collapsed with debts larger than its assets. State the maximum Nasir could lose and explain why.
parts.answer: $36,000. Nasir has limited liability: his loss is limited to the amount paid for his shares (30,000 × $1.20); his personal assets cannot be claimed by the company's creditors.
parts.working: 1 mark amount, 1 mark limited liability, 1 mark personal assets protected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare how owners withdraw profits from (i) a sole trader business and (ii) a limited company.
parts.answer: (i) The sole trader takes drawings, recorded in the capital account. (ii) Shareholders receive dividends declared by the directors out of distributable profits; directors who work in the company also receive salaries treated as expenses.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare how the owners' capital is shown in the statement of financial position of a partnership and of a limited company.
parts.answer: Partnership: each partner has a capital account (often fixed) and a current account for profit shares, interest and drawings. Company: equity shows issued share capital and reserves (share premium, retained earnings and other reserves).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each organisation, state whether it is a sole trader, a partnership, a private limited company, a public limited company or a non-profit organisation.
(i) Three doctors share a clinic, profits and unlimited liability.
(ii) A cricket club funded by members' subscriptions.
(iii) A company whose shares are bought and sold on a stock exchange.
(iv) A family firm whose shares can only be transferred with the directors' permission.
parts.answer: (i) partnership; (ii) non-profit organisation (club); (iii) public limited company; (iv) private limited company.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A hockey club in Sialkot is run for its members, not to make a profit. Which statement does it prepare instead of a statement of profit or loss, and what is the name of its equivalent of capital?
A income and expenditure account; accumulated fund
B receipts and payments account; retained earnings
C statement of changes in equity; accumulated fund
D income and expenditure account; current account
parts.answer: A income and expenditure account; accumulated fund
parts.working: Non-profit organisations prepare an income and expenditure account (accruals basis) and their capital is the accumulated fund. A receipts and payments account (B) is only a summary of cash and does not replace the statement of profit or loss.

practice.stem: Zainab and Kiran are partners in an interior design business in Karachi. Turnover has tripled in three years and they have just won a contract to design the interior of a 200-room hotel, which will need expensive materials bought in advance. A cousin is willing to invest money but does not want to take part in running the business or have unlimited liability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Zainab and Kiran whether they should convert their partnership into a private limited company. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For conversion: limited liability protects their homes against claims (important given the large contract and its risks); the company is a separate legal entity, so it continues if a partner leaves; easier to raise finance — can issue shares to investors such as their cousin and use loan notes; may appear more credible to large clients. Against: set-up costs and legal formalities; must file accounts publicly (loss of privacy) and may require an audit; profits taxed as a company and owners paid through salaries and dividends; banks may still ask for personal guarantees, reducing the benefit of limited liability; shares in a private company cannot easily be sold. Decision: convert, because the growth in contract size and the need for outside capital make limited liability and access to share finance worth the extra cost.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): well-applied points on both sides and a justified decision. Level 2 (4–6): some applied points on both sides or one-sided with a decision. Level 1 (1–3): general features of partnerships/companies.

practice.stem: Hassan bought 40,000 ordinary shares of $1 each in a private limited company at $1.25 per share, fully paid. Salman is a general partner in a firm of architects with one other partner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the maximum amount Hassan could lose as a shareholder, and the maximum Salman could lose as a partner. Explain the difference.
parts.answer: Hassan: $50,000 (40,000 × $1.25 paid). Salman: there is no limit — he could lose his capital and his personal assets, because partners have unlimited liability and are jointly liable for all the partnership's debts (including those caused by the other partner).
parts.working: 1 mark Hassan's 50,000; 1 mark Salman unlimited; 1 mark limited liability explained; 1 mark joint liability/personal assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way in which the law allows a partner to have limited liability, and the condition that applies.
parts.answer: A limited partner (in a limited partnership / LLP structure) may have liability limited to their capital, provided there is at least one general partner with unlimited liability and the limited partner takes no part in managing the business (or the firm is registered as a limited liability partnership).
parts.working: 1 mark limited partner/LLP; 1 mark condition (no management role / at least one general partner / registration).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is capital expenditure for a courier company?
A fuel for the delivery vans
B repainting the office
C purchase of a new delivery motorcycle
D insurance of the vans
parts.answer: C purchase of a new delivery motorcycle
parts.working: Buying a new motorcycle provides a non-current asset used for more than one year, so it is capital expenditure. Repainting (B) only maintains an existing asset, so it is revenue expenditure.

practice.stem: Bano Distributors bought and equipped a warehouse in Gujranwala.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each item as capital expenditure or revenue expenditure.
(i) Legal fees for buying a new warehouse
(ii) Wages of the warehouse staff
(iii) Installing air-conditioning in the warehouse for the first time
(iv) Replacing a broken window pane in the warehouse
parts.answer: (i) capital; (ii) revenue; (iii) capital; (iv) revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Nishat Weaving bought a weaving machine. The invoice and other costs were: price $86,000; delivery $2,400; installation $3,100; staff training on the machine $1,800; first-year maintenance contract $950; insurance for the first year $1,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be capitalised as the cost of the machine.
parts.working: Price 86,000 + delivery 2,400 + installation 3,100 = 91,500. Training, maintenance and insurance are revenue. M1 A1 + 1 for excluding all revenue items.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revenue expenditure and state where it is shown.
parts.answer: $3,950; shown as expenses in the statement of profit or loss.

practice.stem: A school in Abbottabad built an extension to its building costing $40,000. The bookkeeper debited this to repairs and maintenance. Buildings are depreciated at 10% per year on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of acquisition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effect of the error on profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit is understated by $36,000.
parts.working: The 40,000 should be removed from expenses (+40,000) and depreciation of 10% × 40,000 = 4,000 charged; net +36,000. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of the error on the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Non-current assets are understated by $36,000 (cost 40,000 less depreciation 4,000), and capital (via profit) is understated by the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark NCA; 1 mark capital/retained profit.

practice.stem:
Royal Pharmacy spent the following on its building during the year:
1 Replacing worn roof tiles: $6,800
2 Adding a second floor: $95,000
3 Repainting the shop front: $3,200
4 Installing a new lift (not there before): $28,500
5 Architect's fees for the second floor: $7,400
6 Cleaning after the building work: $1,100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Capital $130,900; revenue $11,100
parts.working: Capital: items 2, 4, 5 = 95,000 + 28,500 + 7,400 = 130,900. Revenue: items 1, 3, 6 = 6,800 + 3,200 + 1,100 = 11,100. 1 mark each correct classification group, 1 mark each total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why item 1 is revenue expenditure while item 2 is capital expenditure.
parts.answer: Replacing worn tiles restores the building to its original condition (maintenance), so it is an expense; adding a floor improves/enlarges the asset and increases its earning capacity for more than one year, so it is capital.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Distinguish between a capital receipt and a revenue receipt, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Capital receipt: from sale of non-current assets, loans or capital introduced (e.g. proceeds of selling an old van). Revenue receipt: from normal trading (e.g. sales revenue, rent received, commission).
parts.working: 1 mark each with example.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader records the cost of servicing a delivery van as an addition to the van's cost. What is the effect on the financial statements for the year, ignoring depreciation?
A profit overstated; non-current assets overstated
B profit understated; non-current assets overstated
C profit overstated; non-current assets understated
D profit understated; non-current assets understated
parts.answer: A profit overstated; non-current assets overstated
