parts.working: Revenue expenditure treated as capital means an expense is missing from the statement of profit or loss, so profit is overstated, and the van is shown at too high a cost. D is the effect of the opposite error (capital expenditure treated as revenue).

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the book of prime entry in which each transaction is first recorded.
(i) An invoice received for goods bought on credit for resale
(ii) A credit note sent to a customer for faulty goods returned
(iii) A cheque paid to a supplier
(iv) The purchase of office furniture on credit
parts.answer: (i) purchases journal (day book); (ii) sales returns journal; (iii) cash book; (iv) the journal (general journal).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry
practice.stem: Zara, a wholesaler, sells goods with a list price of $6,400 on credit to Bilal Stores, allowing 15% trade discount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the amount at which the sale is recorded in Zara's books.
parts.working: Trade discount is deducted before recording: 6,400 × 85% = 5,440.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited in Zara's ledger.
(i) the credit sale to Bilal Stores
(ii) Bilal Stores returns goods with a net value of $340
(iii) Bilal Stores pays the balance by bank transfer
parts.answer: (i) Dr Bilal Stores (trade receivable), Cr Sales $5,440. (ii) Dr Sales returns, Cr Bilal Stores $340. (iii) Dr Bank, Cr Bilal Stores $5,100.
parts.working: 1 mark each double entry (amount in (iii) must be correct).

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business receives a credit note from a supplier for damaged goods it returned. In which book of prime entry is the credit note recorded?
A purchases journal
B purchases returns journal
C sales returns journal
D cash book
parts.answer: B purchases returns journal
parts.working: Goods returned to a supplier are returns outwards (purchases returns), recorded from the credit note received. C would be used for a credit note sent to a customer.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why businesses use books of prime entry rather than posting every transaction straight to the ledger.
parts.answer: They group similar transactions (e.g. all credit sales) so that only totals need to be posted to the nominal ledger, saving time and reducing errors; they also provide a chronological record and audit trail back to source documents.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the source document used to write up (i) the sales journal and (ii) the purchases returns journal.
parts.answer: (i) copies of sales invoices sent; (ii) credit notes received from suppliers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Double entry and books of prime entry
practice.stem:
Tahir runs an engineering supplies business.
1 Bought a delivery van for $18,500 on credit from Rahim Motors.
2 Brought his own car, valued at $7,200, into the business for business use.
3 Sent three credit sales invoices: list price $2,400 less 10% trade discount; list price $5,600 less 20% trade discount; $3,150 with no discount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare journal entries, with narratives, for transactions 1 and 2.
parts.answer:
Debit $    Credit $
1 Delivery van                            18,500            
  Rahim Motors (other payable)                        18,500
  Purchase of van on credit                                 
2 Motor vehicles                           7,200            
  Capital                                              7,200
  Owner's car brought into the business
parts.working: 1 mark each correct double entry with amounts (2); 1 mark each narrative (2). Accept 'non-current asset' for the van account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total of the sales journal for the three invoices in transaction 3, and state the double entry for posting the total.
parts.answer: $9,790; Dr each customer's account individually, Cr Sales account with the total $9,790.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name four types of error that are not revealed by a trial balance, giving an example of each.
parts.answer: Any four with examples: omission (invoice not recorded at all); commission (sale debited to the wrong customer); principle (repairs debited to a non-current asset account); original entry (wrong amount from source document in both accounts); complete reversal (debit and credit swapped); compensating errors (two errors cancel out).
parts.working: 1 mark each type with a valid example.

practice.stem:
Nimra, a sole trader, has the following balances at 31 December 2026 (inventory is the opening inventory):
Premises $120,000; Equipment $34,500; Inventory $18,900; Trade receivables $14,250; Bank $6,150; Purchases $96,400; Wages $28,800; General expenses $9,300; Drawings $15,600; Sales $187,200; Trade payables $11,850; Bank loan $40,000. Her capital balance is missing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the trial balance at 31 December 2026, calculating capital as the missing figure.
parts.answer:
Debit $    Credit $
Premises                     120,000            
Equipment                     34,500            
Inventory                     18,900            
Trade receivables             14,250            
Bank                           6,150            
Purchases                     96,400            
Wages                         28,800            
General expenses               9,300            
Drawings                      15,600            
Sales                                    187,200
Trade payables                            11,850
Bank loan                                 40,000
Capital                                  104,850
Totals                       343,900     343,900
parts.working: Debit balances correctly placed (2); credit balances correctly placed (1); capital 104,850 (1); totals 343,900 (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which error will cause the totals of a trial balance to disagree?
A A purchase invoice for $800 was not recorded.
B Sales of $1,250 were credited to the rent received account.
C Wages of $3,400 were debited to the wages account as $4,300 and credited to the bank as $3,400.
D A payment to Saleem of $500 was debited to Salim's account.
parts.answer: C Wages of $3,400 were debited to the wages account as $4,300 and credited to the bank as $3,400.
parts.working: In C the debit (4,300) and credit (3,400) are unequal, so the trial balance does not agree (debit side $900 too high). A is an omission, B an error of commission/principle between income accounts and D an error of commission — in each case equal debits and credits remain.

practice.stem: Imran owns a printing shop. At 30 June 2027 his non-current assets are $186,000, current assets $43,700, non-current liabilities (bank loan) $60,000 and current liabilities $27,450.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Imran's capital at 30 June 2027.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the accounting equation.
parts.answer: Assets = Capital + Liabilities (or Assets − Liabilities = Capital).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
At 1 May 2027, Mehwish's business had assets of $52,000 and liabilities of $14,000. During May:
1 Bought inventory on credit $3,600
2 Paid a supplier $2,100 by bank transfer
3 Sold goods costing $1,500 for $2,300 cash
4 Owner withdrew $900 cash for personal use
5 Took out a bank loan of $10,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show the effect of each transaction on assets, liabilities and capital, and state the closing totals.
parts.answer:
Transaction       Assets $     Liab. $   Capital $
Opening             52,000      14,000      38,000
1 effect             3,600       3,600           0
2 effect           (2,100)     (2,100)           0
3 effect               800           0         800
4 effect             (900)           0       (900)
5 effect            10,000      10,000           0
Closing             63,400      25,500      37,900
parts.working: 1 mark per transaction (5): note 3 increases assets by the net 800 (cash +2,300, inventory −1,500) and capital by the profit of 800. Closing totals: assets 63,400 = liabilities 25,500 + capital 37,900 (1).

practice.stem: Junaid does not keep full double-entry records. At 1 January 2026 his business assets were $148,000 and liabilities $39,500. At 31 December 2026 assets were $176,400 and liabilities $44,200. During the year he withdrew $21,600 and paid in a legacy of $15,000 as extra capital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital at the start and at the end of the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year.
parts.working: Closing capital = opening + capital introduced + profit − drawings. Profit = 132,200 − 108,500 + 21,600 − 15,000 = 30,300. M1 add drawings, M1 deduct capital introduced, A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an increase in capital is not the same as profit.
parts.answer: Capital also changes because of drawings (which reduce it) and extra capital introduced (which increases it); these are owner transactions, not business performance.
parts.working: 1 mark drawings; 1 mark capital introduced.

subtopics.name: Double entry and books of prime entry

subtopics: Double entry and books of prime entry
Double entry and books of prime entry
Double entry and books of prime entry
Double entry and books of prime entry
Double entry and books of prime entry

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bilal owns a mobile phone repair shop in Rawalpindi. He pays the electricity bill for his family home from his own savings account, and it is not recorded anywhere in the shop's books. Which accounting concept is being applied?
A business entity
B duality
C going concern
D money measurement
parts.answer: A business entity
parts.working: Business entity: the owner's private transactions are kept separate from the business's records. Money measurement (D) is wrong because the bill can be measured in money; it is left out because it is private, not because it cannot be valued.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bookshop values a box of last year's diaries at their expected selling price of $140 less selling costs of $20, because this is lower than their cost of $310. Which concept requires this?
A consistency
B matching
C prudence
D realisation
parts.answer: C prudence
parts.working: Prudence: assets must not be overstated and expected losses are recognised as soon as they are foreseen, so inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value ($120). Realisation (D) concerns when revenue is recognised, not the value of unsold goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item would NOT be recorded in the books of a software company because of the money measurement concept?
A a laptop bought on credit from a supplier
B the loyalty and good morale of its programmers
C a loan received from a bank
D an amount owed by a customer who is unlikely to pay
parts.answer: B the loyalty and good morale of its programmers
parts.working: Morale and loyalty cannot be measured objectively in money, so they are not recorded. D is recorded (it is measurable; an irrecoverable debt or allowance would be used).

practice.stem: Nadia runs a printing business in Karachi. She has owned a large printing press for three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the going concern concept.
parts.answer: The assumption that the business will continue to trade for the foreseeable future and has no intention or need to close down or greatly reduce its operations.
parts.working: 1 mark: continue trading; 1 mark: for the foreseeable future / no intention to liquidate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the going concern concept affects the value of non-current assets in a statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Non-current assets are shown at cost less accumulated depreciation (carrying amount), spread over their useful lives, rather than at what they would fetch if sold immediately (break-up value).
parts.working: 1 mark: cost less depreciation over useful life; 1 mark: not at break-up / forced-sale value because the business is not expected to sell them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the money measurement concept.
parts.answer: Only transactions and events that can be measured objectively in monetary terms are recorded in the accounting records.
parts.working: 1 mark: only items measurable in money; 1 mark: measured objectively/reliably are recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items of value to a business that are not recorded because of this concept.
parts.answer: Any two of: skill/experience of the workforce; staff morale; good relations with customers or suppliers; a good location (unless purchased); quality of management.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid non-monetary items.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the duality concept.
parts.answer: Every transaction has two equal and opposite effects on the business, so for every debit entry there is a credit entry of the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark: two aspects/effects; 1 mark: equal debit and credit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Kamran buys a delivery van costing $14,500 on credit from Pak Motors. State the two effects of this transaction on the accounting equation.
parts.answer: Non-current assets (van) increase by $14,500; liabilities (other payable, Pak Motors) increase by $14,500.
parts.working: 1 mark: assets +14,500; 1 mark: liabilities +14,500. Capital unchanged.

practice.stem: Farah's bakery has a year end of 30 June. On 1 July 2026 electricity of $780 was owing for June 2026. During the year to 30 June 2027 she paid electricity bills of $9,640. On 30 June 2027 electricity of $1,120 was owing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the accounting concept that requires the electricity expense to include amounts not yet paid.
parts.answer: Accruals (matching) concept.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electricity expense to be shown in the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2027.
parts.working: Paid 9,640 − opening accrual 780 (belongs to last year) + closing accrual 1,120 = 9,980. M1 deduct opening accrual, M1 add closing accrual, A1.

practice.stem: Ali Traders bought land in 2004 for $85,000. A valuer says it is worth $410,000 today. The business has never revalued the land.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the historical cost concept.
parts.answer: Assets are recorded at their original cost (the price paid to acquire them).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using historical cost for the land bought by Ali Traders.
parts.answer: Advantage: the cost is objective and can be checked against the purchase documents. Disadvantage: the figure is out of date and understates the land's current value, so the SOFP may mislead users.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage (objective/verifiable); 1 mark disadvantage (out of date/understates value).

practice.stem: Saima runs a dental clinic in Peshawar. Her year ends on 31 December. On 1 January 2026 insurance of $2,400 had been prepaid for January to September 2026. On 1 October 2026 she paid $3,600 for twelve months' insurance to 30 September 2027.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the insurance expense for the year ended 31 December 2026.
parts.working: Opening prepayment 2,400 (Jan–Sep 2026) + 3/12 × 3,600 = 900 (Oct–Dec) = 3,300. M1, M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the amount of the prepayment at 31 December 2026 and where it appears in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: $2,700, shown as a current asset (other receivables).
parts.working: 9/12 × 3,600 = 2,700 B1; current asset B1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the realisation concept.
parts.answer: Revenue (and profit) is recognised when it is earned — when goods or services have been transferred to the customer — not when cash is received.
parts.working: 1 mark: recognised when earned / control passes; 1 mark: not when cash received.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A customer orders goods on 3 March, receives them on 9 March and pays on 20 April. State the date on which the revenue is recognised.
parts.answer: 9 March (when the goods are delivered to the customer).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A large hotel company buys a waste-paper bin for $18. It is expected to last five years, but the cost is charged in full to the statement of profit or loss as general expenses. Which concept justifies this treatment?
A historical cost
B materiality
C going concern
D prudence
parts.answer: B materiality
parts.working: Materiality: the amount is too small to affect users' decisions, so the cost of depreciating it over five years is not worth the effort. Prudence (D) is not the reason, because the bin is not being undervalued out of caution; it is simply insignificant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A furniture maker's year ends on 31 December 2026. A customer ordered a table on 10 December 2026 and paid in full on 2 January 2027. The table was delivered to and accepted by the customer on 29 December 2026. In which year should the sale be recognised, and which concept applies?
A year ended 31 December 2026; realisation
B year ended 31 December 2027; realisation
C year ended 31 December 2026; going concern
D year ended 31 December 2027; matching
parts.answer: A year ended 31 December 2026; realisation
parts.working: Realisation: revenue is recognised when control of the goods passes to the customer (delivery and acceptance on 29 December 2026), not when cash is received. B wrongly uses the date of payment.

practice.stem: Omar sells solar lamps. On the last day of his financial year he sent lamps to a retailer on sale or return. The retailer had not accepted them by the year end. Omar included the lamps in revenue at their selling price of $4,800, which is cost plus 20%. They were not included in closing inventory. His draft profit for the year was $41,350.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the treatment of these goods breaks the realisation concept.
parts.answer: Revenue should only be recognised when control passes to the customer, i.e. when the customer accepts the goods. The goods sent on sale or return have not been accepted, so no sale has taken place.
parts.working: 1 mark: revenue recognised when goods accepted / control passes; 1 mark: applied — not yet accepted, so not revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Cost = 4,800 × 100/120 = 4,000. Revenue reduced by 4,800; closing inventory increased by 4,000. 41,350 − 4,800 + 4,000 = 40,550. B1 cost, M1 both adjustments, A1.

practice.stem:
At the end of her financial year, Hina, a clothing retailer in Lahore, has the following inventory.
Item                      Cost $       NRV $
Cotton shirts              6,200       9,100
Silk scarves               3,450       2,800
Leather belts              1,980       1,650
Denim jackets              7,400      11,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory.
parts.working: Each line at the lower of cost and NRV: 6,200 + 2,800 + 1,650 + 7,400 = 18,050. M1 lower of cost/NRV line by line, M1 at least two lines correct, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the accounting concept you have applied and explain why it is applied item by item rather than to the total.
parts.answer: Prudence. If the totals were compared, gains on some items would hide losses on others, so inventory (and profit) would be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: prudence; 1 mark: totals would offset expected losses against unrealised gains.

practice.stem: Zubair Engineering bought a machine two years ago for $48,000. It has been depreciated at 10% per year on cost (straight-line). For year 3 the accountant proposes to use 20% per year on the reducing balance instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the consistency concept.
parts.answer: Once a business has chosen an accounting method (e.g. a depreciation method), it should use the same method from year to year, so that results can be compared over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: same methods each year; 1 mark: allows comparison between periods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depreciation for year 3 under the existing method and under the proposed method.
parts.answer: Straight-line: $4,800. Reducing balance: $7,680.
parts.working: SL = 10% × 48,000 = 4,800. Carrying amount after 2 years = 48,000 − 2 × 4,800 = 38,400; RB = 20% × 38,400 = 7,680. B1 SL, M1 carrying amount, A1 RB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on profit for year 3 if the method is changed, and state one condition under which a change of method is acceptable.
parts.answer: Profit would fall by $2,880. A change is acceptable if the new method gives a fairer (truer) view of the asset's use, and the change and its effect are disclosed.
parts.working: 1 mark: decrease 2,880 (own figure); 1 mark: fairer presentation/disclosed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the materiality concept.
parts.answer: An item is material if leaving it out or misstating it could influence the decisions of users of the financial statements. Immaterial items need not be treated strictly (e.g. small tools may be expensed).
parts.working: 1 mark: could influence users' decisions; 1 mark: immaterial items can be treated in the simplest way.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A stapler costing $25 is material to a small corner shop but not to a multinational bank. Explain this statement.
parts.answer: Materiality is relative to the size of the business: $25 is a large proportion of the shop's profit or assets, but an insignificant fraction of the bank's.
parts.working: 1 mark: relative to size/scale; 1 mark: compared with profit or total assets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two items, other than small value equipment, for which materiality affects the accounting treatment.
parts.answer: Any two: separate disclosure of large unusual items; whether to record small accruals or prepayments; grouping small expenses into 'sundry expenses'; whether to correct a small error.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Rashid owns a grocery shop. During the year he took goods costing $650 from the shop for his family's use, and paid his home electricity bill of $420 from the business bank account. Both amounts were recorded as business expenses: the goods remained in purchases and the bill was debited to the shop's electricity account. His draft profit for the year was $38,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Goods taken: reduce purchases (cost of sales) by 650 → profit +650. Home electricity removed from expenses → +420. 38,200 + 650 + 420 = 39,270. M1 M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how each item should be recorded, and name the concept that has been broken.
parts.answer: Goods taken: Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases $650. Home electricity: Dr Drawings, Cr Electricity (expense) $420. Concept: business entity.
parts.working: 1 mark each double entry; 1 mark business entity.

practice.stem: Crescent Textiles Limited has made losses for three years and its bank has warned it may withdraw the overdraft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two indicators that a company may not be a going concern.
parts.answer: Any two: repeated large losses; net current liabilities / unable to pay debts as they fall due; loss of a major customer or supplier; bank refusing to renew loans; loan repayments in default; key licence withdrawn.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects on the financial statements if a company is no longer a going concern.
parts.answer: Assets are revalued to realisable (break-up) values, often much lower, e.g. specialised machinery and inventory. Non-current liabilities may become current because they must be repaid on closure. Extra liabilities (e.g. closure costs, redundancy) may need to be recognised. Depreciation over useful life no longer applies.
parts.working: 2 marks each effect: identification + explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each situation, name the accounting concept that is applied or broken.
(i) A taxi company changes from straight-line to reducing balance depreciation each year, choosing whichever gives the higher profit.
(ii) The owner records the business's van at the price paid, not its current market value.
(iii) A wholesaler makes an allowance for a customer who has entered liquidation.
(iv) Commission earned in the final week of the year is included in income although it will be received next month.
parts.answer: (i) consistency (broken); (ii) historical cost (applied); (iii) prudence (applied); (iv) accruals/matching or realisation (applied).
parts.working: 1 mark each. (iv) accept accruals, matching or realisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the treatment in (i) could mislead users of the financial statements.
parts.answer: Changes in profit would be caused by the switch in method rather than real performance, so year-to-year comparisons are unreliable and profit may be manipulated upwards.
parts.working: 1 mark: not comparable; 1 mark: profit manipulated / not a fair view.

practice.stem: A wholesaler in Faisalabad has trade receivables of $64,000 at the year end. It keeps an allowance for irrecoverable debts of 2.5% of trade receivables. The allowance brought forward is $1,250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount to be charged to the statement of profit or loss for the allowance for irrecoverable debts.
parts.answer: $350 (increase)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the net figure for trade receivables in the statement of financial position.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the concept that requires an allowance for irrecoverable debts and explain why.
parts.answer: Prudence: receivables should not be overstated, so the expected loss on debts that may not be collected is recognised now. (Accept matching: the expected loss is matched to the year of the sale.)
parts.working: 1 mark concept; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: Kareem is thinking of lending money to a small manufacturing business and is studying its financial statements for the last four years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the consistency concept is important to users of financial statements.
parts.answer: 1 It allows a business's results to be compared from year to year, so trends in profit and performance are real and not caused by changes in method. 2 It prevents managers or owners from manipulating profit by switching methods (e.g. inventory valuation or depreciation) to show the result they want. Also accept: helps comparison with other businesses using similar policies.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: 1 identification + 1 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's financial year ends on 31 March 2027. Rent of $1,850 per month is payable for a shop. During the year she paid $20,350, which covered April 2026 to February 2027. What rent expense should appear in the statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 March 2027?
A $18,500
B $20,350
C $22,200
D $24,050
parts.working: Matching (accruals): the expense is the rent for the 12 months used, 12 × $1,850 = $22,200, whether paid or not; March's $1,850 is accrued. B is the cash paid, which ignores the accrual.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about accounting concepts are correct?
1 The consistency concept means that a business can never change its depreciation method.
2 The going concern concept supports valuing non-current assets at cost less depreciation rather than at their forced-sale value.
3 The duality concept means that every transaction has two equal and opposite effects.
4 The money measurement concept means that the skill of a business's workforce is shown as an asset.
A 1 and 2
B 1 and 4
C 2 and 3
D 3 and 4
parts.answer: C 2 and 3
parts.working: 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong: a method may be changed if the new method gives a fairer view, with the change disclosed. Statement 4 is wrong: the skill of workers cannot be measured reliably in money, so it is not recorded.

practice.stem:
Tariq has decided to close his electronics shop next month. His draft statement of financial position shows: inventory $26,000; equipment (carrying amount) $40,000; trade receivables $15,000; cash $3,800; trade payables $21,400.
If the shop closes: the inventory can be sold for $17,500; the equipment for $22,000; and 10% of the trade receivables will not be collected. Cash and payables are unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Tariq's capital (net assets) on the going concern basis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Tariq's capital if the business is no longer a going concern, and the decrease in capital.
parts.answer: Capital $35,400; decrease $28,000.
parts.working: Inventory 17,500 + equipment 22,000 + receivables 90% × 15,000 = 13,500 + cash 3,800 − payables 21,400 = 35,400. Decrease 63,400 − 35,400 = 28,000. M1 break-up values, M1 receivables 90%, A1 capital, A1 decrease.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the going concern concept no longer applies to Tariq's business.
parts.answer: Tariq intends to close the business within weeks, so it will not continue to trade for the foreseeable future; assets must be valued at what they will realise on sale.
parts.working: 1 mark: closure planned / not foreseeable future; 1 mark: so realisable (break-up) values used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the prudence concept and the realisation concept work together when a business values its closing inventory.
parts.answer: Inventory is valued at cost (not selling price) because the profit on it is not realised until it is sold — realisation. If the net realisable value falls below cost, the expected loss is recognised now — prudence. So gains wait until realised, losses are recognised when foreseen.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost not selling price; 1 mark: profit only recognised when realised (sold); 1 mark: losses recognised at once / lower of cost and NRV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether too much prudence can conflict with the aim of giving a true and fair view.
parts.answer: Excessive prudence (e.g. very large allowances for doubtful debts or undervalued assets) understates profit and assets, so statements are no longer neutral or faithful. Profit is moved to later years, breaking matching and making comparison misleading. Some caution is needed so owners do not withdraw unrealised profits. Conclusion: prudence should mean caution, not deliberate understatement.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 4 developed points: understatement of profit/assets; not neutral/faithful; shifts profit between periods/affects matching; caution still useful to protect capital; a balanced conclusion.

practice.stem: Jamal Kitchens' year ends on 30 June. On 20 June 2027 a customer ordered an industrial oven for $8,000 and paid a deposit of $2,000. The oven, which cost Jamal $5,000, was still in the warehouse on 30 June and was delivered on 5 July 2027. The bookkeeper recorded the full $8,000 as revenue, set up a trade receivable for $6,000, and left the oven out of closing inventory. Draft profit was $63,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with reference to the realisation concept, why this sale should not be included in revenue for the year ended 30 June 2027.
parts.answer: Revenue is recognised when control of the goods passes to the customer. The oven was delivered after the year end (5 July), so the sale belongs to the next year. Receiving the order and deposit does not realise the revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark: control passes on delivery; 1 mark: delivered after year end, so next year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the deposit of $2,000 should be shown in the statement of financial position at 30 June 2027, and state the other correction needed to that statement.
parts.answer: The deposit is a current liability (amount received in advance / contract liability) of $2,000, because the business still owes the customer the oven. The trade receivable of $6,000 recorded for the balance must be removed, and inventory increased by $5,000.
parts.working: 1 mark current liability; 1 mark reason; 1 mark remove receivable / add inventory.

practice.stem: The conceptual framework used for international financial reporting sets out the qualitative characteristics that make financial information useful to investors, lenders and other creditors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the two fundamental qualitative characteristics of useful financial information.
parts.answer: Relevance: information can make a difference to users' decisions because it has predictive value, confirmatory value, or both (and is material). Faithful representation: information depicts what it claims to — it is complete, neutral and free from error.
parts.working: 1 mark each characteristic named, 1 mark each correct explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two enhancing qualitative characteristics and explain how one of them helps an investor comparing two companies.
parts.answer: Any two of: comparability, verifiability, timeliness, understandability. E.g. comparability: if both companies use similar policies consistently and disclose them, the investor can identify real differences in performance rather than differences caused by accounting methods.
parts.working: 1 mark each name (max 2); 1 mark explanation applied to comparing companies.

practice.stem:
Sofia's draft profit for the year is $54,300. The following have been discovered:
1 Revenue includes goods with a selling price of $3,000 sent on sale or return and not yet accepted. They cost $2,250 and are not in closing inventory.
2 Closing inventory includes goods at cost $1,800 which can only be sold for $1,100.
3 Rent expense includes $1,500 paid for the first month of next year.
4 The school fees of Sofia's daughter, $2,400, were paid from the business bank account and charged to general expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item, name the accounting concept that has not been applied.
parts.answer: 1 realisation; 2 prudence; 3 accruals (matching); 4 business entity.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.answer:
Corrected profit $56,750
Draft profit                            54,300
1 Remove sale or return goods          (3,000)
1 Add them to closing inventory          2,250
2 Reduce inventory to NRV                (700)
3 Rent prepaid for next year             1,500
4 Owner's private school fees            2,400
Corrected profit                        56,750
parts.working: 1 mark per correct adjustment line (max 4, item 1 needs both lines); 1 mark corrected profit (own figure).

practice.stem: Indus Agro Limited revalued its land upwards by $30,000 during the year. The land was not sold. The accountant included the gain in the statement of profit or loss, giving a draft profit for the year of $72,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, with reference to accounting concepts, why the revaluation gain should not be included in the profit for the year.
parts.answer: The gain is unrealised: the land has not been sold, so no revenue has been earned (realisation). Prudence means unrealised gains are not reported as profit that could be withdrawn or distributed. The gain is credited to a revaluation reserve in equity (other comprehensive income) instead.
parts.working: 1 mark realisation/unrealised; 1 mark prudence/not available for distribution; 1 mark revaluation reserve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The managing director argues that showing the land at $30,000 more makes the statements more useful. Evaluate this argument.
parts.answer: For: an up-to-date value is more relevant to users assessing the company's worth and security for loans. Against: valuations are subjective and less verifiable than historical cost; future depreciation charges rise. Conclusion: revaluation in the SOFP is acceptable if done for the whole class and by an independent valuer, but the gain must not go through profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for, 1 mark against, 1 mark reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: Leila owns a shoe shop in Islamabad. At her year end she has 1,200 pairs of shoes that cost $14 each and normally sell for $22 each. She wants to apply for a bank loan and proposes to value her closing inventory at selling price to show a higher profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount by which profit would be overstated if Leila used her proposed valuation.
parts.working: At selling price 1,200 × $22 = 26,400; at cost 1,200 × $14 = 16,800; overstatement 9,600. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Leila whether she should value her closing inventory at selling price. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: the profit on unsold goods has not been realised (realisation); prudence says gains are not anticipated, so inventory should be at the lower of cost and NRV; overstated profit could lead her to withdraw cash the business has not earned; the bank would be misled about her performance; next year's profit would be understated when the goods are sold. For: selling price shows what she expects to receive and may impress the bank. Decision: she should not; she should value at cost ($16,800) unless NRV is lower, and explain her expected margin to the bank separately.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points (at least one on each side for full marks), 1 mark for a clear justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which cost is a direct cost for a business that makes wooden tables?
A timber used to make the tables
B rent of the factory
C salary of the factory supervisor
D depreciation of the cutting machines
parts.answer: A timber used to make the tables
parts.working: Timber can be traced directly to each table. Factory rent, supervision and depreciation (B, C, D) are production overheads: they are incurred for the factory as a whole and cannot be traced to a single table.

practice.stem: Mehran Bakery, Lahore, had the following costs in June 2026: flour $18,400; packaging for each loaf $2,300; wages of bakers $26,500; depreciation of ovens $1,900; bakery rent $3,200; wages of the delivery van driver $2,750.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each of the following costs as direct materials, direct labour, production overhead or non-production overhead.
(i) flour
(ii) wages of bakers
(iii) depreciation of ovens
(iv) wages of the delivery van driver
parts.answer: (i) direct materials (ii) direct labour (iii) production overhead (iv) non-production (distribution) overhead
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the prime cost for the month.
parts.working: Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour = 18,400 + 2,300 + 26,500 = 47,200. M1 (packaging included as a direct material, rent excluded) A1.

practice.stem: Shoaib Shoes, Sialkot, values its inventory of finished shoes at production cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between product costs and period costs. Give one example of each for a shoe manufacturer.
parts.answer: Product costs are the costs of making the goods (direct materials, direct labour, production overheads); they are included in the value of inventory and charged as cost of sales when the goods are sold, e.g. leather. Period costs are not part of production (administration, selling and distribution); they are charged in full against profit in the period in which they are incurred, e.g. sales staff salaries.
parts.working: 1 mark each definition, 1 mark each valid example.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A semi-variable cost is $13,000 when 2,000 units are made and $22,000 when 5,000 units are made. What will the cost be when 6,500 units are made?
A $19,500
B $26,500
C $28,600
D $42,250
parts.working: Variable cost per unit = 9,000 ÷ 3,000 = $3; fixed element = 13,000 − 2,000 × 3 = 7,000. At 6,500 units: 7,000 + 6,500 × 3 = 26,500. C treats the whole cost as variable (22,000 ÷ 5,000 × 6,500).

practice.stem:
The production costs of Northern Plastics, Abbottabad, for five months were:
Month          Units  Total cost $
January        4,200        31,860
February       5,600        38,020
March          3,500        28,780
April          6,100        40,220
May            4,800        34,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the high–low method to calculate the variable cost per unit.
parts.working: (40,220 − 28,780) ÷ (6,100 − 3,500) = 11,440 ÷ 2,600 = $4.40. M1 using the highest and lowest output (not the highest and lowest cost) A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fixed cost per month.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the expected total cost for a month in which 7,000 units are made.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one limitation of the high–low method.
parts.answer: It uses only two observations, which may not be typical; the forecast for 7,000 units is outside the range of the data and assumes cost behaviour stays the same.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid limitation.

practice.stem: Punjab Uniform Company receives an order for 500 school uniforms. Costs for the order are: direct materials $6,250; direct labour 550 hours costing $4,400; a design royalty of $350 payable for this order. Production overheads are absorbed at $8 per direct labour hour. Administration and selling overheads are charged at 15% of production cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a cost statement for the order showing prime cost, production cost and total cost.
parts.answer:
Direct materials                                6,250
Direct labour                                   4,400
Direct expenses (design royalty)                  350
Prime cost                                     11,000
Production overheads (550 hours × $8)           4,400
Production cost                                15,400
Administration and selling (15%)                2,310
Total cost                                     17,710
parts.working: 1 mark prime cost; 1 mark overhead absorbed; 1 mark production cost; 1 mark administration and total cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost per uniform.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the selling price per uniform if the company wants a profit margin of 25% on the selling price. Give your answer to the nearest cent.
parts.working: Cost is 75% of the price: 35.42 ÷ 0.75 = 47.23. M1 dividing by 0.75 (not multiplying by 1.25) A1.

practice.stem:
A food processing company in Nairobi records three costs at two levels of output.
Cost      1,000 units $  3,000 units $
X                 6,000          6,000
Y                 4,500         13,500
Z                 5,000          9,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each cost X, Y and Z by its behaviour. Give a reason for each.
parts.answer: X is fixed (total unchanged when output changes); Y is variable (total rises in proportion: $4.50 per unit at both outputs); Z is semi-variable (rises with output but not in proportion: it has a fixed element).
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total of the three costs at an output of 2,400 units.
parts.working: X 6,000; Y 2,400 × 4.50 = 10,800; Z: variable 2 per unit, fixed 3,000, so 3,000 + 2,400 × 2 = 7,800. Total 24,600. 1 mark each cost.

practice.stem: Taj Ceramics, Gujrat, makes tiles. Variable cost is $7.50 per unit. General fixed costs are $18,000 per month. One quality supervisor, paid $3,600 per month, is needed for every 2,500 units (or part of 2,500 units) produced each month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total monthly cost at outputs of 4,000, 5,000 and 6,000 units.
parts.working: Supervisors needed: 2, 2 and 3. 1 mark each total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost per unit at each output.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct, 1 mark for two correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cost per unit falls by much less between 5,000 and 6,000 units than between 4,000 and 5,000 units.
parts.answer: The supervisors' cost is a stepped fixed cost. Above 5,000 units a third supervisor is needed, so fixed costs rise by $3,600 and the benefit of spreading fixed costs over more units is partly lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: stepped fixed cost identified; 1 mark: extra supervisor at 6,000 units increases total fixed cost.

practice.stem: Bengal Shirts, Dhaka, recorded total overheads of $186,000 in a month with 12,000 machine hours and $221,000 in a month with 15,500 machine hours. A new customer offers to buy 2,000 shirts at $11 each. Each shirt needs direct materials $3.20, direct labour $2.40 and 0.5 machine hours. The factory has spare capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the variable overhead per machine hour and the fixed overhead per month.
parts.answer: Variable $10 per machine hour; fixed $66,000 per month

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total variable cost of the special order.
parts.working: Materials and labour 2,000 × 5.60 = 11,200; variable overhead 1,000 hours × 10 = 10,000; total 21,200. M1 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the company whether it should accept the order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Accept, subject to the points below. Revenue 22,000 − variable cost 21,200 = contribution $800; fixed overhead does not change, so profit rises by $800. However the margin is very small; check there is spare machine capacity, that regular customers will not demand the same low price, and whether the order may lead to future work.
parts.working: 1 mark contribution calculated; 1 mark relevant non-financial point(s); 1 mark clear decision consistent with the analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prices of raw materials have risen steadily during the year. Compared with AVCO, what is the effect of using FIFO?
A higher closing inventory and higher gross profit
B higher closing inventory and lower gross profit
C lower closing inventory and higher gross profit
D lower closing inventory and lower gross profit
parts.answer: A higher closing inventory and higher gross profit
parts.working: Under FIFO the oldest (cheapest) units are issued first, so closing inventory is valued at the latest, higher prices. Cost of sales is lower, so gross profit is higher. B forgets that a higher closing inventory reduces cost of sales.

practice.stem:
Kashmir Carpet Weavers records the following movements of wool in January.
Date    Details
1 Jan   Opening inventory 400 kg at $8.00 per kg
6 Jan   Received 600 kg at $8.50 per kg
12 Jan  Issued 700 kg to production
20 Jan  Received 500 kg at $9.00 per kg
27 Jan  Issued 600 kg to production

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using FIFO, calculate the value of each issue of wool.
parts.answer: 12 January $5,750; 27 January $5,250

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the inventory at 31 January.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Rania is choosing a method of valuing the inventory of spare parts for her motorcycle repair business in Amman.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of the FIFO method of inventory valuation.
parts.answer: Any two: follows the usual physical flow of goods; closing inventory is valued at recent prices; easy to understand; no averages need to be recalculated; acceptable under IAS 2.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of the AVCO method.
parts.answer: Any one: it smooths out price changes so that issue prices and profits fluctuate less; all units of the same item are given the same value.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why a company preparing financial statements under international standards may not use LIFO.
parts.answer: IAS 2 Inventories does not allow LIFO.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business had an opening inventory of 200 units costing $5 each. It bought 300 units at $6 each and then 250 units at $6.40 each. It then issued 450 units. Using FIFO, what is the value of the closing inventory?
A $1,600
B $1,760
C $1,900
D $1,920
parts.working: 300 units remain: the latest 250 at $6.40 = 1,600 and 50 at $6 = 300, total 1,900. B is a weighted average value (1,760); A values the closing units at the oldest prices.

practice.stem:
Indus Paints, Karachi, buys solvent for its factory. Movements in March were:
1 Mar opening inventory 1,000 litres at $2.40
3 Mar received 1,500 litres at $2.60
10 Mar issued 1,800 litres
18 Mar received 1,300 litres at $2.80
25 Mar issued 1,200 litres

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the AVCO (weighted average cost) method, calculate the value of each issue. Show the average cost after each receipt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of the closing inventory on 31 March.
parts.working: 1 mark, own figure.

practice.stem:
SunPower Traders, Bahawalpur, sells solar panels.
1 Apr opening inventory 20 panels at $150
5 Apr bought 40 panels at $160
14 Apr sold 45 panels at $240 each
22 Apr bought 30 panels at $170
29 Apr sold 35 panels at $250 each

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory on 30 April using FIFO.
parts.working: 10 panels remain, all from the 22 April purchase: 10 × 170 = 1,700. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of closing inventory on 30 April using AVCO (perpetual). Give your answer to the nearest cent.
parts.working: After 5 Apr: 60 units, 9,400, average 156.67; 14 Apr issue 45 → balance 15 units 2,350. After 22 Apr: 45 units 7,450, average 165.56; 29 Apr issue 35 → balance 10 units = 7,450 × 10/45 = 1,655.56. 1 mark each stage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit for April under each method.

practice.stem:
Falcon Pharma Distributors uses AVCO. Its profits and closing inventory values were:
                                Year 1 $  Year 2 $
Profit for the year (AVCO)        71,200    84,000
Closing inventory: AVCO           45,900    50,100
Closing inventory: FIFO           48,600    52,300
Opening inventory for year 1 was the same under both methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for year 1 if FIFO had been used.
parts.working: Higher closing inventory raises profit: 71,200 + (48,600 − 45,900) = 73,900. M1 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for year 2 if FIFO had been used.
parts.working: Opening inventory is also higher under FIFO, which reduces profit: 84,000 + (52,300 − 50,100) − (48,600 − 45,900) = 83,500. M1 closing adjustment; M1 opening adjustment; A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The directors receive a bonus based on profit and want to change from AVCO to FIFO. Advise them whether they should make this change. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Points for: FIFO is allowed by IAS 2; inventory in the statement of financial position is closer to current prices; profit would have been higher in year 1.
Points against: the consistency concept means a method should be changed only if the new one gives a fairer view, and the change must be disclosed; over time total profit is the same (year 2 would be lower); changing to raise bonuses is unethical and misleading to users.
Decision: do not change merely to increase the bonus.
parts.working: 1 mark points for/against using figures; 1 mark consistency/IAS 2; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem:
Faisal Spinning Mills records cotton yarn using AVCO (perpetual). June movements:
1 Jun opening inventory 2,000 kg at $3.00
4 Jun received 3,000 kg at $3.25
9 Jun issued 3,600 kg to production
13 Jun 200 kg of the yarn issued on 9 June returned to stores unused
17 Jun received 2,400 kg at $3.40
26 Jun issued 2,500 kg to production

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the stores ledger card for June using AVCO.
parts.working: 1 mark each: average 3.15 after 4 June; issue 11,340; return of 200 kg at 3.15 = 630 added; new average (5,040 + 8,160) ÷ 4,000 = 3.30; issue 8,250.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of the inventory at 30 June.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the yarn returned on 13 June is valued at $3.15 per kg.
parts.answer: It is returned at the price at which it was issued on 9 June, so that the cost charged to production is reduced by the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a feature of a just-in-time (JIT) system of inventory management?
A raw materials are delivered in small quantities as they are needed
B large buffer inventories are held in case of supplier delays
C materials are bought in bulk to obtain trade discounts
D suppliers are chosen only on the basis of the lowest price
parts.answer: A raw materials are delivered in small quantities as they are needed
parts.working: JIT aims to hold little or no inventory, so deliveries arrive in small batches just before they are used. B and C describe the opposite approach; under JIT suppliers are chosen for reliability and quality, not only price (D).

practice.stem: Indus Auto Parts, Karachi, assembles brake units for car manufacturers. It currently keeps three months' inventory of components in a rented warehouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages to the business of adopting a just-in-time system.
parts.answer: Any two explained: lower holding costs (storage space, insurance, security); less working capital tied up in inventory, improving cash flow; less risk of obsolescence, damage or theft; storage space can be used for production; close links with suppliers can improve quality.
parts.working: 1 mark each advantage, 1 mark each explanation in context.

practice.stem: Pearl Electronics, Penang, holds average inventory of $300,000. Under JIT this would fall to $60,000. The warehouse no longer needed could be rented out for $2,500 per month. Insurance is 1.5% of average inventory. Annual losses from obsolete inventory would fall from $9,000 to $1,500. A supplier liaison officer would be employed at a salary of $22,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual benefit of introducing JIT.
parts.answer:
Rent from warehouse: 12 × $2,500                       30,000
Insurance saved: 1.5% × (300,000 − 60,000)              3,600
Obsolescence losses saved: 9,000 − 1,500                7,500
Less salary of supplier liaison officer              (22,000)
Net annual benefit                                     19,100
parts.working: 1 mark each item; total own figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two risks of introducing JIT for this business.
parts.answer: Any two: late or failed deliveries stopping production; loss of bulk discounts; supplier price rises once the firm depends on them; sudden increases in demand cannot be met; quality problems.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about just-in-time inventory management are correct?
1 It reduces the cost of storing inventory.
2 It increases the risk that production will stop.
3 It makes it easier to obtain bulk-purchase discounts.
4 It depends on reliable suppliers.
A 1, 2 and 4
B 1 and 3 only
C 2, 3 and 4
D 3 and 4 only
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 4
parts.working: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: JIT orders are small and frequent, so bulk-purchase discounts are usually lost.

practice.stem: Green Valley Foods, Mardan, holds average inventory of raw materials of $240,000. Annual holding costs are 18% of average inventory. Under a proposed JIT system average inventory would fall to $40,000. There would be 500 extra deliveries a year costing $12 each, and suppliers would increase prices by 1% on annual purchases of $1,200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net annual saving from introducing JIT.
parts.answer:
Holding cost saved: (240,000 − 40,000) × 18%       36,000
Less extra delivery costs: 500 × $12              (6,000)
Less price increase: 1% × 1,200,000              (12,000)
Net annual saving                                  18,000
parts.working: M1 A1 holding cost saving; B1 delivery costs; B1 price increase; A1 net saving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the managers whether to introduce JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: The saving of $18,000 supports JIT. But the company must be confident of its suppliers' reliability, since a late delivery would stop production; demand must be steady; and the 1% price rise may grow. Decision: introduce JIT if suppliers can guarantee delivery, perhaps keeping a small buffer at first.
parts.working: 1 mark use of the figure; 1 mark non-financial factor(s); 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: A furniture manufacturer in Chiang Mai, Thailand, is thinking of changing to JIT for its supplies of timber and fittings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two conditions that must exist for a just-in-time system to work successfully.
parts.answer: Any two explained: reliable suppliers that can deliver at short notice; suppliers located close by or good transport links; high and consistent quality of materials (no time to replace faulty items); stable, predictable demand and production schedules; good communication/IT links with suppliers; a flexible, well-trained workforce.
parts.working: 1 mark each condition, 1 mark each explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one effect of JIT on the working capital of a business.
parts.answer: Less money is tied up in inventory, so cash is released (current assets fall).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Atlas Bicycles, Lahore, is considering JIT for its components. Average inventory would fall from $380,000 to $120,000; holding costs are 20% a year of average inventory. The number of orders would rise from 12 to 150 a year, each costing $85 to process. The production manager expects JIT to cause 4 days of production stoppage a year, losing contribution of $6,500 per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net annual financial effect of adopting JIT.
parts.answer:
Holding cost saved: (380,000 − 120,000) × 20%          52,000
Less extra ordering costs: (150 − 12) × $85          (11,730)
Less expected lost contribution: 4 × $6,500          (26,000)
Net annual saving                                      14,270
parts.working: 1 mark holding cost; 1 mark ordering cost (138 extra orders); 1 mark stoppage cost; 1 mark net saving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of days of stoppage per year at which JIT would no longer be worthwhile.
parts.answer: More than 6.20 days, i.e. 7 or more whole days

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise the directors whether to adopt JIT. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: a net saving is expected; less cash tied up in inventory. Against: the saving depends heavily on the stoppage estimate; only about two more days of stoppage would remove it; supplier reliability and transport links must be checked. Decision consistent with these points, e.g. adopt only with a supplier guarantee or penalty clause.
parts.working: 1 mark for points for and against; 1 mark justified decision.

practice.stem: Sindhri Juices, Multan, makes mango juice. Fresh mangoes are available locally only from June to August; the company freezes pulp in a large cold store so that it can make juice all year. Bottles and cartons are bought from a nearby supplier who can deliver daily. The directors have read that JIT reduces costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors whether Sindhri Juices should adopt just-in-time purchasing for fresh mangoes. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
For JIT: less fresh fruit wasted through spoilage; lower cold-storage costs; less cash tied up; fruit used fresher, improving quality.
Against JIT: mangoes are available only in a short season, so supply cannot be called off all year; prices rise sharply out of season; weather can disrupt harvests and transport; juice production must run at full capacity during the season.
Possible compromise: JIT for packaging and bottles, which can be supplied all year, but bulk buying and pulp storage for mangoes.
Decision: do not adopt JIT for mangoes.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for; up to 2 marks for points against (in context); 1 mark for a compromise or further analysis; 1 mark justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A worker is paid $12 per hour for a basic week of 40 hours. Overtime is paid at time-and-a-half. In one week she works 44 hours. What is her gross pay?
A $528
B $552
C $576
D $792
parts.working: 40 × 12 + 4 × 18 = 480 + 72 = 552. A pays all hours at the basic rate; C pays the overtime at double time.

practice.stem: Hassan runs a repair workshop for air-conditioning units in Doha and is deciding how to pay his technicians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to the employer of paying workers a time rate rather than a piece rate.
parts.answer: Advantage (any one explained): quality is not sacrificed for speed; pay is simple to calculate; suitable where output cannot be measured. Disadvantage (any one explained): no incentive to work faster, so supervision is needed; labour cost per unit rises when output falls.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage, 1 mark explanation; 1 mark disadvantage, 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: A garment workshop in Karachi pays machinists $0.85 per garment with a guaranteed minimum of $360 per week. Output in one week was: Asif 520 garments, Bilal 390 garments, Chen 465 garments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross pay of each worker for the week.
parts.working: Asif 520 × 0.85 = 442.00; Bilal 390 × 0.85 = 331.50, below the minimum so paid 360.00; Chen 465 × 0.85 = 395.25. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total labour cost and the labour cost per unit produced. Give the cost per unit to the nearest cent.
parts.working: Total 1,197.25 ÷ 1,375 units = 0.87. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason for paying a guaranteed minimum wage.
parts.answer: Gives workers security of income when output is low for reasons outside their control (machine breakdown, shortage of materials); may be required by law.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Twelve production workers at Margalla Furniture each worked 45 hours last week. The basic week is 40 hours at $10 per hour, and overtime is paid at time-and-a-half. The overtime was needed because of a general increase in orders, not for any particular job.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total gross wages for the week.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much of the gross wages should be treated as direct labour and how much as production overhead.
parts.answer: Direct labour $5,400; production overhead $300
parts.working: All hours at basic rate are direct: 12 × 45 × $10 = 5,400. The overtime premium 12 × 5 × $5 = 300 is overhead because the overtime was due to the general level of work. 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain when the overtime premium would be treated as a direct cost.
parts.answer: When the overtime is worked at the specific request of a customer or for a particular job, the premium can be traced to that job and is charged to it as direct labour.
parts.working: 1 mark specific job/customer; 1 mark charged directly to that job.

practice.stem: Workers at Rose Valley Packaging, Swat, are paid $14 per hour plus a bonus of 50% of the time saved, valued at the hourly rate. The standard time is 0.4 hours per unit. In one week both Farida and Gul worked 38 hours. Farida produced 110 units and Gul produced 92 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross pay of each worker for the week.
parts.answer: Farida $574; Gul $532
parts.working: Farida: standard time 110 × 0.4 = 44 hours, time saved 6 hours, bonus 50% × 6 × 14 = 42; pay 532 + 42 = 574. Gul: standard time 92 × 0.4 = 36.8 hours, no time saved, pay 38 × 14 = 532. 2 marks each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per unit for each worker. Give your answers to the nearest cent.
parts.answer: Farida $5.22; Gul $5.78
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the bonus scheme benefits the company.
parts.answer: Benefit: the faster worker's cost per unit is lower even after the bonus, because time saved is shared 50:50. Drawback: workers may rush and quality may fall; slow workers still receive full time-rate pay, so there is no penalty.
parts.working: 1 mark each point.

practice.stem: Two traders in Karachi, one selling dried fruit and one with a shop in Dubai, agree to work together for one shipment only and share the profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'joint venture'.
parts.answer: A short-term business arrangement in which two or more parties combine resources for a single, specific project and share the resulting profit or loss in an agreed ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: two or more parties for a specific/single project. 1 mark: temporary, sharing profit or loss in agreed ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between a joint venture and a partnership.
parts.answer: A joint venture ends when the project is completed, whereas a partnership continues indefinitely; joint venturers usually carry on their own separate businesses and there is usually no firm name or separate continuing set of books.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: duration (temporary vs continuing); scope (one project vs ongoing business); venturers keep own businesses; no firm name / records often kept in venturers' own books.

practice.stem: A Pakistani rice mill is considering a joint venture with a packaging company in Malaysia to supply a large supermarket order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why the rice mill might enter into the joint venture.
parts.answer: To share the cost and risk of the order; to use the partner's skills, contacts and packaging facilities.
parts.working: 1 mark each: share risk/finance; access to expertise, contacts or market; complete an order too large alone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two risks for the rice mill of entering into the joint venture.
parts.answer: Disagreements over how profit and costs are shared; the other venturer may fail to meet its obligations or may mishandle the money received.
parts.working: 1 mark each: disputes; dependence on partner's performance; loss of control; unlimited liability for shared losses; delays in settlement.

practice.stem: Ikram keeps a 'Joint venture with Salma' account in his own books. The venture has made a profit and Ikram's share is $4,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the double entry in Ikram's books to record his share of the profit.
parts.answer: Debit Joint venture with Salma account $4,600; credit statement of profit or loss (profit on joint venture) $4,600.
parts.working: 1 mark debit; 1 mark credit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After his share of profit is recorded, Ikram's 'Joint venture with Salma' account has a debit balance of $9,300. Explain what this balance shows and how it will be cleared.
parts.answer: Salma owes Ikram $9,300 (she has received more from the venture than her costs plus her share of profit); it is cleared when Salma pays Ikram $9,300 (debit bank, credit the joint venture account).
parts.working: 1 mark: Salma owes Ikram / receivable. 1 mark: cleared by cash received from Salma.

practice.stem: Sialkot Leather sends handbags to an agent in Doha. The agent sells them for a commission and returns the money. A competitor instead works with a Doha trader who shares the profit on the goods equally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which arrangement is a consignment and which is a joint venture.
parts.answer: Sialkot Leather and its agent: consignment. The competitor and the Doha trader: joint venture.
parts.working: B1 both correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two differences between a consignment and a joint venture.
parts.answer: In a consignment the consignor owns the goods until they are sold and bears all the profit or loss; the agent earns only commission. In a joint venture the venturers are co-owners for the project and share profit or loss in an agreed ratio. Also, a consignee acts for the consignor as agent, whereas joint venturers are like temporary partners with equal standing.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per difference: ownership of goods; who bears profit/loss (commission vs share of profit); relationship (principal–agent vs co-venturers).

practice.stem: Asif (Lahore) and Bano (Karachi) agree a joint venture to sell 2,000 cricket bats, sharing profits equally. Asif bought the bats for $36,000 and paid carriage of $1,500. Bano paid advertising of $2,800 and sold all the bats for $52,000, keeping the cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.answer: $5,850 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount that must be paid in settlement, and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Bano pays Asif $43,350.
parts.working: Asif: 37,500 + 5,850 = 43,350 due to him (M1); Bano pays Asif 43,350 (A1).

practice.stem:
Chaudhry and Daniyal entered a joint venture to trade in basmati rice, sharing profits and losses 3:2. Each recorded his own transactions.
Chaudhry: bought rice $64,000; paid transport $3,200; sold rice for $30,000.
Daniyal: paid storage $2,400; paid packing $1,900; sold rice for $52,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account       $
Dr
Purchases of rice (Chaudhry)      64,000
Transport (Chaudhry)               3,200
Storage (Daniyal)                  2,400
Packing (Daniyal)                  1,900
Share of profit – Chaudhry         6,300
Share of profit – Daniyal          4,200
                                  82,000
Cr
Sales (Chaudhry)                  30,000
Sales (Daniyal)                   52,000
                                  82,000
parts.working: B1 purchases and transport; B1 storage and packing; B1 sales 82,000; B1 profit 10,500; B1 shares Chaudhry 6,300, Daniyal 4,200.

practice.stem:
Kashif and Lubna share joint venture profits 2:3. A summary of their joint venture records:
                         Kashif $  Lubna $
Costs paid                 21,500    4,700
Sales proceeds received     9,000   30,200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the joint venture profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.answer: Kashif $5,200; Lubna $7,800.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the settlement payment and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Lubna pays Kashif $17,700.

practice.stem: Usama and Wardah contributed $30,000 and $50,000 respectively to a joint venture importing tiles. They agreed to share the profit in the ratio of their contributions. The profit was $48,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the profit.
parts.answer: Usama $18,000; Wardah $30,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why venturers might agree to share profit in the ratio of the money contributed rather than equally.
parts.answer: The venturer who puts in more money takes more risk and gives up the use of more funds, so a larger share rewards that contribution fairly.
parts.working: 1 mark: reflects risk/finance provided. 1 mark: fairness / equal sharing would favour the smaller contributor.

practice.stem:
Waseem and Yumna are in a joint venture. In Waseem's books the following took place:
1 Waseem paid $15,000 by bank for goods for the venture
2 Waseem received $9,000 by bank from sales of venture goods
3 Waseem's share of the venture profit was $2,750
4 Yumna paid Waseem the amount due to settle the venture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare journal entries in Waseem's books for items 1 to 4. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
Dr $    Cr $
1 Joint venture with Yumna                 15,000
  Bank                                             15,000
2 Bank                                      9,000
  Joint venture with Yumna                          9,000
3 Joint venture with Yumna                  2,750
  Statement of profit or loss (JV profit)           2,750
4 Bank                                      8,750
  Joint venture with Yumna                          8,750
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct entry; settlement 15,000 − 9,000 + 2,750 = 8,750.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the balance on the 'Joint venture with Yumna' account would appear in Waseem's statement of financial position if Yumna had not yet paid.
parts.answer: As a current asset (receivable: amount due from Yumna).

practice.stem: Arif and Bina share joint venture profits equally. Arif paid costs of $12,000. Bina paid costs of $3,000 and received all the sales proceeds of $20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the joint venture profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the settlement payment and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Bina pays Arif $14,500.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Before settlement, state whether the 'Joint venture with Bina' account in Arif's books has a debit or a credit balance, and what it represents.
parts.answer: A debit balance of $14,500, representing the amount Bina owes Arif (an asset/receivable).
parts.working: 1 mark: debit. 1 mark: amount owed by Bina.

practice.stem: Two venturers each record their own joint venture transactions in their own books. At the end of the venture a memorandum joint venture account is prepared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer: It brings together the transactions of all venturers to calculate the profit or loss of the whole venture, so that it can be shared in the agreed ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: combines all venturers' transactions. 1 mark: to find total profit/loss to be shared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the memorandum joint venture account is not part of the double-entry system.
parts.answer: Each transaction has already been recorded in a venturer's own 'Joint venture with …' account; the memorandum account is a working statement prepared from copies of those records, so no entries are posted from it.
parts.working: 1 mark: transactions already recorded in venturers' own books. 1 mark: it is only a statement/memorandum, no double entry.

practice.stem: Joint venture transactions may be recorded either in a separate set of books with a joint bank account, or in each venturer's own books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of keeping a separate set of books with a joint bank account.
parts.answer: Advantage: all receipts and payments pass through one account, so the venture's records are complete and transparent and the profit is easy to calculate. Disadvantage: it costs more time and money to open an account and keep extra books, which may not be worthwhile for a small, short venture.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for an advantage (identify + explain) and up to 2 marks for a disadvantage (identify + explain).

practice.stem: At 31 December 2025, Amjad's joint venture with Bushra had been completed, but Bushra had not yet paid Amjad the $12,400 owed to him. Amjad's share of the venture profit was $5,100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how the $5,100 should be shown in Amjad's statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 2025.
parts.answer: As income: 'share of profit on joint venture' $5,100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the $12,400 should be shown in Amjad's statement of financial position at 31 December 2025, and explain why.
parts.answer: As a current asset (other receivable – amount due from Bushra), because it is money owed to Amjad that he expects to receive within a year.
parts.working: 1 mark: current asset/receivable. 1 mark: reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the accounting concept that requires the profit to be recognised in 2025 even though the cash has not been received.
parts.answer: Accruals (matching) concept.
parts.working: B1 accruals (also accept realisation).

practice.stem: Ejaz and Fatima share joint venture profits equally. Ejaz sent goods from his own inventory costing $24,000 and paid freight of $1,100. He sold some of the goods for $18,000. Fatima paid selling expenses of $2,500 and sold the rest of the goods for $22,000. The venture was then completed and settled in cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Fatima' account in Ejaz's books, including the settlement.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Fatima (Ejaz's books)       $
Dr
Goods from own inventory                  24,000
Freight                                    1,100
Share of profit                            6,200
                                          31,300
Cr
Sales                                     18,000
Bank – received from Fatima               13,300
                                          31,300
parts.working: B1 goods and freight debited; B1 sales credited; B1 share of profit 6,200 debited; B1 settlement received from Fatima 13,300 credited; B1 account balances (totals 31,300).

practice.stem: Ghulam and Hassan bought and resold used cars in Rawalpindi as a joint venture, sharing profits 2:1. Ghulam bought the cars for $45,000 and paid repairs of $3,600. Hassan paid advertising of $1,200 and registration fees of $900, and sold all the cars for $58,500. The venture made a profit of $7,800 and was settled in cash.

parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Hassan' account in Ghulam's books.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Hassan (Ghulam's books)       $
Dr
Purchase of cars                            45,000
Repairs                                      3,600
Share of profit                              5,200

Cr

parts.working: B1 cars and repairs; B1 share of profit 5,200; B1 cash received from Hassan 53,800.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Ghulam' account in Hassan's books.
parts.answer:
