practice.stem: Mehdi and Nida ran a summer camp in Murree as a joint venture, sharing profits equally. They opened a joint bank account: Mehdi paid in $25,000 and Nida $15,000. From the joint bank account they paid: venue hire $18,000; food $12,500; staff $7,300; transport $4,200. Camp fees of $52,000 were paid into the account. At the end, the venturers were paid what was due to them and the account was closed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the joint bank account.
parts.answer:
Joint bank account          $
Dr
Mehdi – capital        25,000
Nida – capital         15,000
Camp fees              52,000
                       92,000
Cr
Venue hire             18,000
Food                   12,500
Staff                   7,300
Transport               4,200
Mehdi – final payment  30,000
Nida – final payment   20,000
                       92,000
parts.working: B1 capital paid in; B1 fees and payments; B1 final payments 30,000 and 20,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the amounts paid to Mehdi and Nida at the end are different although they share profit equally.
parts.answer: Each receives his or her own capital back plus a $5,000 share of profit; Mehdi contributed $10,000 more capital, so he receives $30,000 and Nida $20,000.
parts.working: 1 mark: capital returned plus share. 1 mark: figures.

practice.stem: Usman and Vikram organised a one-night music concert in Dubai as a joint venture, sharing profits 3:2. Usman paid venue hire of $28,000 and sound equipment hire of $6,500, and received all ticket sales of $92,000. Vikram paid the artist's fee of $40,000 and advertising of $5,500, and received sponsorship of $8,000.

parts.answer:

Share of profit – Vikram            8,000

Cr
Ticket sales (Usman)               92,000
Sponsorship (Vikram)                8,000
                                  100,000
parts.working: B1 costs 80,000; B1 income 100,000; B1 profit 20,000; B1 shares 12,000 / 8,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Vikram' account in Usman's books, including the settlement.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Vikram (Usman's books)       $
Dr
Venue hire (Usman)                         28,000

practice.stem: Xenia (Dubai) and Yasir (Karachi) imported a consignment of dates as a joint venture, sharing profits and losses equally. Xenia bought the dates for $32,000 and paid shipping of $4,400. Yasir paid customs duty of $2,100 and warehousing of $1,500. Part of the shipment was damaged and Yasir sold all the dates for only $36,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account       $
Dr
Purchase of dates (Xenia)         32,000
Shipping (Xenia)                   4,400
Customs duty (Yasir)               2,100
Warehousing (Yasir)                1,500
                                  40,000
Cr
Sales (Yasir)                     36,800
Loss – Xenia                       1,600
Loss – Yasir                       1,600
                                  40,000
parts.working: B1 costs 40,000; B1 sales; B1 loss 3,200 shown on credit side; B1 shared 1,600 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Xenia' account in Yasir's books, including the settlement.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Xenia (Yasir's books)       $
Dr
Customs duty (Yasir)                       2,100
Warehousing (Yasir)                        1,500
Bank – paid to Xenia                      34,800
                                          38,400
Cr
Sales (Yasir)                             36,800
Share of loss                              1,600
                                          38,400
parts.working: B1 customs and warehousing debited; B1 sales and share of loss 1,600 credited; B1 cash paid to Xenia 34,800.

practice.stem: Daud and Eman share joint venture profits 3:2. Daud supplied goods from his own inventory at cost, $30,000. Eman paid delivery costs of $1,700 and sold all the goods on credit for $45,000. She allowed cash discounts of $600, and one customer owing $1,500 became bankrupt and paid nothing. Eman collected the rest of the money.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account       $
Dr
Goods supplied (Daud)             30,000
Delivery (Eman)                    1,700
Discounts allowed (Eman)             600
Irrecoverable debt (Eman)          1,500
Share of profit – Daud             6,720
Share of profit – Eman             4,480
                                  45,000
Cr
Sales (Eman)                      45,000
                                  45,000
parts.working: B1 goods and delivery; B1 discount and irrecoverable debt debited; B1 profit 11,200; B1 shares 6,720 / 4,480.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount Eman must pay Daud in settlement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the irrecoverable debt is charged to the joint venture rather than borne by Eman alone.
parts.answer: The sale was made on behalf of the venture, so the risk of non-payment is a cost of the venture shared by both venturers, unless the agreement makes Eman responsible (e.g. through a del credere commission).
parts.working: 1 mark: sale made for the joint venture. 1 mark: losses shared in agreed ratio unless agreement says otherwise.

practice.stem: Jamal and Kinza share joint venture profits 2:1. Jamal bought goods for $33,000 and sent Kinza a cash advance of $8,000 to help her pay the venture's expenses. Kinza paid expenses of $6,700 and sold all the goods for $52,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit on the joint venture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Kinza' account in Jamal's books, including the settlement.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Kinza (Jamal's books)       $
Dr
Goods                                     33,000
Bank – advance to Kinza                    8,000
Share of profit                            8,200
                                          49,200
Cr
Bank – received from Kinza                49,200
                                          49,200
parts.working: B1 goods and advance debited; B1 share of profit 8,200; B1 cash received from Kinza 49,200.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the $8,000 advance does not appear in the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer: The advance is only a transfer of cash between the two venturers; it is not income or a cost of the venture, so it does not affect the profit. It is cancelled out in the settlement.
parts.working: 1 mark: transfer between venturers. 1 mark: no effect on profit.

practice.stem:
Haider Builders, Lahore, wants to bid for a bridge contract worth $2,400,000.
Option 1: bid alone. Haider would have to hire specialist equipment and engineers; total costs are estimated at $2,280,000.
Option 2: form a joint venture with a foreign engineering company. Total costs of the venture are estimated at $1,950,000 and Haider would receive 40% of the profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Haider's expected profit under each option.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Haider Builders which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For the joint venture: higher expected profit ($60,000 more); the foreign partner's expertise lowers the risk of cost overruns and delays; Haider gains experience for future bridge contracts; less finance needed. Against: Haider loses control over decisions; profit depends on the partner's performance; disputes over sharing; Haider builds less of its own reputation. Bidding alone keeps all profit but the margin is only 5% of contract value, so a small overrun would cause a loss. Decision: choose the joint venture, provided a clear written agreement sets out duties, profit sharing and settlement.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for the joint venture; up to 2 marks for points against / for bidding alone; 1 mark for use of the calculated figures (e.g. 60,000 difference, 5% margin); 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: Rashid and Tahir share joint venture profits equally. At the end of their venture in garden furniture, unsold goods that cost $6,000 are taken over by Rashid at an agreed value of $4,000, their net realisable value. Before this item, the memorandum joint venture account showed a profit of $15,000 (all goods counted as sold or taken over at cost).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revised joint venture profit.
parts.working: Taking over at 4,000 rather than cost 6,000 reduces the credit by 2,000 (M1); 15,000 − 2,000 = 13,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's share of the revised profit.
parts.answer: $6,500 each

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether the goods should be taken over at net realisable value rather than cost.
parts.answer: Prudence: goods should not be valued above what they can be sold for, so $4,000 is appropriate if NRV is reliable. However, Rashid benefits if he later sells them for more, so the value must be agreed fairly and independently; Tahir bears half the $2,000 reduction. Conclusion: NRV is acceptable if it is agreed by both venturers or set by an independent valuation.
parts.working: 1 mark: prudence / IAS 2 lower of cost and NRV. 1 mark: conflict of interest – taker benefits from low value. 1 mark: conclusion/agreement needed.

practice.stem:
Iqbal and Javeria entered a joint venture to make and sell embroidered garments in Faisalabad. Profits after commission are shared Iqbal 3, Javeria 1.
Iqbal bought fabric for $40,000 and paid dyeing costs of $6,000.
Javeria paid stitching costs of $9,000 and sold garments for $68,000. She is entitled to a commission of 5% on her sales.
At the end of the venture Iqbal took over the unsold garments at an agreed value of $4,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account         $
Dr
Fabric (Iqbal)                      40,000
Dyeing (Iqbal)                       6,000
Stitching (Javeria)                  9,000
Commission – Javeria (5% × 68,000)   3,400
Share of profit – Iqbal             10,575
Share of profit – Javeria            3,525
                                    72,500
Cr
Sales (Javeria)                     68,000
Unsold garments taken over (Iqbal)   4,500
                                    72,500
parts.working: B1 costs; B1 commission 3,400 debited; B1 sales and goods taken over credited; B1 profit 14,100; B1 shares 10,575 / 3,525.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount paid in settlement and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Javeria pays Iqbal $52,075.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Javeria's commission is charged before the profit is shared.
parts.answer: The commission rewards Javeria for the extra work of selling; it is a cost of the venture, so it is deducted to find the profit that both share.

practice.stem:
Omer and Parveen set up a joint venture to sell solar panels in rural Sindh, sharing profits 3:2. They opened a joint bank account into which Omer paid $30,000 and Parveen $20,000.
From the joint bank account: a generator for the venture was bought for $12,000; solar panels were bought for $48,000; wages of $6,000 were paid. Sales of $70,000 were banked.
At the end of the venture Omer took over the generator at an agreed value of $9,000 and Parveen took over the unsold panels at $5,500. The bank balance was then paid out to the venturers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the joint venture account (in the separate set of books) showing the profit and its division.
parts.answer:
Joint venture account             $
Dr
Generator                    12,000
Solar panels                 48,000
Wages                         6,000
Profit – Omer (3/5)          11,100
Profit – Parveen (2/5)        7,400
                             84,500
Cr
Sales                        70,000
Generator taken over – Omer   9,000
Panels taken over – Parveen   5,500
                             84,500
parts.working: B1 costs debited; B1 sales and items taken over credited; B1 profit 18,500; B1 shares 11,100 / 7,400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount paid from the joint bank account to each venturer at the end.
parts.answer: Omer $32,100; Parveen $21,900.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the generator was taken over at less than its cost.
parts.answer: It had been used during the venture and had lost value (depreciation/wear).

practice.stem:
Qadir and Rizwan built a block of flats in Islamabad as a joint venture. They agreed that each venturer would receive interest at 10% per annum on money he contributed, from the date of payment until the venture ended on 31 December 2025, and that the remaining profit would be shared equally.
Qadir paid $120,000 for the land on 1 January 2025. Rizwan paid $180,000 for construction on 1 April 2025. On 31 December 2025 all the flats were sold and Qadir received the proceeds of $360,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest due to each venturer.
parts.answer: Qadir $12,000; Rizwan $13,500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit to be shared and each venturer's share.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the settlement payment and state who pays whom.
parts.answer: Qadir pays Rizwan $210,750.
parts.working: Rizwan is due 180,000 + 13,500 + 17,250 = 210,750 (M1); Qadir holds the proceeds and pays him (A1).

practice.stem: Sohail and Tania share joint venture profits equally. Sohail's 'Joint venture with Tania' account showed: goods supplied $26,000; expenses paid by Sohail $3,400; sales made by Sohail $15,000; his share of the profit (figure missing); cash received from Tania in settlement $22,600. Tania paid expenses of $4,800 and made all the other sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Sohail's share of the profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total joint venture profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of the sales made by Tania.

practice.stem:

practice.stem: Hamza and Irum entered a joint venture to trade in surgical instruments from Sialkot, sharing the profit after commissions equally. Irum arranged and paid for purchases of $50,000 and receives 4% commission on purchases. Hamza paid shipping and insurance of $3,000, sold all the instruments for $72,000 and receives 6% commission on sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the commission due to each venturer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit to be shared and each venturer's share.
parts.answer: Profit $12,680; $6,340 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate each venturer's total return from the venture.
parts.working: Commission + share (B1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the settlement payment and state who pays whom.

practice.stem:
Latif, a football maker in Sialkot, and Mason, a sports retailer in Manchester, agreed a joint venture for one shipment of match footballs. Profits after commission are shared Latif 3, Mason 2.
Latif supplied footballs from his factory at a cost of $38,000 and paid freight of $5,200.
Mason paid import duty of $3,800 and warehouse charges of $1,600. He sold two-thirds of the footballs for $54,000, on which he receives a commission of 5%. He took over the remaining footballs at an agreed value of $18,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the memorandum joint venture account.
parts.answer:
Memorandum joint venture account         $
Dr
Footballs from own factory (Latif)  38,000
Freight (Latif)                      5,200
Import duty (Mason)                  3,800
Warehouse charges (Mason)            1,600
Commission – Mason (5% × 54,000)     2,700
Share of profit – Latif             12,720
Share of profit – Mason              8,480
                                    72,500
Cr
Sales (Mason)                       54,000
Footballs taken over (Mason)        18,500
                                    72,500
parts.working: B1 costs incl. commission 2,700; B1 sales and takeover credited; B1 profit 21,200; B1 shares 12,720 / 8,480.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare the 'Joint venture with Latif' account in Mason's books, including the settlement.
parts.answer:
Joint venture with Latif (Mason's books)       $
Dr
Import duty (Mason)                        3,800
Warehouse charges (Mason)                  1,600
Commission – Mason (5% × 54,000)           2,700
Share of profit                            8,480
Bank – paid to Latif                      55,920
                                          72,500

Footballs taken over (Mason)              18,500

parts.working: B1 costs, commission and share of profit debited; B1 sales and footballs taken over credited; B1 cash paid to Latif 55,920.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why Latif receives the larger share of profit.
parts.answer: He provided most of the finance/goods ($43,200 of costs) and so bore more risk.

practice.stem: Karakoram Foods Limited has 4,000 shareholders. The company is run by a board of five directors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term stewardship in the context of a limited company.
parts.answer: Stewardship is the responsibility of the directors to look after the company's resources (assets) properly on behalf of the shareholders who own it, and to account to them for how those resources have been used.
parts.working: 1 mark: directors manage/safeguard resources for shareholders; 1 mark: accountability/reporting to owners.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which directors demonstrate good stewardship.
parts.answer: Any two: keeping proper accounting records; preparing annual financial statements that give a true and fair view; safeguarding assets and preventing fraud through internal controls; having the statements audited and presenting them at the annual general meeting; using resources efficiently in shareholders' interests.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between an internal auditor and an external auditor.
parts.answer: Any two: appointment — internal auditor is an employee appointed by management, external auditor is independent and appointed by the shareholders; reporting — internal auditor reports to the directors/audit committee, external auditor reports to the shareholders; purpose — internal audit reviews systems, controls and efficiency for management, external audit gives an opinion on whether the statements give a true and fair view; legal requirement — external audit is required by law for most companies, internal audit is optional; qualification/independence — external auditor must be a registered, independent accountant.
parts.working: 2 marks per difference (both sides compared).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three statutory rights of a company's external auditor.
parts.answer: Any three: right of access at all times to the company's books, records and vouchers; right to require information and explanations from directors and officers; right to receive notice of and attend general meetings; right to speak at general meetings on matters concerning them as auditor; right to make written representations if they are to be removed or not reappointed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the meaning of the phrase 'a true and fair view'.
parts.answer: The financial statements are free from material misstatement and fairly present the company's financial performance and position, prepared in accordance with accounting standards and the law. It does not mean that every figure is exactly correct.
parts.working: 1 mark: free from material misstatement / faithfully presented; 1 mark: in accordance with standards / not absolute accuracy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State who is responsible for preparing a company's financial statements.
parts.answer: The directors (not the auditors).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State who appoints the external auditors of a limited company, and to whom they report.
parts.answer: They are appointed by the shareholders (usually at the annual general meeting) and report to the shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that the external auditor is independent of the directors.
parts.answer: The auditor checks the statements prepared by the directors; if not independent they might be influenced to accept misstatements, so shareholders could not rely on the opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark: checking directors' work / objective opinion; 1 mark: shareholders' reliance/confidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four items normally included in an external auditor's report.
parts.answer: Any four: title and addressee (the shareholders); the auditor's opinion; basis for opinion (statement that the audit was done under auditing standards and the auditor is independent); key audit matters (for listed companies); material uncertainty related to going concern, if any; responsibilities of the directors for the financial statements; responsibilities of the auditor; auditor's name, signature, address and date.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two threats to the independence of an external auditor.
parts.answer: Self-interest: e.g. the auditor owns shares in the client or depends heavily on its fees, so may avoid a qualified opinion. Self-review: the audit firm also prepares the accounts it audits. Familiarity: a long relationship or family ties with directors. Intimidation: directors threaten to remove the auditor. Advocacy: the auditor promotes the client's interests.
parts.working: 2 marks each: threat named + example/explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Other than shareholders, name two groups who rely on a company's audited financial statements, and explain why each relies on the audit.
parts.answer: Any two: banks/lenders — deciding whether to lend and checking loan covenants, need assurance figures are reliable; suppliers — deciding whether to give credit; tax authorities — assessing tax payable; potential investors — deciding whether to buy shares; employees/trade unions — job security and pay negotiations; government/regulators.
parts.working: 1 mark each group; 1 mark each reason linked to reliability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how publishing an audited annual report helps the directors carry out their stewardship responsibility.
parts.answer: The annual report shows shareholders how the directors have used the company's resources and what results they achieved; the audit gives independent assurance that this account is true and fair; shareholders can then question directors and vote on their reappointment at the AGM, so the directors are held accountable.
parts.working: 1 mark: reports use of resources/results; 1 mark: independent assurance; 1 mark: accountability (AGM/votes).

practice.stem:
During the audit of Chitral Tea Limited, the auditor identified the following errors in the draft statement of financial position, which shows net assets of $2,460,000:
• Damaged inventory not yet written down to net realisable value: effect on net assets −$36,000
• Accrued audit fee not recorded: effect on net assets −$18,000
• Prepaid rent omitted: effect on net assets +$12,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected net assets of the company.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The directors agree to make all the corrections. State the type of audit opinion that is likely to be given and explain why.
parts.answer: An unmodified opinion: once the misstatements have been corrected, the statements give a true and fair view in all material respects, so there is no reason to modify the opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark unmodified; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between an unmodified (unqualified) audit opinion and a qualified audit opinion.
parts.answer: Unmodified: the auditor concludes that the financial statements give a true and fair view in all material respects. Qualified: the auditor concludes that the statements give a true and fair view except for the effects of a specific matter, which is material but not pervasive (a material misstatement, or an inability to obtain enough evidence about one area).
parts.working: 2 marks each: meaning + key words ('true and fair', 'except for', material but not pervasive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the three types of modified audit opinion and state when each is given.
parts.answer: Qualified opinion ('except for'): a misstatement or lack of evidence that is material but not pervasive. Adverse opinion: misstatements are material and pervasive, so the statements do not give a true and fair view. Disclaimer of opinion: the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects are material and pervasive, so no opinion is expressed.
parts.working: 1 mark each type named; 1 mark each correct circumstance.

practice.stem: The auditors of Ravi Garments Limited found that closing inventory was overstated by $48,000 because obsolete stock had been valued at cost. The directors refuse to adjust it. Profit before tax was $620,000. The audit firm treats any misstatement above 5% of profit before tax as material. No other problems were found.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the misstatement as a percentage of profit before tax, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the type of audit opinion the auditor is likely to give. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A qualified ('except for') opinion. The overstatement of inventory is material (well above the 5% threshold the firm uses) but it affects only one area of the statements, so it is not pervasive; the rest of the statements give a true and fair view.
parts.working: 1 mark qualified; 1 mark material (with reference to the figure); 1 mark not pervasive / limited to inventory.

practice.stem: Mehran Retail Limited runs 45 supermarkets across Pakistan and has set up an internal audit department.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three functions of an internal audit department.
parts.answer: Reviewing and testing internal controls (e.g. authorisation of purchases, segregation of duties) to see that they work; checking the accuracy and reliability of accounting records and reports to management; detecting and preventing fraud and error; reviewing the efficiency and value for money of operations; checking compliance with laws, regulations and company policies; helping the external auditor, who may rely on its work.
parts.working: 2 marks each: function identified (1) + explanation (1), max 3 functions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two limitations of an external audit.
parts.answer: Auditors test samples of transactions, not every one, so some errors may go undetected; many figures rely on judgement and estimates (e.g. depreciation, allowances, provisions), so the opinion is reasonable not absolute assurance; auditors rely on information and explanations from management, which may be incomplete or deliberately misleading (collusion/fraud); the audit is of past information and is out of date when published; time and cost limits.
parts.working: 2 marks each: limitation + explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why shareholders of a large company need an external audit.
parts.answer: Ownership is separated from control: shareholders do not run the company and cannot check the records themselves. The directors prepare the statements and could present results favourably to protect bonuses or reputation. An independent expert's opinion that the statements are true and fair gives shareholders confidence when assessing directors' stewardship and making decisions (buy/sell/vote). It also helps deter fraud and error.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four points, or 2 marks each for two developed points.

practice.stem: After a cashier at Sadiq Motors Limited was found to have stolen $18,000 over two years, a shareholder complained at the annual general meeting that the auditors 'should have found the fraud'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the responsibility of (i) the directors and (ii) the external auditor in relation to fraud.
parts.answer: (i) The directors are primarily responsible for preventing and detecting fraud, by setting up and monitoring internal controls and a culture of honesty. (ii) The auditor must plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance that the statements are free from material misstatement whether caused by fraud or error; they are not required to find all fraud, but must report material fraud they discover to the appropriate level of management/shareholders.
parts.working: 2 marks each part.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four responsibilities of the directors of a limited company relating to its financial records and statements.
parts.answer: Any four: keep adequate accounting records; prepare annual financial statements that give a true and fair view and follow accounting standards; select suitable accounting policies and apply them consistently; make reasonable judgements and estimates; safeguard the company's assets; take reasonable steps to prevent and detect fraud; assess whether the company is a going concern; file the statements as required by law.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The internal auditor of Indus Hardware Limited attended the year-end inventory count. The inventory records show a book value of $145,600. The physical count, valued at cost, is $138,950.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the inventory shortage and express it as a percentage of the book value, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three possible causes of the shortage.
parts.answer: Any three: theft by staff or customers; goods sent out without being invoiced; recording errors (e.g. purchases recorded twice); damaged goods thrown away and not recorded; count errors; goods returned to suppliers not recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one internal control that would reduce the risk of this happening again.
parts.answer: E.g. regular surprise inventory counts by staff independent of the storekeeper; restricted access to the store; goods-out notes authorised for every dispatch.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term segregation of duties.
parts.answer: Dividing the stages of a transaction between different people so that no one person controls it from start to finish; this makes fraud harder because it would need collusion, and errors are more likely to be spotted.
parts.working: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark benefit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of segregation of duties in the purchases system of a company.
parts.answer: Any two: the person who orders goods is not the person who receives them; the person who records invoices is not the person who authorises payment; the person who signs payments is not the person who keeps the purchases ledger; a different person reconciles supplier statements.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Swat Marble Limited has 2,500 shareholders, none of whom work in the business. This year its external auditor gave a qualified audit opinion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the external auditor's report is addressed to the shareholders rather than to the directors.
parts.answer: The auditor is appointed by, and acts for, the shareholders, who own the company but do not manage it. The report gives them an independent opinion on the statements the directors have prepared, so it is a check on the directors' stewardship.
parts.working: 1 mark appointed by / acts for shareholders; 1 mark checks directors' stewardship for owners who do not run the company.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three possible consequences for Swat Marble Limited of receiving a qualified audit opinion.
parts.answer: Any three: shareholders lose confidence in the directors and may vote against their reappointment; the share price may fall; banks may refuse loans or charge higher interest; suppliers may reduce credit; potential investors may be put off; the company's reputation may suffer.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The honorary auditor of the Peshawar Squash Club checks the treasurer's records for the year. Cash in hand at the start was $3,850. Receipts recorded were: subscriptions $46,200; event ticket sales $18,750; donations $9,500. All recorded payments, supported by receipts, totalled $61,400. The cash counted at the year end was $11,280.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of cash that should be held at the year end, and the amount missing.
parts.answer: Should hold $16,900; missing $5,620

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two controls the club committee could introduce to improve the stewardship of its funds.
parts.answer: Any two developed: all receipts banked intact and promptly, with numbered receipts issued; two signatories required for payments; regular bank reconciliations reviewed by someone other than the treasurer; an independent honorary auditor checks the accounts annually; monthly reports to the committee comparing receipts with members' list.
parts.working: 2 marks each: control + how it protects funds.

practice.stem: Pak Agro Exports Limited has no internal audit department. Last year losses from undetected errors and staff fraud were estimated at $140,000. The finance director proposes an internal audit department costing $95,000 a year, which is expected to reduce such losses by 60%. The external auditor has said it may be able to rely on some of the internal auditors' work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected annual saving in losses and the net annual cost or benefit of the internal audit department.
parts.answer: Saving $84,000; net annual cost $11,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the directors whether they should set up the internal audit department. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: on these figures it costs $11,000 a year more than it saves; the saving is only an estimate; internal auditors are employees, so they are less independent than the external auditor and cannot replace the external audit. For: it reviews and tests internal controls continuously, deterring fraud as well as detecting it; it can improve the efficiency of operations and the reliability of records for management; the external auditor may rely on its work, which could reduce the external audit fee and close the $11,000 gap; it helps the directors show good stewardship of shareholders' assets. Decision: e.g. set it up, because the net cost is small and the non-financial benefits (stronger controls, possible lower audit fee) are likely to outweigh it.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points against (using the $11,000 figure), up to 3 marks for points in favour applied to the company, 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: During the year, the directors of Lahore Builders Limited: (1) bought land for $1.3 million from a company owned by the managing director's brother; an independent valuer had valued it at $1.0 million, and the transaction was not disclosed in the annual report; (2) increased their own bonuses by 40% while reducing the dividend per share from 12 cents to 8 cents; (3) published the annual report four months later than usual. The company's profit for the year rose by 12% and the directors set up an internal audit department.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the directors of Lahore Builders Limited have carried out their stewardship responsibilities properly. Conclude with a judgement.
parts.answer: Against good stewardship: buying land from a company owned by the managing director's brother at 30% above valuation is a conflict of interest and may waste shareholders' funds; failure to disclose the related party transaction; directors' bonuses increased while dividends cut — possible self-interest; the delay in publishing accounts reduces accountability. For: profits rose by 12%; they set up an internal audit department and kept proper records; the land may have strategic value. Judgement: overall the directors have not fully discharged their stewardship duty because of the undisclosed related-party purchase and the bonus/dividend issue, although operational performance improved.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): balanced discussion applied to the case with a justified judgement. Level 2 (4–6): some applied points, may be one-sided, some judgement. Level 1 (1–3): general statements about stewardship.

practice.stem: A flood destroyed the head office of Sindh Rice Mills Limited, including most sales and inventory records for the year. Revenue, trade receivables and closing inventory together make up most of the figures in the financial statements. The directors have estimated these figures, but there is no supporting evidence for the auditor to test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of audit opinion the auditor should give. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: A disclaimer of opinion. The auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence for revenue, receivables and inventory, which affect most of the statements, so the possible effects are both material and pervasive. The auditor therefore does not express an opinion. A qualified opinion would only be suitable if the lack of evidence affected a limited area, and an adverse opinion needs evidence that the statements are actually misstated.
parts.working: 1 mark disclaimer; 1 mark inability to obtain evidence; 1 mark material; 1 mark pervasive; 1 mark distinguishing from qualified/adverse.

practice.stem: The bank has withdrawn all loans from Margalla Shoes Limited and the directors have decided to put the company into liquidation shortly after the year end. However, they have prepared the financial statements on a going concern basis and refuse to change them or to disclose the planned liquidation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of audit opinion the auditor should give. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: An adverse opinion. The company is not a going concern (bank has withdrawn finance, directors intend to liquidate), but the statements are prepared on a going concern basis, so assets are at cost less depreciation rather than realisable values and liabilities may be misclassified. This misstatement is material and affects the statements as a whole (pervasive), so they do not give a true and fair view. It is not a disclaimer because the auditor has sufficient evidence.
parts.working: 1 mark adverse; 1 mark basis of preparation wrong; 1 mark material; 1 mark pervasive; 1 mark sufficient evidence/not a disclaimer.

practice.stem: Thar Coal Services Limited reports profit before tax of $1,150,000. Its mining equipment cost $3,600,000 and has a useful life of 12 years with no residual value, but the directors have decided not to charge any depreciation on it this year. The external auditor disagrees. The directors tell shareholders that "the auditor is responsible for getting the figures right".

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the straight-line depreciation for the year, the corrected profit before tax, and the misstatement as a percentage of the reported profit before tax, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Depreciation $300,000; corrected profit before tax $850,000; misstatement 26.09%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the directors' statement is wrong, and state with reasons the audit opinion likely to be given if the directors refuse to charge depreciation.
parts.answer: The directors are responsible for preparing financial statements that give a true and fair view; the auditor only examines them and gives an independent opinion on them. The misstatement (26.09% of profit) is material, but it is confined to one item (depreciation, carrying amount of equipment and retained earnings) rather than the statements as a whole, so it is not pervasive. The auditor is therefore likely to give a qualified ('except for') opinion.
parts.working: 1 mark directors prepare; 1 mark auditor gives opinion only; 1 mark material with reference to figure; 1 mark qualified because not pervasive.

practice.stem: At the annual general meeting of Kohat Cement Limited, shareholders must vote on reappointing Khan & Co as external auditors. Khan & Co received an audit fee of $85,000 and a further $240,000 for consultancy, including designing the company's new computerised accounting system. The same audit partner has led the audit for 11 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate non-audit fees as a percentage of the total fees received from the company, correct to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the shareholders whether they should vote to reappoint Khan & Co as auditors. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: non-audit fees are almost three times the audit fee (about 74% of total), creating a self-interest threat — the firm may be reluctant to qualify its opinion and risk losing lucrative consultancy work; the firm designed the new accounting system, so it would be auditing its own work (self-review threat); the audit partner has been in charge for 11 years (familiarity threat). For: the firm knows the business well, which may make the audit efficient and cheaper; no evidence of any wrongdoing; changing auditors has costs. Decision: shareholders should not reappoint unless safeguards are put in place (e.g. rotate the audit partner, stop providing system design/consultancy, or have a separate team); otherwise appoint a new independent firm.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for independence threats applied, up to 2 marks for points in favour, 1 mark for safeguards, 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: The directors of Faisal Textiles Limited each receive a bonus equal to 2% of the year's profit before tax. This year the directors postponed essential machine maintenance and changed the estimated useful life of machinery from 8 to 15 years, increasing profit by $1.2 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the conflict of interest between the directors and the shareholders of Faisal Textiles Limited, and suggest how the shareholders could reduce the risk that the directors act in their own interest.
parts.answer: Conflict: the directors' bonus depends on annual profit, so they have an incentive to boost short-term profit (e.g. by delaying maintenance, cutting training, or choosing accounting estimates that increase profit), while shareholders want long-term growth in value and reliable statements; directors also control the information shareholders receive. Ways to reduce it: link part of pay to long-term targets or share price over several years (or pay part in shares); appoint independent non-executive directors and an audit committee; keep a strong independent external audit; require clear disclosure of directors' remuneration and related-party transactions; vote on remuneration at the AGM.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for explaining the conflict with reference to the case, up to 3 marks for suitable safeguards explained.

practice.stem: The directors of Hala Ceramics Limited propose that the company's internal audit department, which reports to the finance director, should take over the work of the external auditor. This would save the external audit fee of $120,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the directors' proposal.
parts.answer: Against: internal auditors are employees who report to the finance director, so they are not independent of the people whose statements they would check; shareholders, lenders and other users need an independent opinion that the statements give a true and fair view; an external audit is normally a legal requirement for a limited company, so it cannot simply be replaced; the external auditor is appointed by and reports to the shareholders, whereas internal audit serves management. For: the saving of $120,000 a year; internal auditors know the business well. Conclusion: reject the proposal; keep both, and instead let the external auditor rely on the internal auditors' work where appropriate, which may reduce the fee.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points (at least one in favour for full marks) applied to the company, 1 mark for using the $120,000 or the reporting line, 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a physical security measure for a computerised accounting system?
A a password on each user account
B encryption of the data files
C a locked room for the server
D a firewall on the network
parts.answer: C a locked room for the server
parts.working: A locked room physically prevents access to the hardware. A, B and D are software (logical) controls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the main purpose of making regular backup copies of accounting data?
A to stop hackers from reading the data
B to allow the data to be restored if it is lost or corrupted
C to check that entries have been input correctly
D to reduce the storage space needed
parts.answer: B to allow the data to be restored if it is lost or corrupted
parts.working: A backup is a copy kept so that lost or damaged data can be recovered. It does not stop unauthorised reading (A, which needs encryption/passwords) or check accuracy (C).

practice.stem: Fatima owns a clothes shop in Hyderabad and keeps her accounts by hand. She is thinking of buying accounting software.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages to Fatima of using a computerised accounting system.
parts.answer: Records and reports (e.g. trial balance, statements to customers) are produced quickly; arithmetic is accurate and ledgers update automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: speed; accuracy of calculations; automatic posting to ledgers; up-to-date information; easy reports; less storage space.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages to Fatima of using a computerised accounting system.
parts.answer: Cost of hardware, software and training; risk of data loss through system failure, viruses or hacking.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: cost; training time; risk of breakdown/data loss; security threats; input errors processed unnoticed.

practice.stem: Ravi Motors, Karachi, keeps its customer and supplier records on a computerised accounting system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two methods the business could use to prevent unauthorised access to its accounting data.
parts.answer: Passwords: each user must enter a secret password, so only authorised staff can log in. Access levels: staff can see or change only the parts of the system they need, e.g. a sales clerk cannot open the payroll. (Also: encryption, biometric log-in, automatic log-out, firewalls.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per method (1 identify, 1 explain).

practice.stem: A trading business in Lahore saves all its accounting data on one office computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways the business could reduce the risk of losing its accounting data.
parts.answer: Make regular backups; store a backup copy off-site or in the cloud.
parts.working: 1 mark each: regular backups; off-site/cloud storage; antivirus software; uninterruptible power supply; fire-proof storage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a backup copy should be stored away from the office.
parts.answer: If the office suffers a fire, flood or theft, both the computer and an on-site backup could be destroyed; an off-site copy can still be used to restore the records.
parts.working: 1 mark: risk of physical disaster/theft at the office. 1 mark: off-site copy allows restoration.

practice.stem: The finance manager of a school in Islamabad prepares the annual budget on a spreadsheet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways a spreadsheet helps in preparing budgets.
parts.answer: Formulas recalculate totals automatically when any figure is changed, saving time and avoiding arithmetic errors. 'What-if' analysis lets the manager test different fee levels or salary increases and see the effect on the budget straight away. (Also: easy charts, copying layouts for each month, sharing.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per way (1 identify, 1 explain).

practice.stem: The external auditor of Indus Foods Ltd asks whether its accounting software keeps an audit trail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'audit trail'.
parts.answer: A record kept by the system of every transaction and change, showing who made it and when, so that each entry can be traced from the source document to the financial statements.
parts.working: 1 mark: record of transactions/changes with user and time. 1 mark: allows tracing source to final accounts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an audit trail is useful to the auditor.
parts.answer: The auditor can check that recorded figures are supported by source documents and can identify unauthorised or suspicious changes, which helps detect errors and fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark: verify figures to evidence. 1 mark: detect unauthorised changes/fraud.

practice.stem: A computerised accounting system needs both hardware and software.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between hardware and software, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Hardware is the physical equipment, e.g. a computer or printer; software is the programs that run on it, e.g. an accounting package.
parts.working: 1 mark each, with example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two reports that accounting software can produce automatically.
parts.answer: Trial balance; aged trade receivables report (also: statement of profit or loss, customer statements, VAT/tax return, inventory report).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Sunrise Bakery, Peshawar, is introducing a computerised accounting system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why staff should be trained before the system is used.
parts.answer: So that they enter transactions correctly and avoid input errors that would make the accounts wrong. So that they can use the system efficiently and obtain the reports needed, getting the expected time savings. (Also: understand security procedures such as passwords and backups; reduce resistance to change.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per reason (1 identify, 1 explain).

practice.stem: The accounts department of a hospital has a payroll clerk, a purchases clerk and an accountant, all using one computerised system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'access levels'.
parts.answer: Each user is allowed to view or change only the parts of the system that their job needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: restricted rights per user. 1 mark: related to job role/view vs edit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of how access levels could be used in this department.
parts.answer: The purchases clerk cannot open or change payroll records.
parts.working: B1 any sensible example.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one physical control that would protect the accounting system.
parts.answer: Lock the server room (also: CCTV, lockable cabinets for backups, fire protection).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business's purchase system will not accept a single invoice above $10,000. A clerk keys in an invoice for $85,000 instead of $8,500.
Which validation check will reject the entry?
A format check
B range (limit) check
C presence check
D check digit
parts.answer: B range (limit) check
parts.working: A range or limit check tests that a value lies within set limits. A format check only tests the pattern of characters, which 85,000 still matches; a presence check only tests that a value has been entered.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a disadvantage of a computerised accounting system compared with a manual system?
A ledger balances are updated automatically
B reports such as the trial balance can be produced quickly
C an input error may be repeated in every record that uses that data
D arithmetic errors in totalling the ledgers are eliminated
parts.answer: C an input error may be repeated in every record that uses that data
parts.working: If wrong data is input, the system processes it faithfully and the error flows through all linked records ('garbage in, garbage out'). A, B and D are advantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the purpose of an audit trail in a computerised accounting system?
A to prevent staff from changing their passwords
B to allow each transaction to be traced from its source document through to the financial statements
C to make a copy of all files at the end of each day
D to stop viruses from entering the system
parts.answer: B to allow each transaction to be traced from its source document through to the financial statements
parts.working: An audit trail records who entered or changed each transaction and when, so it can be traced. C describes a backup; D describes antivirus software.

practice.stem: A wholesaler's clerks key in customer account codes (format: two letters followed by four digits, e.g. KH2041) and invoice amounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name and describe three validation checks that would be suitable for this data.
parts.answer: Format check: tests that the account code is two letters followed by four digits. Existence (lookup) check: tests that the account code matches an existing customer. Range check: tests that the invoice amount is within set limits, e.g. above $0 and below the customer's credit limit. (Also: presence check that no field is left blank.)
parts.working: For each of three checks: 1 mark name, 1 mark description applied to the data.

practice.stem: Zaitoon Traders uses an integrated accounting package in which the sales, purchases, inventory and nominal ledgers are linked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what happens in the system when a credit sales invoice is entered.
parts.answer: The customer's account in the sales ledger is debited; the sales account in the nominal ledger is credited and the sales ledger control (trade receivables) account is updated; the inventory records are reduced by the quantity sold.
parts.working: 1 mark each: customer account debited; sales/control accounts updated in nominal ledger; inventory updated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of the ledgers being integrated.
parts.answer: Each transaction is entered only once, so all records agree and are up to date.
parts.working: B1 (single entry, consistency, saves time, fewer posting errors).

practice.stem: A garment exporter in Sialkot has received emails that appear to come from its bank, asking staff to confirm the company's online banking log-in details. Last month another firm in the city had its accounting files locked by ransomware.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'phishing' and suggest one way to protect the business against it.
parts.answer: Phishing is a fraudulent message pretending to be from a trusted organisation to trick staff into revealing passwords or bank details. Protection: train staff never to give log-in details by email and to check messages with the bank directly.
parts.working: 1 mark explanation; 1 mark protection (training, spam filters, two-factor authentication).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'ransomware' and suggest one way to protect the business against it.
parts.answer: Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts or locks files and demands payment to release them. Protection: keep regular backups stored separately so files can be restored without paying, and keep antivirus software and updates current.
parts.working: 1 mark explanation; 1 mark protection (separate backups, antivirus, updates, not opening unknown attachments).

practice.stem: An online retailer in Karachi stores customers' names, addresses, phone numbers and payment records in its accounting system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two responsibilities the business has when holding this personal data.
parts.answer: Keep the data secure: use passwords, encryption and access controls so it cannot be stolen or misused. Use the data only for the purpose it was collected and keep it accurate and up to date, deleting it when no longer needed. (Also: obey data protection law, do not share without consent.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per responsibility (1 identify, 1 explain).

practice.stem: The owner of a computerised business says, 'The computer never makes mistakes, so our accounts must be correct.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify and explain two types of error that can still occur in a computerised accounting system.
parts.answer: Error of original entry: a wrong amount is keyed in from the invoice, and the system posts the wrong figure to both accounts. Error of commission: a payment is posted to the wrong supplier's account; debits still equal credits so the system does not detect it. (Also: error of omission, error of principle, compensating errors.)
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per error (1 identify, 1 explain why the system does not detect it).

practice.stem: A pharmacy in Rawalpindi uses its accounting software to keep a running record of inventory. The software automatically produces a purchase order when inventory of an item falls to its reorder level. For one medicine, maximum daily usage is 120 packs and the maximum time for delivery is 5 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the reorder level for this medicine, using maximum usage × maximum lead time.
parts.answer: 600 packs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit and one risk of the software producing purchase orders automatically.
parts.answer: Benefit: the pharmacy will not run out of medicines because orders are made on time without staff having to check shelves. Risk: if the recorded inventory is wrong (e.g. theft or input error), orders may be wrong, so physical counts are still needed.
parts.working: 1 mark benefit; 1 mark risk.

practice.stem:
Ravi Builders spent the following when introducing a computerised accounting system:
                                             $
Computers and printers                   9,000
Accounting software (permanent licence)  3,000
Installation of the network                600
Staff training course                    1,200
Annual maintenance contract                800
Temporary staff to key in old records      700

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure.
parts.answer: Capital $12,600; revenue $2,700.
parts.working: Capital: hardware 9,000, software 3,000, installation 600 (B1 B1) = 12,600. Revenue: training 1,200, maintenance 800, temporary staff 700 (B1) = 2,700 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on the profit for the year if the training course were treated as capital expenditure.
parts.answer: Profit would be overstated by $1,200 this year (less any depreciation charged), and non-current assets would also be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit overstated by 1,200. 1 mark: assets overstated / breaks the rule that training is revenue expenditure.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business uses an integrated computerised accounting system in which every entry must have equal debits and credits.
Which error could still occur?
A a sales ledger total that is added up incorrectly
B a debit entry with no corresponding credit entry
C a trial balance that does not agree
D a sales invoice posted to the account of the wrong customer
parts.answer: D a sales invoice posted to the account of the wrong customer
parts.working: Posting to the wrong customer is an error of commission: debits still equal credits, so the system cannot detect it. The software performs the arithmetic and enforces double entry, so A, B and C cannot occur.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A batch of supplier invoices has a manually calculated batch total of $23,640. After the invoices were keyed in, the computer total was $23,910.
Which single error would explain the difference?
A an invoice for $4,580 was keyed in as $4,850
B an invoice for $270 was not keyed in
C an invoice for $4,850 was keyed in as $4,580
D a credit note for $270 was keyed in as an invoice
parts.answer: A an invoice for $4,580 was keyed in as $4,850
parts.working: The computer total is 270 too high (23,910 − 23,640). Keying 4,850 for 4,580 adds 270. B and C would make the total 270 too low; D would make it 540 too high.

practice.stem:
Noor Pharmacy, Quetta, is considering a computerised accounting system. Estimated costs and savings:
                                                   $
Software (one-off)                             4,800
Hardware (one-off)                             7,200
Staff training (one-off)                       1,500
Annual software licence                          900
Annual saving in part-time bookkeeper's wages  6,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total initial cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the payback period in years, correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.65 years

parts.label: d
parts.text: Advise the owner whether to introduce the system. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: the cost is recovered in under three years, after which $5,100 a year is saved; faster, more accurate records and up-to-date inventory and receivables information. Against: hardware may need replacing in about three to five years; staff must learn the system; risks of breakdown and data loss; savings are estimates. Decision: introduce the system, as payback is short compared with the system's likely life, but plan backups and training.
parts.working: 1 mark: financial point using figures. 1 mark: non-financial benefit. 1 mark: drawback/risk. 1 mark: justified decision.

practice.stem: Kaghan Supplies gives every customer a four-digit account number followed by a check digit. The check digit is calculated as follows: multiply the four digits by the weights 5, 4, 3 and 2 in order; add the results; divide by 11; the check digit is 11 minus the remainder. When an account number is entered, the computer multiplies the five digits by 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 and accepts the number only if the total is exactly divisible by 11.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the check digit for account number 3725.
parts.answer: 7 (full number 37257)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A clerk keys in 37527 instead of 37257. Show that the computer will reject it.
parts.answer: Weighted total = 69, which is not divisible by 11, so the number is rejected.
parts.working: 3×5 + 7×4 + 5×3 + 2×2 + 7×1 = 69 (M1); 69 ÷ 11 leaves remainder 3, so rejected (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of input error this check is designed to detect.
parts.answer: Transposition errors (digits swapped) and single-digit keying errors.

practice.stem: Margalla Engineering Ltd is replacing its old accounting software with a new system. The finance director must choose between direct changeover (switching completely on one day) and parallel running (running both systems together for three months).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'parallel running'.
parts.answer: Operating the old and new systems at the same time, with the same data, so their results can be compared before the old system is dropped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise the finance director which method to use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Parallel running: results from the new system can be checked against the old, and if the new system fails the old one is still available, so the risk of losing accounting records is low; but staff must enter everything twice, which is costly, slow and may cause mistakes. Direct changeover: cheap and quick, and staff concentrate on one system; but if the new system fails there is no fallback and records, payments to suppliers or payroll could be disrupted. Decision: for a company's main accounting records, use parallel running (perhaps for one month-end close only) because the cost of failure is greater than the extra staff time.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points on parallel running; up to 2 marks for points on direct changeover; 1 mark for applying to the company (size, importance of records, staff time); 1 mark for a justified decision.

practice.stem: Bolan Distributors issues 2,400 sales invoices a month. Preparing an invoice by hand takes 6 minutes; with the proposed system it would take 1.5 minutes. Invoicing clerks are paid $9 an hour. The new system would cost $12,000 a year to rent and maintain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of clerk hours saved each month.
parts.answer: 180 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual saving in clerks' wages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving after the cost of the system.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Discuss non-financial factors the directors should consider before introducing the system.
parts.answer: Staff may resist the change or fear job losses, affecting morale; staff need training and there may be early errors; faster, more accurate invoices may improve customer service and cash collection; dependence on the system creates risks of breakdown and data loss.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to three relevant factors, developed (staff morale/redundancy; training; customer service; security/reliability).

practice.stem:
The accounting software of Chenab Wholesalers produced this aged trade receivables report at 31 March 2026:
Age of debt        $
0–30 days     45,200
31–60 days    21,000
61–90 days    10,500
Over 90 days   7,300
Total         84,000
The business creates a provision for doubtful debts of 2% on debts up to 30 days, 5% on 31–60 days, 10% on 61–90 days and 40% on debts over 90 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of trade receivables that are more than 60 days old. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the provision for doubtful debts at 31 March 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the computerised aged receivables report helps credit control.
parts.answer: It is produced instantly and accurately at any time, so the credit controller can quickly see which customers are overdue and by how long, and chase them or stop further credit before debts become irrecoverable.
parts.working: 1 mark: quick/accurate/up to date. 1 mark: identifies overdue customers for action.

practice.stem: At Khyber Steel Ltd one purchases clerk can set up new suppliers in the computerised purchase ledger, record invoices and authorise payments. Last year the clerk created a false supplier account and paid $18,000 into his own bank account before the fraud was discovered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two weaknesses in the control system that allowed the fraud.
parts.answer: There was no segregation of duties: one person could create suppliers, record invoices and approve payments. Access levels were too wide and no one else reviewed new supplier accounts or payments.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend controls to prevent such a fraud happening again. Justify your recommendations.
parts.answer: Separate duties so that different staff create suppliers, record invoices and authorise payments, so fraud needs collusion. Set access levels so the clerk cannot add suppliers; new suppliers approved by a manager with checks on bank details. Review the audit trail and exception reports of new suppliers and payments regularly. Require two authorisations for payments above a set limit.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per developed recommendation (control + why it works), max 4.

practice.stem: Sadia & Co. Ltd introduced a computerised accounting system last year. A director says: 'Now that the software does all the double entry, we no longer need to prepare bank reconciliations or check control accounts.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the director's statement.
parts.answer: Partly true: the software keeps debits equal to credits, posts to ledgers and control accounts automatically and removes arithmetic errors, so some manual checks are no longer needed. However, the bank reconciliation compares the business's records with an independent source (the bank statement); it still finds unpresented cheques, bank charges, direct debits not entered, keying errors and fraud. Errors of commission, omission and original entry are not detected by the software. Control accounts and reconciliations are also internal controls that auditors expect. Conclusion: the statement is not justified; reconciliations should continue, although the software makes them quicker.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points supporting the statement; up to 3 marks for points against (independent check, errors not detected, fraud, audit expectations); 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Rehman Electricals, a small business in Multan, is thinking of moving from accounting software on one office computer to a cloud-based accounting package paid for by monthly subscription.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the business should move to cloud-based accounting.
parts.answer: For: data can be reached from anywhere, e.g. by the owner at home or the accountant; the provider makes automatic backups and updates; no large up-front cost; can link to online banking for automatic bank feeds. Against: depends on a reliable internet connection, which may be a problem in some areas; monthly fees continue for ever; data held by a third party raises security and confidentiality concerns; staff need retraining. Conclusion: move to the cloud if the internet is reliable and the provider has strong security, because backup and access benefits outweigh the subscription cost.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for advantages and up to 2 marks for disadvantages applied to the business; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.
